value: developed by Martin Silverudd, his first and most successful autosexing breed
day-old males show blonde down on the back of the head
adult males are largely white; females show a spotted 'flowery' pattern

history_summary.value: The 55 Flowery Hen was created in Sweden in 1955 by Father Martin Silverudd as an autosexing breed producing commercial quantities of large, round, cream-colored eggs.

summary.value: The 55 Flowery Hen is a Swedish laying breed created in 1955 by Martin Silverudd, a priest and poultry breeder who made several new breeds. It was his first design and the one that worked best. He wanted a bird that sexes itself at hatch and still lays eggs in commercial numbers, and this breed does both. Newly hatched cockerels can be picked out by a patch of blonde down at the back of the head. Grown roosters are mostly white, while hens carry a speckled pattern that looks like small flowers, which is where the name comes from. Hens lay large, round, cream colored eggs. Because chicks can be sorted by sex on day one, the breed appeals to keepers who want only laying hens and no surprise roosters.

history_summary.value: The Alsacienne was developed as a dual-purpose fowl in Alsace during the 1890s, at a time the region was part of the German Empire, and it resembles the older Bresse Gauloise. It nearly disappeared in the twentieth century and was still considered at risk as of 2007.

summary.value: The Alsacienne, or Poule d'Alsace, is an old French chicken from Alsace in the east of the country. Its modern form was fixed in the 1890s, when Alsace belonged to the German Empire, and it may be related to the German Rheinlander, which has a different comb. Unlike most French breeds it carries no Asian blood. Birds have a red rose comb that ends in a spike, and the French standard allows black, blue-laced, golden salmon and white, in both large and bantam size. Hens weigh roughly 4.5 to 5.5 pounds and cocks 4.5 to 6.5. It is a dual-purpose bird: hens lay large white eggs of at least 60 grams, and chefs in a French tasting ranked its meat second only to Bresse chicken. The breed nearly vanished in the last century and is still counted as at risk.

low egg output makes it unsuited to commercial farming

history_summary.value: The Altsteirer, or Styrian Hen, is native to the Styria region spanning Slovenia and Austria, with capons of this type recorded as far back as 1352 and the breed formally described in 1894. Its numbers collapsed after the Second World War under industrial poultry farming, and it was later rebuilt in Slovenia from surviving farm flocks.

summary.value: The Altsteirer, or Styrian hen, is an old dual-purpose chicken from Styria, the region shared by northern Slovenia and southern Austria. Records of Styrian capons go back to 1352, breeders in Graz described the breed in 1894, and a standard followed in 1902. Numbers fell hard after the Second World War, and Slovenian experts rebuilt the breed from farm flocks after 1991. Most birds today are partridge colored, though white and barred types also exist. They have a single upright comb, white earlobes and white legs. Hens weigh about 4 to 4.8 pounds and cocks 5.5 to 6.6. Estimates of laying vary from about 130 to 200 white to ivory eggs a year, of medium size, and hens seldom go broody. Styrian capons were long prized for their meat. The breed does best free ranging on a farm rather than in commercial housing.

value: well suited to extensive free-range small farms

history_summary.value: The Amarela, also known as the Minhota, is a traditional Portuguese farm breed from the Minho region that fell sharply in numbers during the twentieth century as diets and farming changed. Conservation efforts since 2013 have grown its numbers, and by 2024 it was no longer considered at risk.

summary.value: The Amarela, also called the Minhota, is a traditional farm chicken from Portugal and one of the country's four native breeds. It comes from the north-west, mainly the old province of Minho. The breed was once kept across most of Portugal, but numbers fell badly during the last century as farming and eating habits changed. A conservation effort has since brought it back, and it is no longer rated at risk. There is only one color, a buff or golden shade that gives the breed its name, meaning yellow. Birds have a single comb and bare yellowish legs. Hens weigh about 3.7 to 5.5 pounds and cocks 5 to 6.8. It is kept for both meat and eggs. The birds are hardy, resist disease and do well on free range, which suits small family farms.

history_summary.value: The Ameraucana was developed in the United States during the 1970s from Chilean Araucana stock, with the aim of keeping the unusual blue-egg gene while breeding out the parent breed's lethal tufted and rumpless traits. It was added to the American Poultry Association's Standard of Perfection in 1984 as a breed distinct from the Araucana.

summary.value: The Ameraucana is an American breed made in the 1970s from Araucana stock that came from Chile. Breeders kept the blue egg gene but bred away the rumpless and ear tuft traits that carry lethal genes in the parent breed. The APA accepted it in 1984. Birds have a tail, a beard and muffs, a small pea comb and slate legs, in colors such as black, blue, wheaten, buff, silver and white. Large fowl roosters weigh about 6.5 pounds and hens about 5.5, and there is a bantam version too. Hens lay roughly 150 to 200 medium blue eggs a year and can be fairly broody. Many keepers find them friendly and docile, though temper varies between lines. They handle heat and cold well. Real Ameraucanas come from breeders; feed store "Americanas" are usually Easter Egger mixes.

history_summary.value: The American Game was bred in the United States for cockfighting, and its bantam version was created separately in New Jersey during the 1940s by crossing wild red jungle fowl with pit-game bantams. The bantam was admitted to the American Poultry Association's standard in 2009, while the full-size bird remains unrecognized by major registries.

summary.value: The American Game is a game fowl developed in the United States for cockfighting. The full size bird comes in a wide range of plumage colors, and cocks carry long, curved sickle feathers in the tail. Cocks weigh about 5.5 pounds and hens about 4.4. Major poultry standards do not list the large fowl, but the bantam version was accepted by the American Poultry Association in 2009 in ten colors, including birchen, black, black-breasted red, blue and white. That bantam has its own origin: a New Jersey breeder made it in the 1940s from wild red jungle fowl and small pit game birds. The hens produce medium to large brown eggs, and the birds make a decent table fowl. For shows, the comb, wattles and earlobes of males are trimmed off. Today the breed is kept mostly by game fowl fanciers and exhibitors.

history_summary.value: The Ancona originated in central Italy but was refined into its modern form mainly in England after birds were exported there in 1851. By 2025 the breed was considered at risk worldwide, with only a few hundred birds remaining, most of them in Australia.

summary.value: The Ancona is a Mediterranean egg breed named for the port city of Ancona on the east coast of Italy. English fanciers took it up around 1850 and shaped the modern bird, and it reached America in 1888. Its black feathers carry small white V-shaped tips, giving a speckled look that grows whiter with age. Combs may be single or rose, and a hen's single comb flops to one side. It is a small, Leghorn-sized bird: hens weigh about 4.5 pounds and roosters about 6. Hens lay around 220 white eggs a year, medium to large, start at about five months and almost never go broody. Anconas are active, lively and a little wild; they fly well and like to range over wide ground. They handle frost and snow, though single combs need protection from frostbite. They suit keepers who want eggs and have space to let birds roam.

history_summary.value: The Appenzeller Barthuhn was bred from about 1860 in Switzerland's Appenzell region, largely by a breeder named Zust who wanted a bearded, rose-combed bird with better frost resistance. It gained formal recognition in 1898 and remains a small-population breed today.

summary.value: The Appenzeller Barthuhn is a bearded chicken from the Appenzell area of north-eastern Switzerland. A breeder named Zust developed it from the 1860s, drawing on Leghorn, Russian Bearded and Polverara stock, with the aim of a bird that could stand Alpine winters. The beard, rose comb and small wattles help protect it from frostbite. It was recognized in 1898, nearly died out during the Second World War, and is still rare. Colors include partridge, black and blue-laced, and a bantam exists. It is a light breed: hens weigh about 3.5 to 4 pounds and cocks 4.5 to 5. Hens lay roughly 100 to 150 white eggs a year, medium to large, and seldom go broody. The birds are calm, docile and friendly, forage eagerly, and cope very well with cold, so they suit keepers in cold regions with room to range.

history_summary.value: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben has been bred in the Swiss Alps for centuries, though its exact origins are unclear and it may relate to the Brabanter of the Low Countries. It nearly went extinct around 1950 but was revived from 1983 with help from ProSpecieRara, hatching 230 chicks that year.

summary.value: The Appenzeller Spitzhauben is a small crested chicken from the Appenzell district of north-eastern Switzerland, where it has been kept for centuries and is seen as the national chicken. Its name comes from a pointed lace hat once worn by local women, which the forward sweeping crest resembles. It also has a red V-shaped comb, blue legs and white skin. Silver spangled birds are the most common, with gold spangled, black, blue and other colors also bred. The breed almost vanished after the Second World War and was saved by a German breeder. Hens weigh about 3.5 pounds and roosters about 4.5 in US flocks, and European birds run lighter. Hens lay some 150 to 180 white eggs a year, medium to large, including through winter. The birds are active, flighty and fly well, so they need a covered run or free range. They cope with both cold and heat.

history_summary.value: The Araucana originated among the Mapuche people of Chile's Araucania region and was first scientifically described in the 1920s after the Spanish aviculturist Salvador Castello studied local flocks. Separate British and American lines developed during the twentieth century, with the American line kept tufted and rumpless, and it is closely related to the newer Ameraucana breed.

summary.value: The Araucana is a blue egg chicken from Chile, named for the Araucania region where Mapuche farmers kept it. A Spanish poultry scientist described the birds in 1914, and the first ones reached North America in 1924. The American type is rumpless, with no tail, and carries odd tufts of feathers sticking out beside the ears. Both traits come from lethal genes, so many chicks die before hatching and breeding them is hard work. British birds differ: they can have tails and wear a beard and muffs. Under the US standard, roosters weigh about 5 pounds and hens about 4. Hens lay around 150 to 200 medium to large blue eggs a year, and some flocks do better. They are calm, curious and friendly, and a longtime breeder says they cope with both summer heat and winter cold. The breed is rare in the US and suits dedicated keepers more than casual ones.

history_summary.value: The Ardennaise is a traditional breed of the Ardennes plateau spanning Belgium and France, first described in 1882. It nearly disappeared by 1940 after crossbreeding with Leghorn stock, and was gradually rebuilt over about three decades following the Second World War.

summary.value: The Ardennaise is an old farm chicken of the Ardennes uplands, a region shared by southern Belgium and north-eastern France. It was first written up in 1882, did well under a Liege breeders' club from 1893, then declined as Italian laying hens flooded in and local birds were crossed with Leghorns. By 1940 the pure breed had gone, and breeders spent about thirty years after the war rebuilding it. It is related to the Bresse Gauloise and is bred in twelve colors, often with a dark face. A bantam form dates from the early 1900s, and a rumpless strain lacks a tail entirely. Hens weigh about 3.5 pounds and cocks about 4.5. Hens lay around 140 to 180 white eggs a year, medium in size. The birds are slender, lively and hardy, and are kept for both eggs and meat by conservation minded keepers.

history_summary.value: The Asil is among the oldest game fowl breeds of the Indian subcontinent, its name derived from the Arabic word for purebred. Stock of this type was exported to Europe from around 1750 and helped give rise to related breeds, including a European bantam line re-created in Belgium during the 1980s.

summary.value: The Asil, also spelled Aseel, is an old game fowl from the Indian subcontinent, bred there for fighting for well over 2,000 years. Its name comes from an Arabic word for purebred. The bird is compact and very muscular, with short hard feathers held tight to the body, an upright stance, yellow legs, a small pea comb and a hooked beak. It looks lighter than it is. US standards put cocks at about 6 pounds and hens near 5, while Indian village birds can run heavier. Hens lay very few eggs, often under 70 a year and sometimes far fewer, small and cream to light brown. They are superb broody hens and fierce mothers. Asils fight other chickens, even as chicks, but many bond well with their keepers. They handle heat and range well. This is a bird for experienced keepers, not beginners.

history_summary.value: The Augsburger was created around 1870-1880 by Julius Meyer near Augsburg, Bavaria, by crossing the French La Fleche with the now-extinct Italian Lamotta to combine good meat with good egg-laying. It fell out of favour from the 1960s as specialized commercial breeds took over and is now listed as extremely endangered in Germany.

summary.value: The Augsburger is a rare German dual-purpose chicken and the only breed that comes from Bavaria. Julius Meyer of Haunstetten, now part of Augsburg, made it around 1870 to 1880 by crossing the French La Fleche, known for its meat, with a laying type from Italy called the Lamotta, which no longer exists. Its most unusual feature is a cup-shaped rose comb, quite different from the horn-like comb of the La Fleche. Birds are black with a green sheen, and a blue-laced form was added in 1990. Earlobes are white, and a bantam exists. Hens weigh about 5 pounds and cocks about 6. Hens lay around 180 large white eggs a year. Numbers fell from the 1960s as high output commercial breeds took over, and it is now listed as extremely endangered in Germany, so it mostly interests conservation breeders.

history_summary.value: The Australian Game was developed in New South Wales during the nineteenth century by crossing Australian Pit Game, Malay Game, Old English Game, Modern Game and Asil stock, originally for cockfighting and meat. It is now principally kept as an exhibition bird.

summary.value: The Australian Game, also called the Colonial or simply the Aussie, is a large hard feathered game fowl from New South Wales. Breeders put it together during the 1800s from several fighting types: Australian Pit Game, Malay, Old English Game, Modern Game and Asil. The Malay blood gave it long legs, a trait that was prized at the time. It was first raised for cockfighting, where it had a name for courage and stamina, and also for the table. Despite that past, it was said to be gentle and tame with its keeper. The Australian standard sets cocks at about 12 pounds and hens at about 10, which makes it a heavy bird. Today it is kept mainly for exhibition, and national records list it as at risk, with only a few hundred birds counted.

history_summary.value: The breed was developed in Australia in the early 20th century by crossing Croad Langshans, Orpingtons, Wakfer Chinese Langshans and Modern Langshans. It gained wide popularity in Australia by the 1950s and was formally admitted to the Australian Poultry Standard in 1998.

summary.value: The Australian Langshan is a show and utility chicken bred in Australia in the early 1900s. Breeders built it from Croad Langshans, Orpingtons, Chinese Langshans imported in 1905 and Modern Langshans. It was widely kept across Australia by the 1950s and entered the first Australian Poultry Standard in 1998, but it is little known elsewhere. The bird stands tall and upright on long legs, with a medium red single comb and, ideally, a feathered outer toe on each foot. It comes in glossy black with a green sheen, an even blue grey, and pure white, and there is a bantam version. Hens weigh about 6 pounds and cocks about 7. Hens lay brown eggs. Early birds were valued as utility layers, while modern lines are leggier and kept mainly for exhibition, so the breed now suits show keepers most.

history_summary.value: The breed was developed in Australia in the early 1900s by British soldiers in New South Wales for cockfighting, likely from English Pit Fowl, Malay Game and Asil stock. It was first standardised in 1936, with a bantam version following in 1981.

summary.value: The Australian Pit Game is a fighting chicken that British soldiers based in New South Wales developed in the early 1900s. The Australian standard traces it to English Pit Game or Old English Game, Malay and Asil, and the breed club adds that Sumatra blood may be in the mix. A standard was first written in 1936, a bantam version followed in 1981, and the breed joined the national standard in 1998. It is one of the most loosely defined breeds in Australia: birds may be large or small, carry a single or pea comb, show any color, and have muffs or tassels. Judges look instead for health, vigor, a heart-shaped muscular body and quick, upright bearing. Heavy cocks weigh over about 6 pounds and heavy hens over about 4.4. Hens lay tinted eggs. Numbers are small, and it is kept by game fowl breeders.

history_summary.value: The Australorp was developed in Australia from imported Black Orpington stock crossed with breeds such as Rhode Island Red, Minorca, White Leghorn and Langshan to improve egg-laying utility. It became famous worldwide in the 1920s after a record-setting egg-laying trial and was added to the American Poultry Association's Standard of Perfection in 1929.

summary.value: The Australorp is an Australian utility breed made from Black Orpingtons imported from England between about 1890 and the early 1900s. Local breeders added a little Minorca, Leghorn, Langshan and Rhode Island Red blood and selected hard for laying, and the name, short for Australian Orpington, was in use by the early 1920s. A team of six hens then set a world record of 1,857 eggs in a year, and one hen later laid 364 eggs in 365 days. Today a backyard hen lays about 250 to 300 tinted to light brown eggs a year, medium to large in size. Birds are glossy black in the US, with blue and white in other countries. Roosters weigh about 8.5 pounds and hens about 6.5. Australorps are friendly and gentle, even the roosters, and good with children. They handle cold well but need shade in hot weather.

history_summary.value: The Ayam Cemani is a rare Indonesian breed from Java that has likely been used for religious and mystical purposes since around the 12th century. Dutch breeder Jan Steverink first imported the breed to Europe in 1998.

summary.value: The Ayam Cemani is a rare chicken from the island of Java in Indonesia, where it has likely been kept for religious and ceremonial use for centuries. Its name means a chicken that is black right through. A gene that causes heavy pigment makes the feathers, beak, comb, face and skin black, and even the meat, organs and bones are black or dark gray. The birds have a gamey, upright build and a single comb. Roosters weigh about 4.4 to 5.5 pounds and hens about 3.3 to 4.4. Hens lay cream or tinted eggs, fairly big for their size, but seldom sit on them. In Bali the fast, muscular cocks are used for fighting. The first birds reached the Netherlands in 1998 and Britain in 2008. They are usually friendly, though a little skittish, and they are hard to find and costly. They suit keepers who want a striking, unusual bird.

history_summary.value: The Ayam Kampong is a diverse indigenous chicken population of Indonesia and Malaysia, resulting from uncontrolled crossbreeding of red jungle-fowl, local Southeast Asian chickens and exotic chickens introduced by Dutch and British settlers in the late 1800s. It has traditionally been raised as free-range village poultry for meat and eggs.

summary.value: Ayam Kampong, or Ayam Kampung, means village chicken, and the name covers the free ranging native chickens kept by almost every rural household in Indonesia and Malaysia. The population is very mixed, the result of red junglefowl, local Southeast Asian birds and imported European stock crossing freely since the late 1800s. Looks vary widely, but three main types are recognized: black-red, red and naked neck. Birds are small and grow slowly. Hens weigh roughly 3 to 4 pounds and cocks 3.5 to 5, depending on the flock. Hens lay only about 55 to 100 small light brown eggs a year, largely because they go broody so often. Meat birds reach market weight of 2 to 3 pounds in three or four months, and the meat sells for more than commercial chicken. Families prize these birds for meals at celebrations and special occasions.

history_summary.value: The Ayam Kedu originates from the village of Kedu on the Kedu Plain in Central Java, Indonesia, and is regarded as one of the ancestors of the Ayam Cemani. It is valued in Indonesia as a ritual bird and is also used in Chinese medicine.

summary.value: The Ayam Kedu is a native chicken of Indonesia, named after the village of Kedu on the Kedu Plain in Central Java, where local families have kept it for generations. It is counted among the ancestors of the all black Ayam Cemani. It is a medium sized, hard feathered bird with a large upright single comb. Three main types are known: the Kedu Kedu, a big white skinned bird; the Kedu Cemani, black skinned with a black comb; and the Kedu Hsian, a white skinned partridge type. Plumage may be black, white or partridge. Roosters weigh about 5 to 8 pounds and hens about 2.6 to 6. Estimates put laying at roughly 100 to 200 eggs a year, usually described as brown. The bird is valued in Indonesia for rituals and ceremonies, is used in Chinese medicine, and is also kept for eggs and meat.

history_summary.value: The Ayam Ketawa, or laughing chicken, comes from Sidenreng Rappang in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, and was originally kept as a status symbol by Buginese royalty. It remains a symbol of courage and social status and is entered into crowing contests judged on the clarity and length of its call.

summary.value: The Ayam Ketawa, or laughing chicken, comes from Sidenreng Rappang in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it was developed from local junglefowl long ago. It belongs to the group of long-crowing breeds, and its cocks are famous for a crow that sounds much like a person laughing. In the Bugis language it is called Gaga, meaning a stammering chicken, and keepers sort birds by the speed and rhythm of the call, with names such as dangdut, gretek and disco. The breed was once a status symbol of the Bugis royal family and has spread more widely since the monarchy ended. It still stands for courage and social rank, and birds compete in crowing contests for the Governor's Cup. Birds have a single comb and white skin and come in several plumage colors. Hens weigh about 2 to 4.5 pounds and cocks about 4.5 to 6.5.

history_summary.value: The Barbezieux is a French breed considered rare, recreated by four breeders between 1980 and 1985 after near-disappearance. It is raised mainly in its region of origin around Barbezieux under the 'Poulet de race Barbezieux' quality label, prized for firm, gamey meat.

summary.value: The Barbezieux is a rare French meat chicken from the area around Barbezieux in the Charente, where it has been kept since at least the 1800s and possibly far longer. It ranks among the tallest chickens native to Europe, with roosters standing up to about 2 feet. Plumage is a glossy beetle black, set off by a very large comb and wattles, white earlobes, white skin and blue legs. Roosters weigh about 10 pounds and hens close to 8. The breed nearly died out, and four breeders rebuilt it between 1980 and 1985. Today birds that meet the standard are raised in their home region under a quality label, with around 10,000 to 12,000 sold each year after at least 110 days of growth. The meat is firm with a gamey taste. Hens lay a fair number of white eggs, and no bantam form exists.

history_summary.value: The Barbu d'Anvers is one of the oldest bantam breeds, thought to have originated in the Antwerp province of Belgium from small bearded chickens of the Low Countries. It is the ancestor of other Belgian bantam breeds such as the Barbu de Grubbe and Barbu d'Uccle.

summary.value: The Barbu d'Anvers is a tiny Belgian chicken that exists only as a bantam, with no large version. It ranks among the oldest bantams anywhere and is linked to the Antwerp area, where small bearded fowl were kept for centuries. The name means bearded bird of Antwerp, and a thick muff of feathers hides the earlobes. It stands upright, pushes a round chest forward, carries an arched tail, and wears a small rose comb on clean legs. Cocks weigh about 1.5 pounds and hens a little over 1.3 pounds. Belgium recognizes dozens of color patterns, including quail, porcelain and cuckoo. Hens lay small cream colored eggs and make good sitters and mothers. The birds are friendly and do well as pets, especially with room to roam, but most keepers raise them for shows. It remains the most secure of the Belgian bantam breeds.

history_summary.value: The Barbu de Boitsfort is the most recent Belgian true bantam breed, created by crossing the Barbu de Watermael with the tail-less Barbu de Grubbe. It was first shown in 1997 and received full recognition in Belgium in 2001.

summary.value: The Barbu de Boitsfort is a very small Belgian bantam with no large form. It takes its name from Watermael-Boitsfort, a district of Brussels. It is the youngest of the Belgian bearded bantams: breeders made it in the 1990s by crossing the Barbu de Watermael with the tailless Barbu de Grubbe. It was first shown at Bruges in 1997 and gained full Belgian recognition in 2001. The bird matches the Watermael in every way except one: it has no tail and no tail bone. Like its relatives it wears a full beard. Cocks weigh roughly 1.3 to 1.5 pounds and hens about 1 pound. Twenty-three color patterns are accepted in Europe. Its eggs are tiny, about one ounce each. Numbers are critically low, so it is mainly a bird for dedicated show breeders who want to help keep a rare line alive.

value: tail-less variant of the Barbu d'Anvers

history_summary.value: The Barbu de Grubbe arose around 1904 when a tail-less Barbu d'Anvers was born to breeder Robert Pauwels near Kortenberg, Belgium, who then bred a population of tail-less birds. The breed nearly disappeared after the First World War but survives today as a rare breed, recognised in Germany since 2008.

summary.value: The Barbu de Grubbe is a Belgian true bantam, meaning it has no full sized version. It is simply a Barbu d'Anvers without a tail. Around 1904 a tailless chick hatched on the farm of breeder Robert Pauwels near Kortenberg, between Brussels and Leuven, and he bred more birds from it. They appeared at shows until the First World War, then vanished for decades. Today the breed is rare; Belgium counted only 170 breeding birds in 2012. Apart from the missing tail and tail bone, it looks like the d'Anvers: a full beard, a rose comb, clean legs and the same wide range of colors. Cocks weigh about 1.5 pounds and hens about 1.3 pounds. Hens lay small cream colored eggs. It is kept mostly for shows, and it suits fanciers in Britain, the Netherlands and Germany who want an unusual bantam.

comb.value: rose comb with three small spikes

value: one of the smallest of all bantams
closely related to but smaller than the Barbu d'Anvers
known as the Watermaal in the United States

history_summary.value: The Barbu de Watermael was created by Antoine Dresse at Watermael-Boitsfort, Belgium, in the early twentieth century, likely with some contribution from the Barbu d'Anvers. It is among the most recent and among the smallest of the Belgian bantam breeds.

summary.value: The Barbu de Watermael is a Belgian bantam and one of the smallest chickens kept anywhere. Antoine Dresse developed it early in the 1900s on an estate at Watermael-Boitsfort, near Brussels, and it was first exhibited in 1922. He never said which breeds he used, though the Barbu d'Anvers was certainly one of them. The Watermael looks much like the d'Anvers but is smaller and carries a narrow crest swept back over the head, a three part beard and muff, and a rose comb ending in three little points. Cocks weigh about 1.3 to 1.5 pounds and hens 1 to 1.2 pounds. Belgium accepts more than thirty colors, and in the United States it is known as the Watermaal, shown in black, blue, buff, mottled, quail and white. It is kept almost only as an ornamental and show bird and is considered in danger in its home country.

conservation_status.value: critical (2010, among the most endangered breeds in Belgium)

value: tailless variant of the Barbu d'Uccle
true bantam with no large counterpart
considered a variant of the Barbu d'Uccle rather than a separate breed in Britain and the Netherlands

history_summary.value: The Barbu d'Everberg was bred around 1906 at the Chateau d'Everberg near Kortenberg, Belgium, as a tailless variant of the Barbu d'Uccle. It is one of the most endangered chicken breeds in Belgium.

summary.value: The Barbu d'Everberg is a Belgian true bantam, so it comes only in a small size. It is the tailless form of the Barbu d'Uccle, the bearded, feather footed bantam with a single comb. The line was developed around 1906 at the Chateau d'Everberg in Kortenberg, a town between Brussels and Leuven. Apart from lacking a tail, it follows the d'Uccle closely, and in Britain and the Netherlands it is treated as a d'Uccle variety rather than a breed of its own. European poultry bodies do list it as a separate breed. Cocks weigh about 1.5 to 1.8 pounds and hens about 1.2 to 1.4 pounds. Because the feet are feathered, the birds need a dry, clean run. It is among the rarest chickens in Belgium and was rated critical in 2010, so it appeals mainly to show breeders working to save rare lines.

value: true bantam with no large fowl counterpart

history_summary.value: The breed was created in Uccle, Belgium in the early 1900s, likely by crossing Sabelpoot and Barbu d'Anvers bantams. It spread abroad after 1911 but declined through the World Wars and remains a critically rare breed today.

summary.value: The Barbu d'Uccle, often sold in the US as the Belgian d'Uccle, is a bearded bantam from Uccle, a town on the edge of Brussels. Michael Van Gelder bred it in the early 1900s, probably from two older Belgian bantams, and it was first shown in 1905. It is a true bantam with no large version. The bird sits low, with a full beard and muffs around the face and thick feathers down the legs and feet. The Mille Fleur, meaning a thousand flowers, is the best known of the seven US colors; porcelain, white and self blue are others. Under the American standard, hens weigh about 22 ounces and cocks about 26. Hens lay tiny cream eggs. They have sweet, friendly natures and odd, quizzical faces, which makes them good pets for people with little space and a favorite of bantam fanciers.

value: developed from Asian 'Shanghai' stock crossed with local Dutch fowl

history_summary.value: The breed formed in the Barneveld area of the Netherlands from crosses of local farmyard chickens with imported Asian stock such as Brahma, Cochin and Croad Langshan from the 1850s onward. It was named and shown from 1911, standardised in the 1920s, and later exported to Britain for its brown egg production.

summary.value: The Barnevelder comes from the area around the town of Barneveld in the central Netherlands. Farmers there crossed their local hens with big Asian birds, then called Shanghai fowl, from the 1860s on, and the breed was named in 1911 and recognized in 1923. Britain began importing it around 1921 because shoppers there wanted brown eggs. The best known pattern is double laced, where each brown feather carries two rings of black with a green sheen; black, blue and silver forms also exist, and there are bantams. Hens lay about 175 to 200 large brown eggs a year and keep laying through the winter. The birds are calm and docile, hens often go broody, and they tend to be a little lazy, so free ranging helps keep them fit. They suit backyard keepers who want steady brown eggs from a quiet, good looking bird.

value: yellow legs, feet and skin, bright red single comb

history_summary.value: The Basque hen comes from the Basque region spanning southern France and northern Spain, a hardy dual-purpose bird found in five color varieties and increasingly popular with homesteaders in North America for its foraging ability and friendly temperament.

summary.value: The Basque hen, called Euskal Oiloa in the Basque language, is the old farmyard chicken of the Basque Country, the region that straddles northern Spain and southwestern France. It is a sturdy dual purpose bird that gave rural families both meat and eggs, and Spain began a formal breeding program for it in 1975. It has yellow legs and skin, red earlobes and a bright red single comb. Five color forms exist: black, red, a red brown naked neck, golden cuckoo and a white bird with a black tail. Cocks weigh about 8 to 9 pounds and hens about 5.5 pounds. Hens lay roughly 200 to 220 large brown eggs a year. The birds are friendly, like being around people and handle well. They are tough and forage well, which suits homesteads and free range flocks.

conservation_status.value: at risk of extinction (unknown status as of 2025)

value: larger than most bantams but smaller than full-sized breeds

history_summary.value: The breed developed in the Liege area of Wallonia from small partridge-coloured bantams crossed with local chickens, valued for hatching partridge and pheasant eggs. William Collier began selective breeding around 1917 and a standard was set in 1930, but the breed remains rare and at risk of extinction.

summary.value: The Bassette Liégeoise, often just called the Bassette, is a small Belgian chicken from the Liège area of Wallonia. It counts as a true bantam because no large version exists, yet it is bigger than most bantams: cocks weigh about 2.2 pounds and hens about 2 pounds. Local people once kept these little birds to hatch partridge and pheasant eggs. From around 1917 a Brussels breeder, William Collier, selected them for a fixed type and better laying, and a standard followed in 1930. The bird has a single comb, white earlobes and slate blue beak and legs. Quail and silver quail are the usual colors. Hens lay about 125 to 180 small eggs a year and make reliable sitters and mothers. Very few birds remain, so the breed mainly interests keepers who want to preserve a rare Belgian line.

conservation_status.value: in danger of extinction (168 birds counted in Belgium in 2010)

value: true bantam with no full-sized counterpart

history_summary.value: Like the Dutch Bantam, the breed descends from small partridge-coloured European bantams and was selectively bred in the Liege area of Wallonia from around 1900. Its standard was set in 1934, and it remains rare with only around 168 birds counted in Belgium in 2010.

summary.value: The Belgian Bantam, known in Belgium as the Belgisch kriel or Naine belge, is a tiny chicken with no large form. The name can confuse people, since it is also used loosely for every bantam from Belgium, but here it means one particular breed. It comes from the old European stock of small partridge colored bantams, the same roots as the Dutch Bantam, and breeders around Liège shaped it from about 1900. Its standard dates from 1934. It looks much like the Dutch Bantam but is a little bigger, with cocks near 1.4 pounds and hens near 1.2 pounds. It has a single comb and slate blue legs, and partridge is by far the usual color. Hens lay small white eggs and are good sitters and mothers. Only 168 birds were counted in Belgium in 2010, so it is a breed for dedicated conservation breeders.

origin_year_or_period.value: bred for hundreds of years, standardised 1885

conservation_status.value: extremely endangered (GEH Rote Liste category I)

value: unusually long crow, up to five times longer than other breeds

history_summary.value: The breed has been kept in Germany's Bergisches Land for centuries, likely brought from south-east Europe or the Middle East and spread by Cistercian monks, and was selectively bred for its unusually long crow. A breed association formed in 1884 and it remains a rare, extremely endangered breed today.

summary.value: The Bergische Kräher is an old German chicken from the Bergisches Land, a hilly region east of Düsseldorf and Cologne. Its name means Bergish crower, and it belongs to the long crowing group of breeds: a cock's crow can last up to five times longer than an ordinary rooster's. Local clubs have held crowing contests for centuries, judging each crow for length and beauty, and a breed society has existed since 1884. The accepted color is gold laced black, with slate blue legs, a single comb and white earlobes. Cocks weigh roughly 6.5 to 7.5 pounds and hens 4.5 to 5.5 pounds. It is a dual purpose bird with good meat, and hens lay about 130 medium white eggs a year and seldom go broody. Only a few hundred birds remain, so it suits conservation minded keepers who do not mind a loud rooster.

conservation_status.value: extremely endangered (GEH Rote Liste category I)

comb.value: single, flops from side to side

value: single comb flops from side to side, giving the breed its name
one of three chicken breeds native to the Bergisches Land

history_summary.value: The breed has been known since the eighteenth century in Germany's Bergisches Land, likely resulting from crossing Spanish birds with local Bergische Krahler stock, and nearly went extinct in the early 1800s due to competition from imported multi-purpose breeds. A breed association formed in 1916, and it remains critically endangered with around 250 birds recorded in 2013.

summary.value: The Bergische Schlotterkamm is a rare German chicken from the Bergisches Land in North Rhine-Westphalia, the same district that produced the Bergische Kräher and the German Creeper. Its name comes from its large single comb, which flops loosely from one side of the head to the other. The breed has been known since the 1700s and probably came from crossing Spanish imports with the local Kräher. Imported breeds nearly wiped it out, and a breeders' club was formed in 1916 to save it. The body is long and fairly rectangular, and four colors are recognized: plain black, cuckoo, and black laced with either silver or gold. Cocks weigh about 4.5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4 to 5 pounds. Hens lay around 150 medium white eggs a year and rarely go broody. A rare bantam form also exists. With only about 250 birds counted in 2013, it is a breed for conservation keepers.

history_summary.value: This traditional Italian breed from the Piemonte region was once abundant around Saluzzo but declined in the 1960s with industrialised farming, since it suits only free-range keeping. A recovery effort began in 1999, though breeding stock numbers remain low.

summary.value: The Bianca di Saluzzo is a traditional white chicken from Piedmont in northwest Italy. It is named after the town of Saluzzo, or the old marquisate around it, and is also called the Bianca di Cavour after a nearby town. It was once common on local farms, but intensive poultry farming in the 1960s pushed it aside, because it only does well when it can range outdoors. An agricultural school in Verzuolo started rebuilding the breed in 1999, and numbers are still small. The bird is pure white with yellow skin, legs and earlobes and a big single comb. Cocks weigh about 5.5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4.5 pounds. It is a dual purpose breed: hens start laying at six to seven months and give about 180 medium white eggs a year. It suits free range keepers interested in rare Italian poultry.

value: autosexing chicks distinguishable by colour at hatch
developed from Malines, Welsumer and Barred Rock crosses

history_summary.value: The breed was developed in the 1970s near Bielefeld, Germany by Gerd Roth, who crossed Malines and Welsumer stock with American Barred Rocks. Because of its Barred Rock ancestry it is autosexing, and it was formally recognised under its current name in 1980.

summary.value: The Bielefelder is a modern German chicken created in the 1970s near Bielefeld by breeder Gerd Roth. He blended Malines, Welsumer and Barred Rock lines, among others, and the breed gained German recognition in 1980. Its main selling point is that it is autosexing: at hatch, female chicks show a dark chipmunk stripe down the back, while males are paler with a light spot on the head. Adults wear a crele pattern, a barred red and black mix, and a silver form without red also exists. The birds are large, grow fast and carry a good amount of meat, so they work as a dual purpose breed. Hens lay about 230 large brown eggs a year. Bielefelders are friendly and like human company, and their camouflage coloring helps them on free range. A bantam version is available too.

value: buff plumage with black or blue tail
used to produce the traditional Cappone di Morozzo capon

history_summary.value: This traditional dual-purpose breed from Piemonte, Italy, declined sharply in the 1960s as farming intensified since it needs free-range conditions. A recovery program began in 1999 and a formal breed standard followed in 2007, though total numbers remain modest.

summary.value: The Bionda Piemontese is an old farm chicken from Piedmont in northwest Italy. Bionda means blonde, a nod to its buff feathers, which are set off by a black or blue tail. Local names include Bionda di Cuneo and Bionda di Villanova. The breed faded in the 1960s when poultry farming moved indoors, since it needs outdoor range to thrive. A school in Verzuolo began restoring it in 1999, and Italy's poultry federation approved a standard in 2007. It has yellow skin and legs and a large single comb. Cocks weigh about 5.5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4.5 to 5 pounds. As a dual purpose bird it grows quickly for meat and is the base of the traditional Morozzo capon. Hens lay about 180 to 200 pinkish brown eggs a year of medium to large size. It suits free range keepers who value rare heritage stock.

value: typically a cross of a Rhode Island Red (or other non-white, non-barred) rooster onto a Barred Plymouth Rock hen, which carries both extended-black and barring genes
chicks are sex-linked: color at hatching differs by sex, so pullets and cockerels can be told apart immediately

history_summary.value: Black sex-links are crossbred hybrids bred so that chick down color is linked to sex, removing the need to vent-sex chicks. The cross combines heterosis (hybrid vigor) from two purebred lines into a heavy brown-egg layer.

summary.value: The Black Sex Link, often sold as the Black Star, is not a breed that breeds true but a first-generation cross. A Rhode Island Red or New Hampshire rooster is mated to a Barred Plymouth Rock hen, a pairing American breeders pushed after World War II to get a stronger layer. Chick color depends on sex, and males hatch with a white spot on the head, so buyers can tell pullets from cockerels on day one. Adults are mostly black, and hens may show gold on the neck. Hens weigh about 5 pounds and roosters about 8. A good hen lays more than 250 large to extra large brown eggs a year and seldom goes broody. The birds are quiet, docile and easy to handle, and they stand up to both cold and hot weather. They suit beginners and families who want plenty of eggs from a hardy, easygoing bird.

value: early maturing, laying starts around 145-173 days

history_summary.value: The breed developed from black Mediterranean-type chickens traditionally kept in Shumen Province, Bulgaria, and was formalized through selective breeding at the Agricultural Institute of Stara Zagora between 1951 and 1989, including an early cross with Minorca. Numbers fell sharply after 1989, and today only one flock of about 200 birds survives, making it an endangered breed.

summary.value: The Black Shumen is a light, egg laying chicken from Shumen Province in north-eastern Bulgaria. Local black farm hens of a Mediterranean type were improved at the Agricultural Institute of Stara Zagora from 1951, first by crossing with Black Minorca cocks, and the result was recognized as a breed. It spread widely across Bulgarian farms and schools, but numbers crashed after 1989, and today a single flock of about 200 birds is kept at that institute. The plumage is black with a green sheen, the legs slate grey and the skin white. The large red single comb flops to one side in hens. Hens weigh about 3.3 pounds and cocks about 4.2. They mature early and lay around 150 to 155 small white eggs a year. The breed is rare and endangered, so it matters mostly to conservation breeders.

value: slate-blue plumage from a dilution gene

history_summary.value: Blue chickens from Andalusia in southern Spain reached England by 1851, where breeders developed the blue-laced type through selective and cross-breeding over many years. The breed spread to the United States, South America and Germany in the second half of the 19th century, and Spain officially recognised the Andaluza Azul in 2007.

summary.value: The Blue Andalusian is a Mediterranean chicken from Andalusia in southern Spain. Birds from there reached England in the 1840s, and English fanciers spent decades refining the sharp blue lacing seen on show birds today. The breed reached America in the 1850s and entered the American standard in 1874. Its slate blue color comes from a dilution gene, so blue parents also produce black and splash or off-white chicks. It has white earlobes, a single comb and dark legs. Roosters weigh about 7 pounds and hens about 5.5 pounds. Hens lay roughly 160 to 200 medium to large chalk white eggs a year, keep laying in winter and seldom go broody. These are active, lively birds that forage hard and dislike confinement, so they suit free range setups more than small runs. They handle heat well and can live in colder areas, though warm regions suit them best.

comb.value: single, upright, five to seven points

value: vulture hocks (long downward feathers on the thighs)
short compact body with a U-shaped topline

history_summary.value: Feather-footed bantams of this type have been depicted in European art since the 17th century and were described in English poultry books by the mid-1800s. The breed was established in the United Kingdom and the United States through the 19th century and later used to help create the Barbu d'Uccle.

summary.value: The Booted Bantam, called Sabelpoot in Dutch, is a true bantam known for its heavily feathered legs and feet and its vulture hocks, stiff feathers that sweep down and back from the thighs. Feather-footed bantams like it appear in European paintings from the 1600s, and birds were being bred in Massachusetts by 1836. It is closely related to the Barbu d'Uccle but has no beard and runs a little larger. Hens weigh about 22 ounces and cocks about 26. It has a single upright comb, a short back and a tail held high. The APA accepts white, mille fleur, porcelain, black and self blue. Hens lay around 120 small white to tinted eggs a year and often go broody. Booted Bantams are calm, friendly and alert, and they scratch very little, so they spare gardens. They dislike cold and damp and need dry, soft ground to keep foot feathers clean.

value: grows quickly, reaching adulthood by six months

history_summary.value: The breed comes from the Bourbonnais region of France, where white poultry such as the Gatinaise had long been kept. Crossing these local birds with Brahmas produced the Bourbonnaise herminee, while the plain white birds kept the Gatinaise name.

summary.value: The Bourbonnaise is a French farm chicken from the old province of Bourbonnais in central France. White poultry had been kept there for a long time, and crossing those local birds with Columbian Brahmas near the end of the 1800s produced the Bourbonnaise, a white bird with dark markings like the Brahma. It is a semi heavy breed with fairly long legs. Cocks weigh about 7.7 pounds and hens about 5.5 pounds. It is a practical dual purpose bird: hens lay up to 200 cream colored eggs a year, and the young grow fast, reaching adult size by about six months. The birds are vigorous, forage well and look after themselves, yet they also cope with life in a coop. That mix of hardiness and productivity makes the breed a good choice for small farms and backyard keepers, and it is listed on the Slow Food Ark of Taste.

value: trilobar beard and muff hiding the earlobes and wattles

history_summary.value: The Brabanter is an old Dutch breed from the Brabant region, appearing in a 1676 painting by Melchior d'Hondecoeter, and it nearly went extinct in the early 1900s before being restored by cross-breeding with other crested, bearded birds. A bantam version was created around 1934 by crossing it with bearded Poland bantams.

summary.value: The Brabanter is an old crested chicken from Brabant, a region split between the Netherlands and Belgium. Birds very like it appear in Dutch paintings from the 1600s. It nearly died out early in the 1900s and was rebuilt by crossing in other crested, bearded fowl. Its crest is narrow and stands up and slightly forward, like that of the Swiss Appenzeller Spitzhauben, and it also has a full three part beard that hides the small white earlobes. The comb is a small V shape. This is a light breed: cocks weigh about 4 to 5.5 pounds and hens about 3.5 to 4.5 pounds. Hens lay around 170 medium white eggs a year and keep laying fairly well in winter. Brabanters are calm and clever, and their tiny comb and wattles make them a good fit for cold climates. A bantam version has existed since about 1934.

value: rare breed after decline in and after World War II

history_summary.value: The Braekel likely originated near Brakel in East Flanders, Belgium, from the same population of gold and silver chickens that produced similar German breeds, and it gave rise to the UK's Campine. Two regional types were split into separate breeds in 1884 and reunited under one standard in 1926, but the breed declined sharply during and after the Second World War and is now rare.

summary.value: The Braekel, also spelled Brakel, is an old laying breed from East Flanders in Belgium, named after the Brakel area near the villages of Opbrakel and Nederbrakel. It was once kept on nearly every farm in the district. It shares its roots with the German East Frisian Gull and the Westphalian Totleger, and it gave rise to the British Campine. Unlike Campine roosters, Braekel males have normal cock feathering. The feathers show straight bars of color with a plain, solid neck, in gold or silver. It is a light breed: cocks weigh about 4.5 to 5.5 pounds and hens about 4 to 5 pounds. Hens start laying at six or seven months and give about 180 to 200 large white eggs a year. The birds are active, fly well and forage hard, so they suit free range keepers. Numbers fell sharply after the Second World War, and the breed is now rare.

value: distinctive head shape from cross-breeding with Grey Chittagong stock
one of the largest chicken breeds

history_summary.value: The Brahma developed in the United States in the 1840s from large, heavily-feathered 'Shanghai' birds imported from China, crossed with Grey Chittagong stock from Bengal that gave it its pea comb and head shape. It became the leading American meat breed from the 1850s until around 1930, after early export stock also shaped the dark variety bred in England.

summary.value: The Brahma is a giant, heavily feathered chicken that American breeders developed in the mid 1800s from big birds shipped out of Shanghai, with a little Chittagong blood from India that gave it a pea comb and a heavy brow. Roosters reach about 12 pounds and hens about 10, so it ranks among the largest breeds you can keep. Feathers run down the legs and over the toes, and the usual colors are light, dark and buff. Hens lay around 150 to 200 medium to large brown eggs a year and keep laying through winter better than most. Brahmas are calm, docile birds that rarely fly and stay put behind a low fence. They cope well with cold but suffer in hot summers, and they need a dry run to keep their foot feathers clean. They suit families and beginners who have room for a big, gentle bird.

value: considered the same breed as the Campine until distinguished in 1884
nearly extinct by the 1960s; revived from just 2 hens, 2 roosters and a dozen eggs starting in 1971

history_summary.value: The Brakel dates back to 1416 in the Flanders region spanning northern France, Belgium and Holland. Its population collapsed after both World Wars, and the breed was rebuilt from a handful of surviving birds beginning in 1971.

summary.value: The Brakel is a Belgian chicken with a long history; records trace it back to the early 1400s in Flanders, a region that once reached from northern France into Belgium and Holland. It takes its name from a village northwest of Brussels. For centuries it was a common farm bird, and it was long lumped together with the Campine until the two were split in 1884. Both World Wars cut numbers badly, and by the 1960s it was almost gone. A rescue started in 1971 with just two hens, two roosters and a dozen eggs. Brakels come in silver or gold, with a solid colored neck and barred body feathers. Cocks weigh about 4.5 to 5.5 pounds and hens about 4 to 5 pounds. Hens lay around 180 to 200 large white eggs a year. The birds are active, strong fliers and keen foragers, best suited to free range.

value: naked neck with bare bright red skin
good sitters with strong maternal behaviour

history_summary.value: The Branca is a traditional white naked-neck breed from north-western Portugal, kept on small family farms in the Entre Douro e Minho region for eggs and meat. It was the most endangered of the four Portuguese chicken breeds in 2016, with only a few hundred breeding birds, but its population had grown substantially by 2024.

summary.value: The Branca is a white naked neck chicken from northwest Portugal, and its name simply means white. It is one of four native Portuguese breeds, along with the Amarela, Pedrês Portuguesa and Preta Lusitânica. Families in the Entre Douro e Minho region have long kept it on small farms for their own eggs and meat. The top of the neck has no feathers and shows bright red skin, matching the red face, earlobes and single comb. Legs are bare and pale yellow. Cocks weigh roughly 5 to 7 pounds and hens about 3.3 to 5 pounds. The birds are active and tough, resist disease well and cope with poor conditions. Hens sit well and make caring mothers. The breed does best on free range or in a roomy run. Numbers were very low in 2016 but grew strongly, and it was rated not at risk by 2024.

value: white variety raised in Bresse has appellation d'origine contrôlée status as poulet de Bresse
regarded as a premium meat product

history_summary.value: Chickens from the Bresse region of eastern France were recorded as early as 1591 and gained a reputation as a premium table bird, but the breed nearly disappeared around 1900 before fancy breeders rebuilt it from white stock under a 1904 standard. The Bresse name received legal protection in 1936 and full appellation d'origine contrôlée status in 1957.

summary.value: The Bresse Gauloise is a French chicken from the old province of Bresse in eastern France, famous as one of the finest table birds in the world. Only white birds raised inside the legally defined Bresse area may be sold under the Bresse name, as poulet de Bresse, and they fetch premium prices. The same birds raised elsewhere are called Gauloise. Four colors exist: white, black, grey with silver pencilling, and a newer blue. White birds show a red comb, white feathers and slate blue legs. Records of these chickens go back to 1591, and fanciers rebuilt the breed after it nearly vanished around 1900. Although prized for meat, hens also lay a good number of large white eggs and seldom go broody. The birds mature quickly and are hardy. They suit keepers who want a quality meat bird that still lays well.

value: bred for very fast growth and high feed conversion
reaches slaughter weight around 2 kg in 5 to 7 weeks
prone to skeletal and heart-related welfare problems from rapid growth
slow-growing free-range/organic strains reach slaughter weight at 12-16 weeks

history_summary.value: The modern broiler emerged from pedigree breeding that began around 1916 and a Cornish x Plymouth Rock cross introduced in the 1930s, which became the dominant meat bird by the 1960s. Breeding programs since the 1950s, such as Donald Shaver's, further refined growth rate and traits like colour-sexing to produce today's fast-growing commercial broilers.

summary.value: A broiler is not a single breed but any chicken raised mainly for meat. Before modern meat strains existed, broilers were mostly young cockerels culled from farm flocks. Organized pedigree breeding started around 1916, and in the 1930s breeders crossed Cornish males with large white Plymouth Rock hens, a cross that dominated meat production by the 1960s. Today's commercial strains come from company breeding programs and are usually white feathered with yellowish skin. They grow very fast, turn feed into meat efficiently and move little, reaching about 4.4 pounds in five to seven weeks. Slower growing strains used for free range and organic systems take closer to 12 to 16 weeks. That rapid growth brings real welfare problems, including leg and skeletal disorders and heart trouble, so housing, ventilation and stocking density need careful management. Most are raised in large mixed sex flocks in sheds.

value: deeply pigmented face from purplish-red to almost black

history_summary.value: The Brugse Vechter is the oldest of Belgium's three gamecock breeds, developed in West Flanders in the early 19th century for cock-fighting and first documented as 'the Bruges breed' in 1858. It is now endangered, having given rise to the Luikse Vechter and Tiense Vechter, with a bantam version created in the second half of the 20th century.

summary.value: The Brugse Vechter, or Bruges Fighter, is a Belgian game chicken from the area around Bruges in West Flanders. It appeared in the early 1800s, was bred for cockfighting, and is the oldest of Belgium's three fighting breeds; the Luikse and Tiense Vechter both come from it. Cockfighting is now illegal in Belgium, and many birds are kept only for shows. It is a big, strong bird, with cocks around 11 to 12 pounds and hens near 9 pounds. The back is broad, flat and nearly level, the face is dark, anywhere between purplish red and near black, the small comb is triple, and the thick legs are slate blue. Hens lay about 150 extra large cream eggs a year but are poor sitters. The birds are hardy yet often aggressive, so cocks and hens may need separate pens. It is endangered and best left to experienced keepers.

value: developed at Cambridge by Professor Punnett and Mr. Pease to add autosexing to Light Sussex-type utility birds
distinctive crele plumage: copper and gold body color with barring
never became popular and barely survived the 1960s

history_summary.value: The Brussbar was bred at Cambridge in the early-to-mid 20th century from Brown Sussex and Barred Rock stock crossed with utility Light Sussex, aiming for an autosexing dual-purpose bird. It was standardized in 1952 but never achieved popularity and remains very rare.

summary.value: The Brussbar is a rare British chicken developed at Cambridge before 1950 by Professor Punnett and his colleague Mr. Pease, pioneers of autosexing breeds. Their goal was a bird with the useful qualities of the Light Sussex whose chicks could be sorted into males and females by color at hatch. They began by crossing Brown Sussex with Barred Rocks, then added productive Light Sussex lines. The breed was standardized in Britain in 1952. Adults have crele plumage, a barred mix of copper and gold. A silver form once existed, but only the gold survives. Autosexing breeders rated the Brussbar among their best dual purpose birds for eggs and meat, yet it never gained a real following and barely made it through the 1960s. Interest is growing again, though only one known pure flock remains, so it suits dedicated rare breed keepers.

value: mahogany red plumage with black tail, resembling buckeye seeds
only American Class breed with a pea comb
tolerates confinement well but prefers to range
good at hunting mice and other pests
created by a woman, Nettie Metcalf, predating the Rhode Island Red

history_summary.value: The Buckeye was created in 1896 by Nettie Metcalf of Warren, Ohio, who crossed Barred Plymouth Rocks, Buff Cochins and black-breasted red games to make a cold-hardy dual-purpose bird, and it is the only known American breed developed by a woman. It was admitted to the American Poultry Association's Standard of Perfection in 1904 and is now listed as Watch by the Livestock Conservancy.

summary.value: The Buckeye is an American dual purpose chicken bred in Warren, Ohio, in the 1890s by Nettie Metcalf, the only woman credited with creating a breed in the American class. She named it for the Buckeye State, and its deep mahogany red feathers and black tail match the color of the buckeye nut. It carries a small pea comb and a broad, compact body with meaty thighs. Roosters weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 6.5 pounds. Hens lay roughly 150 to 200 medium to large brown eggs a year, and some modern lines lay more. They can go broody and make protective mothers. Buckeyes are active, friendly birds that forage hard and are known for catching mice. The pea comb makes them very tough in cold winters, and they can get used to heat over time. They do best with room to roam and suit homesteads and backyard flocks.

value: true bantam with no corresponding large fowl
smaller and lower to the ground than the similar Booted Bantam

history_summary.value: The Burmese Bantam apparently originated in Myanmar and reached the UK in the 1880s, but was believed extinct by the First World War. Surviving birds found in the 1970s were crossed with white Booted Bantams to recreate the breed, which the Poultry Club of Great Britain now recognises only in white.

summary.value: The Burmese is a tiny ornamental chicken with no large fowl version. A British army officer brought the first white birds home from Burma around 1880. The breed was thought lost before 1914, but a small group turned up with an old keeper in Wiltshire in 1970. Andrew Sheppy, founder of the Rare Poultry Society, crossed them with white Booted Bantams and brought the line back. The bird looks like a small Booted Bantam that sits lower, with a longer shape and a low tail. It has a single comb topped by a small crest, short legs covered in feathers, small earlobes and long wattles. White is the only color the British standard accepts, and a black copy has been made in the Netherlands. It is a rare show bird, and little is published about its eggs or nature.

history_summary.value: Developed in the 1930s in Modesto, California by Horace Dryden, who crossed Barred Plymouth Rock and White Leghorn birds to make a dual-purpose, autosexing chicken. It was never recognized by the American Poultry Association and remains a rare breed today.

summary.value: The California Gray is a rare American chicken bred in Modesto, California, during the 1930s. The Dryden poultry breeding work crossed Barred Plymouth Rocks with White Leghorns to get a bird that could give both meat and a steady supply of large white eggs. Adults wear barred gray feathers. The breed is autosexing, so chicks can be sorted into males and females at about one day old by their down. Birds weigh roughly 4 to 6 pounds. Cocks are also mated to White Leghorn hens to make the California White, a commercial laying hybrid. The American Poultry Association never accepted the breed into its standard, and it is not on the Livestock Conservancy priority list. It suits keepers who want white eggs from a bird with some table value and who like sexing chicks at hatch.

value: developed in the 1930s by crossing a Barred Plymouth Rock rooster with a White Leghorn hen
never recognized by the American Poultry Association

history_summary.value: The California Grey was developed in California in the 1930s by the Dryden poultry breeding program to be a dual-purpose hen laying large white eggs that stayed productive for more than two years. Its Barred Rock x White Leghorn cross gave naturally autosexing grey barred plumage, but it was never recognized by the American Poultry Association and is now rare.

summary.value: The California Grey is an uncommon American breed first produced in California during the 1930s. Breeder Dryden mated a Barred Plymouth Rock rooster to White Leghorn hens, aiming for a hen that laid large white eggs and kept up production past her second year while still giving some meat. The result has gray barred plumage and is autosexing, which lets keepers tell cockerels from pullets soon after hatch. Grown birds weigh about 4 to 6 pounds, lighter than most dual purpose breeds. Cocks of the breed are also used with White Leghorn hens to make the California White laying hybrid. It never won a place in the American Poultry Association standard and remains rare today. It fits a small flock owner who values white eggs and easy chick sexing over show points.

comb.value: large single red comb, can flop to one side

history_summary.value: A Flemish breed closely related to the larger Braekel, it was formally split off as its own breed in the early 1900s and imported to Britain and the United States soon after. It later played a role in early autosexing genetics research, though it remains one of the rarer chicken breeds today.

summary.value: The Campine comes from the Kempen district of northern Belgium, near Antwerp, and is a smaller, slimmer cousin of the Braekel. English breeders took it up around 1900 and made hen feathering in males the standard, so cocks look much like hens, without long sickle or hackle feathers. It comes in Silver and Golden, each with a plain colored head and neck over a body barred with black. Roosters weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4 pounds in the US standard. Hens rarely go broody and lay 140 to 200 medium white eggs a year, big for such a small bird. Campines are active, flighty and curious, love to forage, and do not like being held. They prefer warm weather and struggle in hard cold. They can work for beginners with room to free range.

history_summary.value: A Spanish black chicken breed thought to date back to Moorish Spain, it nearly disappeared once imported commercial layer hybrids and intensive farming spread. A national conservation program from the 1970s onward, plus a formal breed standard first set in 1930 and revised in 2010, helped it survive.

summary.value: The Castellana Negra is an old Spanish laying breed, often linked to the Moorish period, when it was called the moruna. It was once the common farm hen of central and southern Spain, then nearly vanished when caged hybrid layers took over. Conservation flocks built from a handful of birds in the 1980s brought it back, and about 2,200 were counted in 2024, still a vulnerable number. It is a light, Mediterranean type bird dressed in solid black with a green sheen, a red single comb with five or six points, white earlobes and dark slate legs. Roosters weigh about 6 to 6.5 pounds and hens about 5 pounds. Hens start laying at four to five months and give around 200 to 225 large white eggs a year. They are hardy, resist disease well and seldom go broody.

comb.value: large single comb with six upright points on males, flops over on hens

history_summary.value: Developed in Catalonia's El Prat area in the second half of the nineteenth century by crossing local landrace fowl with imported Asian stock, it was showcased at the 1902 Madrid World's Fair and admitted to the American Poultry Association's standard in 1949. Prized for its heat tolerance, it also became a commercial breed in parts of Latin America such as Argentina.

summary.value: The Catalana, also called the Catalana del Prat, was bred near Barcelona in Catalonia, Spain, during the late 1800s from local farm hens crossed with Asian birds. It was shown to the world at the 1902 fair in Madrid and joined the American standard in 1949. Birds are a rich buff to reddish gold with black tails that shine green, white earlobes and slate blue legs. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6. Hens lay roughly 200 to 240 white to pale pink eggs a year, medium to large in size, and seldom go broody. The meat is also well regarded, so it serves as a dual purpose bird. Catalanas are alert, active and wary of people, fly readily and dislike being penned. They handle extreme heat very well, which makes them a strong pick for hot climates.

value: only chicken breed native to Canada

history_summary.value: Bred from 1908 by the Cistercian monk Wilfrid Chatelain at the Oka Agricultural Institute in Quebec, it was designed as a cold-hardy dual-purpose fowl and shown publicly in 1918, joining the American Poultry Association standard in 1921. Its population nearly vanished by the late 1970s and it remains an endangered breed today, kept mostly in Quebec.

summary.value: The Chantecler is the only chicken breed that comes from Canada. Brother Wilfrid Chatelain, a monk at the abbey in Oka, Quebec, started work on it in 1908 and showed it to the public in 1918. He wanted a sturdy farm bird that could handle Canadian winters, so the breed has tight, dense feathers, a tiny cushion comb and almost no wattles, which keeps frostbite away. White is the original color, and a partridge version came later from Alberta. Roosters weigh about 7.5 to 8.5 pounds and hens about 5.5 pounds. Hens lay around 200 to 220 large light brown eggs a year and keep laying in winter. They are gentle, calm birds that grow friendly when handled young, and some hens go broody. The breed is rare today. It is a strong pick for cold northern climates but does poorly in hot weather.

value: best broody breed, especially for hatching ducks and turkeys

history_summary.value: Descended from large feather-legged chickens brought from China to Europe and North America in the 1840s and 1850s, the Cochin sparked a mid-19th-century poultry craze after imported birds were given to Queen Victoria. Bred mainly for its impressive fluffy appearance rather than production, it remains popular today as an ornamental and broody breed rather than a meat or commercial egg bird.

summary.value: The Cochin comes from big, feather-legged chickens shipped out of China in the 1840s and 1850s, first called Shanghai fowl. Their size set off the "hen fever" craze in England and America. Today it is kept mainly for show and as a pet. Soft, loose feathers give it a round, heart-shaped outline, and the feathering runs down the legs onto the toes. Roosters weigh about 11 pounds and hens about 8.5, and bantams are common in the US. Hens start slowly, often around eight months, then lay roughly 150 to 200 medium to large brown eggs a year. They are among the most broody of all breeds and will happily hatch duck or turkey eggs. Cochins are gentle, docile and easy to tame, and a two-foot fence holds them. They do well in cold but need shade in summer heat.

history_summary.value: An old Belgian breed of unclear origin, possibly linked to the Malines chicken of the Mechelen area, it vanished by the First World War and was recreated before the Second World War. It is now critically endangered in Belgium but more common in nearby northern France.

summary.value: The Coucou des Flandres, known in Dutch as the Vlaamse Koekoek, is an old farm chicken from Flanders in Belgium, tied to the Dender river area. It is probably close kin to the Malines and may show what that breed looked like before Asian birds were crossed in during the 1800s. The breed died out around the First World War and was rebuilt in the years before the Second. A 2005 count found only 53 birds in Belgium, though it is more common across the border in northern France. Every bird is cuckoo patterned, with a single comb and bare, pinkish white legs. Hens weigh about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds and roosters about 6.5 to 7.5 pounds. Hens lay around 150 cream eggs a year, each near 60 grams, and they sit well and raise chicks as good mothers.

history_summary.value: One of the oldest French chicken breeds, named after the Normandy commune of Crevecoeur-en-Auge, it won prizes at the 1855 Paris exposition and was later added to the American Poultry Association's standard in 1874. Its numbers collapsed during the world wars and recovery only began in 1976, with separate bantam versions later bred in the United States and Germany.

summary.value: The Crevecoeur is one of the oldest French chicken breeds, named after the village of Crevecoeur-en-Auge in Normandy. For centuries it was a prized table bird in France, known for fine white breast meat and small bones. It wears a crest and beard like the Houdan, but it has four toes and a V-shaped comb that looks like a pair of small horns. Black is the usual color, and France also recognizes blue, white and cuckoo. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6.5 pounds. Hens lay 120 to 150 white or lightly tinted eggs a year, medium to large in size, and some go broody. The birds move in a quiet, deliberate way and are gentle and docile, which makes them good pets when handled young. They are content in small covered pens, but wet crests can freeze in winter. The breed is endangered and kept mostly for shows today.

origin_year_or_period.value: origins unknown, among the oldest French breeds; standard accepted 1909

history_summary.value: The Crevecoeur is among the oldest French chicken breeds, from the Pays d'Auge in Normandy. It suffered heavy losses in both World Wars and was thought nearly extinct after the second, before Jean-Claude Perriquet began a recovery effort in 1976; it remains a Livestock Conservancy-listed endangered breed.

summary.value: The Crevecoeur is one of the oldest French chickens, raised for centuries in Normandy and named for a small town there. It was prized for its table meat, with fine bones and white breast meat, and it won early prizes in Paris before joining the American standard in 1874. Wartime losses in France left it close to extinction, and it is still rare. The usual bird is solid black, with a full crest, a beard and a small red comb shaped like a V or pair of horns; blue and white also exist. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6.5. Hens lay 120 to 150 white to tinted eggs a year, medium to large, and go broody at times. Crevecoeurs are quiet and gentle, take confinement well and make good pets, but their crests need covered pens and protection from winter wet.

history_summary.value: Descended from fowl from the Langshan area near Nantong, China, it was imported to Britain in 1872 by Major F.T. Croad and became a popular utility breed in the early twentieth century. Numbers fell after the Second World War but the breed was kept going by the Rare Poultry Society and its own club was revived in 1979.

summary.value: The Croad Langshan is a large, soft feathered chicken from the Langshan, or Wolf Hill, district near Nantong in eastern China. Major Croad brought the first birds to Britain in 1872, and his name now separates this original utility type from the taller Modern Langshan bred for shows. American Langshans descend from the same Croad birds. The usual color is black with a green sheen, and white and blue are also recognized. The back and rising tail form a deep U shape, and the shanks carry light feathering. Cocks weigh about 9.5 pounds and hens about 7.5 pounds. Hens lay around 140 to 150 large, dark brown eggs a year and keep laying through winter. The birds are calm, friendly and easy to tame, and they take confinement well. They like dry, well drained ground and cope with warm climates better than most Asian breeds.

history_summary.value: Developed in Cuba during the 1800s by crossing Malay and Sumatra gamefowl brought from the Philippines with European gamefowl, it is the only chicken breed officially recognized as native to Cuba and joined the American Poultry Association's standard in 1939. Originally a triple-purpose bird raised for meat, eggs and cockfighting, it is mostly kept today as an ornamental exhibition breed outside Cuba.

summary.value: The Cubalaya is the one chicken breed native to Cuba. Breeders there made it in the 1800s by mixing Malay and Sumatra game birds from the Philippines with European game stock, and it reached the American standard in 1939. Its best known feature is the long, drooping lobster tail, paired with a pea comb and a flowing mane of neck feathers. The US standard colors are black, white and black-breasted red. Cocks weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4, and they can take up to three years to fill out. Hens lay roughly 125 to 175 small to medium white or tinted eggs a year and make good mothers. The birds are unusually tame with people but can pick on other chickens, and they can be noisy. They handle heat and humidity well, like to forage on grass, and suit warm regions and exhibition keepers.

history_summary.value: A very old Bohemian breed, first mentioned in 1205 when a flock was given as a wedding gift to the Danish king Valdemar II. It is now considered an endangered breed.

summary.value: The Czech Gold Brindled Hen is a very old farm breed from Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic. It appears in records from 1205, when a flock went to the Danish king Valdemar II as a wedding present on his marriage to the Bohemian princess Dagmar. Today it is rare and counted as endangered. Hens are light brown flecked all over with gold. Roosters have gold neck feathers, a brown to red gold back, dark wings with a green bar, a black tail and a breast speckled with gold. Both sexes carry a red single comb and slate blue legs, and chicks hatch light brown. Hens weigh about 4.5 to 5.5 pounds and roosters about 5 to 6 pounds. A hen lays around 160 eggs a year, each 55 to 60 grams. Little is recorded about its temperament.

value: created from Gournay and Crevecoeur genetics to re-create the extinct Normande breed
