fine white meat and delicate bones

history_summary.value: The Dampierre was created in France in 1996 from Gournay and Crevecoeur stock, an attempt to re-create the Normande breed that had gone extinct more than a century earlier. It remains rare and expensive, only beginning to appear in the United States.

summary.value: The Dampierre is a young French breed made in 1996 by fanciers who wanted to bring back the Normande, an old Normandy chicken that had died out more than a hundred years before. They could not revive the exact bird, so they built a close likeness from Gournay and Crevecoeur stock. The result is mottled black and white like the Gournay and wears a feather crest on its head. It is a dual purpose bird, with fine white meat on light bones. Hens lay a good number of large white eggs and will go broody and sit on a clutch. The breed is still very rare, especially outside France, and published details on its weight, laying totals and temperament are hard to find. It suits keepers who enjoy uncommon heritage style birds.

history_summary.value: The Deathlayer, or Totleger, comes from the old farm chickens of Westphalia in Germany, mainly around Bielefeld and Herford. It was widespread until more productive foreign breeds arrived and is now seriously endangered, with fewer than 1,000 registered birds in 2016.

summary.value: The Deathlayer, known in Germany as the Westfaelischer Totleger, is an old laying breed from the farms of Westphalia, mainly around Bielefeld and Herford. The grim English name is a mistranslation. It grew out of older words meaning a daily or long lasting layer. Birds come in gold pencilled or silver pencilled plumage and carry a rose comb. They are small and light, with hens around 3.5 to 4.5 pounds and roosters around 4.5 to 5.5 pounds. Hens rarely go broody and lay about 180 medium white eggs a year. The breed is closely related to the East Frisian Gull and the Braekel. Once common, it faded when more productive foreign breeds arrived, and in 2016 fewer than a thousand registered birds remained, so it is counted as seriously endangered. Birds like to roost up in trees when allowed.

history_summary.value: Not a formally recognized chicken breed but a blue strain of American gamecock tied to a Delaware regiment in the Revolutionary War, with a name dating to 1775; it became Delaware's official state bird in 1939. The flock kept today by the University of Delaware has been crossbred with Blue Andalusian stock and no longer looks like the original fighting birds.

summary.value: The Delaware Blue Hen is a blue strain of American game chicken rather than a recognized breed. Its name goes back to 1775 and the Revolutionary War, when soldiers of a Delaware regiment from Kent County were linked with blue fighting cocks, though several versions of the story exist. Delaware made the Blue Hen Chicken its official state bird in 1939, and the University of Delaware teams are named after it. In the 1960s a breeder gave the university twelve birds, not from the old Kent County line, and it has kept a small flock since, about forty birds in 2007. That flock was crossed with Blue Andalusians and now looks Mediterranean, with a different body, less gold in the neck feathers and white earlobes in place of red. No laying or weight figures are published for it.

history_summary.value: Bred by George Ellis in Delaware starting in 1940 from light-colored 'sport' offspring of Barred Plymouth Rock and New Hampshire crosses, it was first called the Indian River and became the dominant broiler chicken on the Delmarva Peninsula for roughly two decades. It was displaced by the Cornish-Rock cross in the late 1950s and is now an endangered heritage breed, though its conservation status has improved from critical in 2010 to recovering by 2024.

summary.value: The Delaware is an American chicken created in 1940 by George Ellis of Delaware. He noticed pale sports among his Barred Plymouth Rock and New Hampshire crosses and bred them into a new line, first called the Indian River. For about twenty years it was the leading broiler on the Delmarva Peninsula, until Cornish crosses took over in the late 1950s, and it later became rare. The bird is mostly white with black barring on the neck, wings and tail. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6. Hens lay about four large to jumbo brown eggs a week, up to 200 a year, and rarely go broody. Delawares are calm and friendly with people and firm but not bullying with other hens. They can be noisy, cannot fly well, and suit small farms that want both meat and eggs.

history_summary.value: A Turkish long-crowing breed closely tied to the city of Denizli for at least nine centuries, with roosters capable of crows lasting 20 to 25 seconds in their first year. Its population has been declining, prompting an active conservation program run by Turkey's Lalahan Central Livestock Research Institute.

summary.value: The Denizli is a long crowing chicken from Turkey, named after Denizli, a city in the southwest of the country. The rooster has been the emblem of the city and province for at least 900 years, backed by an old relief found at the ruins of Laodicea, and a large glass statue of one went up in the city square in 2013. Young cocks can hold a single crow for 20 to 25 seconds. Birds have black eyes, dark gray or purple legs and silver or red neck feathers, sometimes with red on the wings, and breeders sort them into three groups by color, build and comb. Adults weigh roughly 6.5 to 7.5 pounds. The birds are kept for eggs and meat as well as for their crowing. Numbers are falling, and a Turkish state research institute runs a conservation flock.

history_summary.value: An old English breed from Derbyshire and the Pennine area, likely descended from Golden Spangled Hamburghs, Dorkings, Old English Pheasant Fowl and Black-Breasted Red Games, and prized in the 1800s for heavy egg production. It nearly vanished in England by 1900 and remains rare today, listed as Vulnerable in the UK and Critical in the US.

summary.value: The Derbyshire Redcap is one of England's oldest farm breeds, raised for generations in Derbyshire and the southern Pennines. Its name comes from a huge red rose comb, covered in small points and finished with a spike at the back, which counts for a quarter of the judging points in British shows. Feathers are deep red to black with dark half moon tips, and there is only one color. Roosters weigh about 7.5 pounds and hens about 6. Unusually, the hens have red earlobes yet lay white eggs, around 150 to 200 a year, medium to large, and they keep laying for years. They seldom go broody. Redcaps are lively, alert and a little wild, fly well and forage hard. They need space and dislike being shut in. They handle cold well but not heat, and they suit roomy free range farms more than small yards.

history_summary.value: Considered the oldest American chicken breed, likely descended from birds brought over by English colonists and well established by about 1750, it was later crossed with Black Java to create the Plymouth Rock in the 1860s. Numbers nearly collapsed by the 1970s, but a breed-rescue effort from the 1980s onward brought it back, and its status had improved to watch by 2021.

summary.value: The Dominique is counted as the oldest American chicken breed. Its roots are unclear: it may come from fowl that colonists brought from southern England, and barred birds of this kind were common on American farms by the 1750s. In the 1860s Dominiques were crossed with Black Javas to create the Plymouth Rock, and later rules reserved the Dominique name for rose combed birds. The feathers are barred in light and dark gray, a pattern called cuckoo or hawk colored, and the low rose comb ends in a short spike. Roosters weigh about 7 pounds and hens about 5. Hens lay roughly 230 to 275 medium brown eggs a year; some lines go broody and make good mothers. Dominiques are calm, friendly birds and forage well. Their tight feathers and small comb resist frostbite, and they also cope with hot, humid summers. They are a solid pick for families and first time keepers.

history_summary.value: A rare Vietnamese breed from Dong Tao village near Hanoi known for its unusually large legs and feet, historically raised exclusively for the royal family and mandarins. It remains a prized, expensive delicacy today, though its bulky legs make natural incubation difficult.

summary.value: The Dong Tao, sometimes called the Dragon Chicken, is a rare meat breed from Dong Tao village in Khoai Chau District, Hung Yen Province, near Hanoi in northern Vietnam. Its trademark is a pair of hugely thick, scaly legs and feet on a heavy frame. The meat is a costly delicacy in Vietnam, and in the past these birds were raised only for the royal court and high officials. They are hard to breed. Hens tend to crush their own eggs under those bulky feet, so keepers usually hatch the eggs in an incubator, and the birds cope poorly with sudden shifts in temperature. Growth is slow, taking eight months to a year to reach a table weight of about 6.5 to 11 pounds, and males can top 13 pounds. It suits specialist breeders more than casual backyard keepers.

history_summary.value: One of Britain's oldest chicken breeds, named after the Surrey market town of Dorking and possibly linked to the five-toed fowl described by the Roman writer Columella. It was Britain's leading meat breed until displaced by the Sussex in the early twentieth century, came close to extinction by the Second World War, and was revived when its breed club restarted in 1970.

summary.value: The Dorking is one of the oldest British chickens, named for the market town of Dorking in Surrey, which once sent its birds to London. Some writers link it to five-toed fowl praised in Roman times, and a fifth toe is still its trademark. For centuries it was England's top table bird, known for tender meat, before the Sussex and later the Plymouth Rock took its place. The body is long, deep and set on short legs. Colors include white, silver-gray, colored, red and cuckoo. Under the US standard, roosters weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 7. Hens lay 170 to 190 white or cream eggs, medium to large, and keep laying in winter, but they go broody often and make devoted mothers. Dorkings are calm, gentle and friendly, and may be picked on by pushier breeds. Single combs need frostbite protection in cold areas.

history_summary.value: A true bantam with no large-fowl counterpart, likely descended from Southeast Asian bantams brought home by Dutch East India Company sailors, first documented as a distinct breed in 1882 and recognized by the Dutch national poultry club in 1906. It later spread abroad, reaching the United States in the 1950s and Britain by the late 1960s, and remains popular with hobbyists for its friendly nature and good laying for its size.

summary.value: The Dutch Bantam, or Hollandse Kriel, is a true bantam from the Netherlands, meaning there is no full sized version. Its forebears were probably small Southeast Asian birds carried home by Dutch sailors, and it was first written up as a breed in 1882. It reached the United States in the 1950s and Britain in the late 1960s. It is one of the tiniest breeds, with cocks no more than about 1.2 pounds and hens about 1 pound. The original color was partridge, and many others now exist; Britain standardizes thirteen. Birds have a five point single comb, white earlobes and slate blue legs, and they fly well. Hens lay around 160 small cream or white eggs a year, a lot for a bantam, and go broody readily. They are friendly but a bit flighty and do not like hard cold, and they suit hobby keepers and families.

history_summary.value: Easter Eggers are American hybrids created by breeding a bird carrying the blue-egg gene, descended from Chilean Araucana stock, with brown-egg-laying breeds. They are not recognized as a breed by the American Poultry Association or American Bantam Association, but became popular backyard and hatchery birds for their variable, colorful eggs.

summary.value: The Easter Egger is not a true breed but an American hatchery mix. It comes from crossing a bird that carries the blue egg gene with a brown egg layer, so no poultry standard covers it, and it is sometimes sold as "Americana", which is a different thing from the Ameraucana breed. Birds come in any color, and many have muffs, beards and a small pea comb. Their legs may be gray, yellow or greenish. The big draw is the eggs: shells may be blue, green, olive, brown or even pinkish, and each hen keeps the same shade for life. Hens lay about 200 to 280 medium to large eggs a year and seldom go broody. They are friendly, docile and curious, cope with both hot and cold weather, and make an easy choice for beginners and families.

well suited to hot Mediterranean climates

history_summary.value: The Empordanesa is a Mediterranean egg breed from Catalonia, Spain, bred for hot-climate hardiness and known for laying unusually dark, terracotta-to-chocolate-brown eggs.

summary.value: The Empordanesa is a Spanish chicken from the Emporda area of Catalonia, in the far northeast of the country. It is a Mediterranean laying breed that copes well with hot weather. Its best known feature is the egg, which ranges from a warm reddish terracotta to a deep chocolate brown, far darker than most brown eggs. Hens lay roughly 160 to 180 eggs a year, and improved lines can reach about 220, with each egg weighing around 60 grams. Reported sizes vary: roosters weigh from about 5.5 to 7.5 pounds and hens from about 4 to 5.5 pounds. The comb is unusual. It starts as a normal single comb in front but splits into several points at the back, so it looks like a small crown. Red, white, buff and partridge colors are kept. The breed nearly vanished in the twentieth century and was rebuilt from farm flocks starting in 1982.

history_summary.value: Created between 1959 and 1965 at an experimental poultry station in Rovigo, Veneto, by crossing Rhode Island Red and Sussex stock, it resembles a Light Sussex but has the yellow skin and legs favored by Italian consumers. It remains a rare regional breed with only a few hundred breeding birds, now conserved as part of a Veneto biodiversity project.

summary.value: The Ermellinata di Rovigo is a modern dual purpose chicken from Rovigo in the Veneto region of northeast Italy. Breeders at the local poultry research station made it between 1959 and 1965 from Sussex and Rhode Island Red birds. It looks much like a Light Sussex: a white body with black neck feathers, wing tips and tail. Unlike the Sussex, it has yellow skin and yellow legs, which Italian meat buyers prefer. The comb is a large single comb with five or six points, and the earlobes are red. Roosters weigh about 7 to 8.5 pounds and hens about 5 to 6.5 pounds. Hens lay some 170 to 190 pinkish brown eggs a year, each around 55 to 60 grams. Young birds grow quickly, and the hens are used to breed chicks that can be sexed by color. The breed is rare and is kept under a regional conservation program.

history_summary.value: A French regional variant of the Langshan breed, descended from birds imported to England from China in 1872 and later raised around Estaires in the Nord-Pas-de-Calais region. A breeders' club was formed in 1999, and the breed has been under regional genetic conservation protection since 2004.

summary.value: The Estaires, or Poule d'Estaires, is a French farm chicken from the far north of the country, named after the town of Estaires near Lille. Its roots lie in the Langshan, a Chinese breed that reached England in 1872 and spread to mainland Europe soon after. Farmers around Estaires, La Gorgue, Laventie and Merville raised these birds and sold them to the Lille market, and local fowl and the northern French game bird may also have played a part. The breed faded after the Second World War and has since been rebuilt by breeders in the region, with a club founded in 1999 and regional genetic protection since 2004. It looks much like a Croad Langshan: glossy black with a green sheen, a small evenly toothed comb and dark slate legs with light feathering. Gold and silver necked forms also exist. It is raised mainly for meat.

much meat production is capons, without chemical castration
added to the Slow Food Ark of Taste in 2008

history_summary.value: The traditional dual-purpose farm chicken of the Basque Country, it survived early competition from white-egg commercial hybrids because local consumers preferred brown eggs, but later declined once brown-egg hybrids appeared. Conservation breeding began in 1975, and it gained an official Spanish breed standard in 2001.

summary.value: The Euskal Oiloa, or Basque hen, is the old farmyard chicken of the Basque Country in northern Spain. It is a hardy dual purpose bird of the Atlantic type, so unlike the Mediterranean breeds of Spain it has yellow legs, red earlobes and brown eggs. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 5.5 pounds. Its single comb carries five to seven sharp points, and its skin is yellow. Five colors are recognized: black, red, golden cuckoo, black tailed white, and a red brown naked neck type. Hens lay roughly 209 to 220 brown eggs a year, each around 60 grams. Many males are raised as capons for the table. The breed lost ground to commercial brown egg hybrids, and a conservation program began in 1975. Spain approved its official standard in 2001 and lists it as a breed at risk.

history_summary.value: Developed in the 1860s near the villages of Houdan and Faverolles in north-central France from a mix of breeds including the Houdan, Dorking, Brahma and Malines, it became a leading supplier of eggs and meat to the Paris market by the early 1900s. It reached Britain in the mid-1890s and the United States around 1901, and while it is now kept mainly for exhibition and as a pet for its gentle nature, it remains a good dual-purpose layer.

summary.value: The Faverolles is a French chicken named after a village southwest of Paris. Breeders built it in the 1800s by crossing the Houdan, Dorking, Brahma and other birds, aiming for a fowl that gave both meat and winter eggs for the Paris market. It has a beard, muffs, feathered legs and an unusual fifth toe on each foot. Salmon is the best known color, and white is also accepted in the US. Under the American standard, cocks weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6.5. A hen lays roughly 150 to 200 tinted or light brown eggs a year, medium to large, and keeps going in winter. The birds are gentle and so docile that pushier breeds may pick on them. They handle cold well but not heat, and they make good pets for families and first time keepers.

history_summary.value: An ancient Egyptian breed from the Fayoum region south-west of Cairo, valued for its hardiness and believed disease resistance; some stock was imported to the United States in the 1940s and crossbred with American chickens, and it reached the United Kingdom in 1984. It remains outside the American Poultry Association's standard but is popular for hot climates and free-range keeping.

summary.value: The Fayoumi is an old Egyptian chicken named for the Fayoum area southwest of Cairo. It is a small, light bird: roosters weigh about 4 pounds and hens about 3 pounds. Two colors are kept, silver penciled and gold penciled, and every chick hatches brown whatever its adult color. The comb is single and bright red. Hens mature very fast and can start laying at around four to five months. Their eggs are small and white to cream, they come in good numbers, and young hens seldom go broody. Fayoumis are lively and very flighty, fly well, like to roost in trees and complain loudly when picked up, so they rarely become pets. In return they are tough, forage well and need little feed. They handle hot climates well and suit free range keepers more than beginners who want a lap chicken.

history_summary.value: An old Dutch breed from the isolated Friesland coastal region, related to several other northern Dutch breeds, it was overtaken as an egg-layer by more productive breeds such as the Leghorn and Rhode Island Red from the early twentieth century. Numbers fell further during the First World War, but a Dutch breed society formed in 1922 helped preserve it, and it later gained followings in Germany and the UK.

summary.value: The Friesian is an old Dutch chicken from Friesland, a once isolated stretch of the North Sea coast in the northern Netherlands. It is a small, light breed: roosters weigh about 3.3 to 3.5 pounds and hens about 2.6 to 3 pounds, so large fowl are sometimes mistaken for bantams at shows. Bantams exist too and are tiny. The bird stands fairly upright with its tail carried high. It has a small single comb, white earlobes and big orange eyes. Many colors are recognized in Europe, and penciled forms in chamois, gold and silver are the most common in Britain. Hens lay about 150 to 200 small white eggs a year and seldom go broody. Friesians are active, flighty and fly well. They are hardy foragers that find much of their own food, which makes them a good fit for free range flocks.

value: poor heat retention, struggles in cold climates

history_summary.value: A breed defined by its curled plumage, from a frizzle gene believed to have arisen in Asia and reported there since the eighteenth century. Selective breeding for exhibition turned it into a distinct breed recognised in nine European countries and Australia, though in the United States frizzled birds are judged as a feather type within their own breed rather than as a separate breed.

summary.value: The Frizzle is a chicken whose feathers curl outward and forward toward the head instead of lying flat, giving it a ruffled, windswept look. The curl comes from a single gene that most likely arose in Asia, and curled birds were noted in Europe by the late 1600s. Several European countries and Australia treat the Frizzle as its own breed, while in the United States frizzling counts as a feather type found in breeds such as Cochins, Polish and Silkies. Birds have a single comb, clean legs and come in many colors, and bantams are more common than large fowl. Hens lay white or tinted eggs. They are gentle birds, mostly kept for showing. The curled feathers hold little warmth and the birds cannot fly, so they need shelter in cold weather and low perches. They suit exhibitors and keepers who want an unusual, friendly bird.

value: white feathers, red comb and wattles, yellow beak and feet
prized for exceptional meat quality from specific feeding techniques

history_summary.value: The Gallina di Saluzzo, meaning 'the white hen of Saluzzo', is a rustic dual-purpose breed from the Piedmont region of Italy, once common on small family farms and nearly lost to intensive agriculture before recovery efforts began in 1999.

summary.value: The Gallina di Saluzzo, also called the Bianca di Saluzzo, is an old farm chicken from Piedmont in northern Italy. Its name means the white hen of Saluzzo. It was once kept on many small farms in the region, then almost vanished as factory poultry took over. A farm school near Cuneo began bringing it back in 1999. The bird is fully white with a red single comb and wattles, and a yellow beak, legs and skin. It is a small to medium bird: cocks weigh about 5.5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4.5 pounds. Hens start laying at six or seven months and give around 180 white eggs a year, mostly in spring and summer. Locally the breed is valued above all for its meat, sold as young birds and as Christmas capons. It is a hardy bird that forages well on open ground.

origin_year_or_period.value: developed from Croad Langshan stock imported in 1879, completed by the early 20th century

value: "wine glass" profile from long legs and upright posture

history_summary.value: Developed in Germany from Croad Langshan stock imported in 1879, with some Minorca and Plymouth Rock influence, it became a distinct, tall, brown-tinted breed completed by the early twentieth century and given its own breed club in 1895. It is mostly kept for exhibition today, and the bantam version is more popular than the standard size in Britain.

summary.value: The German Langshan is a tall, heavy chicken that German breeders built from Croad Langshans brought over from England in 1879, with Plymouth Rock and other blood added along the way. A breed club formed in 1895. Seen from the side, the bird has a high head, a curved back and a raised tail, a shape often compared to a wine glass. Unlike the Croad, its legs carry no feathers. Black, blue and white are the usual colors. Cocks weigh about 6.5 to 10 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 7.5 pounds, and the weight keeps them from flying much. Hens lay roughly 150 to 200 fairly large, tinted eggs a year. Chicks grow fast, and the adults tame without much trouble. Today the breed is kept mostly for shows, and in Britain the bantam is far more common than the large fowl.

history_summary.value: Developed by Karnataka Veterinary, Animal and Fisheries Sciences University in Bengaluru by crossing purebred exotic lines to resemble native desi birds. It is a dual-purpose breed suited to backyard and free-range farming, growing faster than local varieties while still needing little special care.

summary.value: Giriraja is a modern Indian chicken bred at the Karnataka veterinary university in Bengaluru. Scientists crossed pure exotic lines to get a bird that looks and lives like a village desi chicken but grows and lays better. It is a dual purpose bird. By six months, hens reach about 6.5 pounds and cocks about 9 pounds. Hens lay around 180 to 190 brown eggs a year, each about 52 to 55 grams. The shells are thicker than those of shop eggs, so they crack less, and most eggs hatch, which lets farmers breed their own replacements. The birds forage well on insects, greens and kitchen scraps, need little special care and can range freely. They resist most common diseases, though not Newcastle disease. The breed is aimed at backyard and small mixed farms, where a flock of five hens and one cock is typical.

origin_country.value: United States (developed by the Hubbard hatchery)

history_summary.value: A commercial sex-linked hybrid created by crossing a White Rock or Rhode Island White hen with a New Hampshire Red rooster, originated by the Hubbard hatchery. It is not recognized as a true breed by the American Poultry Association because it is a crossbreed, and while prized for very high egg production, its productive lifespan is short, typically two to three years.

summary.value: The Golden Comet is a sex-linked hybrid layer, not a true breed, first produced by the Hubbard hatchery in the United States. It comes from mating a New Hampshire Red rooster with a White Rock or Rhode Island White hen, and chicks can be sexed by color at hatch. It is sold under many names, including Red Star, Golden Buff and Cinnamon Queen. Hens are reddish brown to gold, with a single red comb and yellow, clean legs. They can start laying at about 16 weeks and give roughly 260 to 330 brown eggs a year, but output drops after about two years, and they rarely go broody. Golden Comets are calm, friendly and easy to handle. They manage both cold and hot weather if given shade and water, though the comb can frostbite. They suit beginners who mainly want eggs.

value: evenly mottled black-and-white feathers, orange eyes, thick beak
reduced to near-extinction in the World Wars, revived by local enthusiasts in the early 2000s to roughly 15,000 birds

history_summary.value: The Gournay is an old breed from Upper Normandy, France, with possible ancestry dating to the Viking era. It nearly went extinct during the World Wars and was revived by dedicated enthusiasts starting in the early 2000s.

summary.value: The Gournay is an old farm chicken from upper Normandy in northern France, named after the market town of Gournay-en-Bray. Its roots may go back a very long way, possibly to Viking times. The two World Wars left it close to extinction, and local breeders rebuilt the flocks from the early 2000s. The plumage is black with even white flecks, the only color allowed, set off by a red single comb, white earlobes, orange eyes and a stout beak. Cocks weigh about 5.5 to 7 pounds and hens about 4.5 to 5 pounds, and a bantam form exists. Hens lay about three white eggs a week, and the eggs are big. They are gentle birds that do go broody. The French value the breed for both its tasty meat and its eggs, which makes it a good all round farmyard bird.

history_summary.value: An old Polish breed identified by its unusual green legs, first described in 1879 and officially recognised in 1923; it was once raised across roughly 70 percent of Poland but declined sharply once it failed to adapt to intensive farming. It was used between 1946 and 1954 to help create the autosexing Polbar breed, and today survives only in two small closed conservation flocks.

summary.value: Named for its pale green shanks, the Green-legged Partridge is a traditional farm chicken from Poland. It was first written up in the late 1800s and got a Polish standard in the early 1920s. Hens wear brown partridge feathering, while cocks show a gold head and hackle, an orange saddle and a black breast and tail with a green sheen. It is a light bird: cocks weigh about 5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4 to 5 pounds. Hens mature at six months and lay roughly 140 to 180 eggs a year, a modest total, and the yolks are low in cholesterol. Meat and eggs both taste good. The breed thrives on free range, forages well and resists disease, but it stresses when crowded and may pull feathers. It was once common across Poland and is now held mainly in conservation flocks.

history_summary.value: A Vietnamese local chicken breed originating in Bac Ninh Province, one of several traditional Vietnamese chicken varieties alongside breeds such as the ga Ri, ga Dong Tao and ga Mia.

summary.value: The Ho chicken, called ga Ho in Vietnamese, is a rare native breed from Bac Ninh Province in the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam. Most birds are kept in and around one village community near the town of Thuan Thanh. It is a big, heavy bird for a local Asian breed, with thick, short legs and a large frame. Cocks stand tall with a broad chest and weigh about 10 to 12 pounds, while hens weigh about 8 to 9 pounds. Cocks are either glossy greenish black or deep plum red, and hens come in muted clay, sparrow and dried longan shades. The comb is small, red and shaped a little like a strawberry. Because the hens are so heavy and slow, they make clumsy sitters and hatch few chicks. The breed is raised for prized meat and as a hobby bird, and local shows are held each spring.

history_summary.value: An old breed of uncertain origin, found in Holland by the fourteenth century and later refined further in England, taking its modern name in the 1840s. Once valued for egg production, it lost favor after the Leghorn arrived around 1890 and today survives mainly as an active, ornamental exhibition breed.

summary.value: Despite its German name, the Hamburg is an old Dutch breed, known in Holland by the 1300s and further developed in northern England, where it was once called the Pheasant Fowl. It is small and trim, with a red rose comb ending in a long spike, white earlobes and slate gray legs. Colors include silver spangled, the most popular, plus gold spangled, silver and gold penciled, black and white. Roosters weigh about 5 pounds and hens about 4. Hens lay 120 to 225 small to medium white eggs a year, start at four to five months and keep laying well for several years, but they do not go broody. Hamburgs are very active, alert and flighty, fly well and like to roost high in trees. They handle both hot and cold weather, dislike confinement, and are show and egg birds rather than pets for children.

history_summary.value: The Holland was developed at Rutgers Breeding Farms in New Jersey by crossing chickens imported from Holland with White Leghorns, Rhode Island Reds, New Hampshires and Lamonas, producing White and Barred varieties accepted by the APA in 1949. It remains one of the rarest American breeds.

summary.value: The Holland is an American chicken created at Rutgers Breeding Farms in New Jersey in the 1930s. At the time, buyers paid more for white eggs, but most farm breeds laid brown ones, so the goal was a meaty farm bird that laid white eggs. Breeders crossed stock from Holland with Leghorns, Rhode Island Reds and other breeds, and the APA accepted it in 1949. It comes in barred and white, and the white may now be gone. The skin and legs are yellow and the single comb is bright red. Hens lay about 200 to 240 white, medium to large eggs a year. The APA standard calls for an 8.5 pound cock and a 6.5 pound hen. Hollands are calm, quiet and friendly, forage well and handle cold, though cocks can get frostbitten combs. They suit homesteads and families but dislike tight confinement. It is one of the rarest American breeds.

history_summary.value: A traditional French breed named for the town of Houdan west of Paris, likely developed from old five-toed French fowl combined with crested birds from Caux, Normandy, and refined in the 1800s with Crevecoeur and Dorking blood. Once one of France's leading meat breeds, it declined through the twentieth century and is now an endangered breed kept mainly for exhibition.

summary.value: The Houdan is an old French chicken named after the town of Houdan, west of Paris. It stands out for its full crest, beard and muffs, a small comb shaped like a leaf or a V, and five toes on each foot instead of four. Most birds are mottled, black spotted with white, and American breeders later added a white form. In the 1800s it ranked among the leading meat breeds of France, and today it is rare and kept mostly for shows. Under the American standard, cocks weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6.5 pounds, while European birds run lighter. Hens lay around 140 to 230 white eggs a year. Houdans are calm, gentle birds that children can handle easily. They like warm, dry weather, but wet crests can freeze in winter, and a large crest can block a bird's view of predators.

history_summary.value: A Croatian breed developed in 1917 by Ivan Lakus in the village of Torcec in the Podravina region, now widespread across Croatia and the wider Balkans.

summary.value: The Hrvatica is a Croatian farm chicken. It was bred in 1917 by Ivan Lakus at Torcec, a Podravina village, starting from local hens and crossing them with Leghorn cocks. White birds were culled, leaving black, red, brown and speckled birds, and Welsummer blood later set the final type. Today it is kept across Croatia and much of the Balkans. It is a solid dual purpose bird: cocks weigh about 7.5 to 9 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. With good feed and care, hens can lay more than 200 eggs a year. The meat is well regarded, especially from birds with access to green feed. Hens still go broody readily and are careful mothers, which is now rare in chickens. The breed resists disease and breeds well, making it a practical choice for small farms that want to hatch their own chicks.

history_summary.value: A landrace fowl brought to Iceland by Norse settlers around the ninth or tenth century and kept largely unchanged for a thousand years, until commercial strains crossed into the population in the 1930s threatened its purity. Conservation efforts from the 1970s preserved pure lines, and DNA studies later showed the breed carries unusually high genetic diversity not found in any other chicken breed.

summary.value: The Icelandic chicken is a landrace that Norse settlers carried to Iceland around a thousand years ago. For centuries it was the only chicken on the island, chosen for thrift and good mothering rather than for looks, so there is no fixed standard. A flock shows almost every color and pattern, several comb types, and some birds wear a small crest, but true Icelandics never have feathered legs. They are small birds: cocks weigh about 4.5 to 5.25 pounds and hens 3 to 3.5. Hens lay around 180 white to cream eggs a year, small to medium in size, and keep laying through winter. Many hens go broody and raise their own chicks. The birds are lively and curious, turn friendly when handled young, fly well and forage hard. They are very hardy in cold, harsh weather and suit free range homesteads and beginners, though not a closed pen.

foundation breed of the commercial Cornish Rock broiler cross
thin, hard feathers with no down, susceptible to cold

history_summary.value: Developed around 1820 in Cornwall, England, by Sir Walter Gilbert crossing game breeds such as the Aseel and Old English Game, it failed as a fighting bird but proved an excellent meat breed thanks to its unusually broad breast. Renamed Cornish in the United States in 1910, it became the foundation of the modern Cornish Rock broiler that dominates commercial chicken production worldwide.

summary.value: The Indian Game, known in the United States as the Cornish, was bred in Cornwall in southwest England around 1820. Sir Walter Gilbert crossed Asil and English game birds hoping for a fighting cock, but the result had no taste for fighting. Instead it proved to be a superb meat bird. It is short legged, wide set and packed with breast muscle, with tight, hard feathers that carry almost no down. Cocks weigh about 10.5 pounds and hens about 8 pounds, though the close feathering makes them look smaller. Hens are poor layers, giving perhaps 80 small, light brown eggs a year. Most birds are calm, but hens push to the top of the pecking order and some cocks turn aggressive. The thin feathering leaves them poorly suited to harsh cold or heat. The white strain became a parent of the modern broiler and of the small game hen sold in stores.

roosters are notably good hawk fighters and flock guardians

history_summary.value: A rare American dual-purpose breed of uncertain origin from near Decorah, Iowa, in the early twentieth century, surrounded by an improbable folk legend involving a pheasant sire. Never officially recognized by any poultry association, it nearly disappeared once Iowa hatcheries stopped selling it, but has been kept going by a small group of dedicated breeders.

summary.value: The Iowa Blue is a rare American dual-purpose chicken that first turned up near Decorah, Iowa, in the early 1900s. Its true origin is unknown, and the local story that a pheasant fathered the first chicks cannot be true, since pheasants and chickens do not interbreed. Despite the name, the birds are not blue: they have a silvery white head and a dark body with white penciling, plus a single comb and red earlobes. Roosters weigh about 7 pounds and hens about 6. Hens lay a fair number of brown eggs and often go broody and raise chicks well. The birds are fairly docile, though some are a bit skittish, and they forage well on free range. Roosters are known as bold guards against hawks. The breed nearly died out after Iowa hatcheries dropped it and has never been accepted into a show standard, so it suits homesteaders who want a working bird.

origin_country.value: France (developed by Institut de Selection Animale)

history_summary.value: A commercial sex-linked hybrid developed in 1978 by the French company Institut de Selection Animale for battery egg production, bred from a closely guarded mix of breeds including Rhode Island Red and Rhode Island White stock. It is prized for laying about 300 eggs in its first year, and the company behind it later merged into what became Hendrix Genetics.

summary.value: The ISA Brown is a commercial hybrid layer, not a breed. The French firm Institut de Selection Animale created it in 1978 for large egg farms, and the company is now part of Hendrix Genetics. The exact recipe is kept secret, but Rhode Island Red and Rhode Island White stock are thought to be in the mix. The cross is sex-linked, so chicks can be sorted by color at hatch. Hens are small, about 4.3 pounds, and a flock reaches half production at about 21 weeks. A hen lays roughly 300 brown eggs in her first year, and the breeder reports close to 480 over a full commercial cycle to 100 weeks. The eggs average about 62 grams, which is a US large. The breeder says the hens adapt to many climates and housing systems.

value: the only single-combed breed known to lay green eggs
roosters have deep blue body feathers and shimmering metallic hackles; splash patterns are also common

history_summary.value: The Isbar was developed in 1950s Sweden by Martin Silverudd, who aimed to create autosexing breeds that lay unusually colored eggs in volume. It is the only single-combed breed known to lay green eggs.

summary.value: Now more often called the Silverudd Blue, the Isbar (said like ice-bar) is a scarce chicken from Sweden. Martin Silverudd, a monk and poultry breeder in Smaland in southern Sweden, worked on it from the 1950s. He wanted hens that laid plenty of eggs in unusual colors. Its main roots are New Hampshire and Rhode Island Red, with Cream Legbar crosses bringing in the colored shell. Hens lay about 200 eggs a year in shades of green, sometimes with brown speckles, and each egg weighs about 50 to 65 grams. It is a single-combed bird. Most are blue, with black and splash birds also common, and cocks show bright metallic neck feathers. Because Silverudd died in 1986 before the work was finished, birds still vary in size and egg shade. They handle cold weather well and forage actively, which suits small farms in cool climates.

value: pea comb and small wattles aid cold hardiness

history_summary.value: Created in 1932 by Reginald Appleyard in the Suffolk village of Ixworth from white Sussex, Minorca, Orpington and Indian Game stock, it was bred as a fast-growing, high-quality dual-purpose table bird. It nearly disappeared in the 1970s and remains a rare, endangered breed today, valued for meat that commands premium prices.

summary.value: The Ixworth is an all-white English chicken made in 1932 by Reginald Appleyard, the breeder behind the Silver Appleyard duck, at his farm in Ixworth, Suffolk. He crossed white Sussex, white Orpington, white Minorca and several kinds of Indian Game to get a quick-growing table bird that still laid well. The bird is stocky, with white feathers, white legs and skin, a bright red pea comb and tiny wattles, so frostbite is rarely a problem and it copes well with cold. Cocks weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 7 pounds. Hens lay around 160 to 200 tinted eggs a year. Birds are alert and active and forage well. The breed nearly died out in the 1970s and is still rare, kept by a small band of fans. It suits smallholders who want both good meat and a fair supply of eggs.

history_summary.value: The only chicken breed indigenous to Norway, historically the country's principal breed until foreign imports began in the nineteenth century. It was refined at a state breeding station in Jaeren between 1916 and 1973, work that made it autosexing, and it is now recognized as a conservation-worthy national breed.

summary.value: The Jaerhons is Norway's only native chicken breed. It takes its name from Jaeren, a farming district on the southwest coast in Rogaland. It was the main chicken on Norwegian farms until foreign breeds arrived in the 1800s. From 1916 to 1973 a state breeding station at Bryne worked to improve it, and that work made the breed autosexing, so chicks can be sorted by sex at hatching. Two color types are accepted, both mixing brown with yellow, one dark and one light. Birds have a single comb and bright yellow beaks and legs, and a bantam version was approved in 1994. Hens lay about 215 white eggs a year, each at least 55 grams, which is only about a fifth fewer than modern commercial layers. Norway lists it as a national breed worth conserving.

history_summary.value: An ancient Korean heritage breed famous for its extremely long tail feathers, nearly wiped out in the early 1900s by the rise of commercial non-native chicken farming. It survived thanks to one dedicated farmer, and as of 2021 only about 250 birds remained in conservation.

summary.value: The Jangmigye, also called Ginkkori-dak or long-tail chicken, is an old Korean heritage breed kept for its extraordinary tail. A cock's tail can reach about 4.9 feet, longer than many people are tall. The breed is thought to date back to around the middle of the third century. Early in the 1900s, commercial farms stocked with imported breeds pushed it almost to extinction, and it is said that a single stubborn farmer kept a flock going. By 2021 only about 250 birds were held in conservation, and the breed appears on the FAO list of livestock breeds. Unlike the Japanese Onagadori, whose tail keeps growing, the Jangmigye cock sheds and regrows its tail feathers every year after the rainy season. It is kept today as an ornamental and heritage bird rather than for eggs or meat.

history_summary.value: An ancient true bantam breed with no large-fowl counterpart, depicted in Japanese art since the early 1600s and possibly descended from old fighting fowl. It reached Europe and the United States after Japan reopened to foreign trade around the Meiji Restoration in 1868, and it carries a lethal short-leg gene that means it never breeds fully true.

summary.value: The Japanese Bantam, or Chabo, is a tiny ornamental chicken from Japan, where it has appeared in art since the early 1600s and was kept as a living garden ornament. It is a true bantam with no large form. Its look is extreme: very short legs, a big comb and a tall upright tail that rises well above the head. The short legs come from a lethal gene, so a quarter of eggs from two short-legged parents never hatch and another quarter grow normal legs. Hens weigh about 22 ounces and cocks about 26. Hens lay small cream eggs and make excellent broody mothers. Young birds can be jumpy, but they settle with handling and make good pets and 4H show birds. They need solid floors, dry housing and extra warmth in northern winters to protect their combs. Their short legs do little harm to lawns and gardens.

value: foundation breed for the Jersey Giant, Rhode Island Red and Plymouth Rock

history_summary.value: The second-oldest chicken breed developed in the United States, first mentioned in print in 1835 despite its name suggesting Javan origin, and a major foundation breed for the Jersey Giant, Rhode Island Red and Plymouth Rock. It nearly vanished by the late twentieth century but has been revived since the 1990s, notably through conservation work at the Garfield Farm Museum in Illinois, though it remains critically endangered.

summary.value: The Java is one of the oldest American chicken breeds, second only to the Dominique. Its name points to the island of Java, but the breed was developed in the United States from Asian stock and was known here by 1835. It helped create the Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island Red and Jersey Giant. Javas have a long back and deep breast that give them a solid, boxy shape. Black birds show a green sheen, and mottled and white birds also exist. Roosters weigh about 9.5 pounds and hens about 7.5 pounds. Hens lay 150 to 180 large brown eggs a year, keep laying into winter and often go broody. The birds are calm and friendly, which makes them a good choice for families with children. They forage well, handle both cold and heat with basic shelter, and suit homesteads and small farms. The breed is critically rare.

originally bred to replace the turkey as a premium table bird
black variety has a beetle-green sheen
slow growing, takes 8-9 months to reach harvest size

history_summary.value: Created in Burlington County, New Jersey between 1870 and 1890 by John and Thomas Black, who crossed Black Java, Black Langshan and Dark Brahma stock hoping to produce a chicken that could replace the turkey as a premium table bird. It became one of the heaviest chicken breeds and joined the American Poultry Association's standard in 1922, and while it declined with the rise of faster-growing commercial broilers, its conservation status has since improved to recovering.

summary.value: The Jersey Giant is an American chicken bred in Burlington County, New Jersey, between about 1870 and 1890. John and Thomas Black crossed Black Javas, Black Langshans and Dark Brahmas, hoping to make a chicken big enough to stand in for the turkey at the table. It is one of the heaviest breeds alive: mature roosters weigh 13 to 15 pounds and hens 10 to 11. The APA accepts black, white and blue, and the black has a green sheen. Hens lay about 150 to 200 extra large eggs a year, ranging from light cream to dark brown, and keep laying in winter. These are calm, friendly birds that rarely fight. They handle cold well but need shade and cooling in hot weather. Owners need larger nest boxes and low roosts, and meat birds take 8 to 9 months to fill out.

history_summary.value: An Indian breed native to the Dhar and Jhabua districts of Madhya Pradesh, prized for its black meat, which many believe has health benefits, and protected by a geographical indication tag since 2018. Rising demand has driven overconsumption and price scams, prompting a state-backed breeding program to prevent the breed's decline.

summary.value: The Kadaknath is an Indian chicken from the Dhar and Jhabua districts of Madhya Pradesh, where rural and tribal families have long kept it. Its local name, Kali Masi, means the bird with black flesh. Melanin colors almost everything about it grey-black, from the beak, legs, comb and tongue to the meat, bones and blood. Three varieties exist: jet black, golden and pencilled. It is a small bird, with roosters at about 4 to 4.4 pounds and hens at about 2.6 to 3.3 pounds. It is kept mainly for its dark meat, which carries an Indian geographical indication tag granted in 2018. Hens lay small brown eggs with a faint pink tint and seldom sit on them long enough to hatch a brood. Heavy demand has shrunk its numbers, and the state now runs a breeding program to protect it.

value: cocks have unusually long crows lasting up to 60 seconds

history_summary.value: A little-known Indonesian breed from the Solok area of West Sumatra, thought to descend from the red junglefowl and kept above all for the unusually long crow of the cocks, which can last up to 60 seconds.

summary.value: The Kokok Balenggek is a native Indonesian chicken from the Solok area of West Sumatra. It is thought to descend from the red junglefowl and is well adapted to its home hills. Its fame comes from its voice: cocks give a long, drawn-out crow that can last as long as 60 seconds. The birds are sturdy, with fairly long legs, wild-type colored feathers, golden sickle feathers in the tail and large red wattles. Most have a single comb, though some carry a rose comb, and leg color runs from white through yellow to black, with yellow common. Local keepers value it mainly as a hobby and show bird for its crow, but it is also used for eggs and meat and has been studied by researchers. It remains little known outside Indonesia.

history_summary.value: A landrace long-crowing breed that developed in the Drenica region of Kosovo, historically known locally as the Rooster of Drenica. Rarely kept before 2011, it has since spread in popularity across the Balkans and wider Europe thanks to its distinctive, unusually long crow.

summary.value: The Kosovo Longcrower is a landrace chicken from the Drenica area of Kosovo, where Albanian speakers call it the Rooster of Drenica. Few people kept it before 2011, but its unusual voice has since made it popular with breeders across the Balkans and in countries such as Austria, Germany, Poland and Sweden. Cocks start crowing at six or seven months, and a typical crow lasts 20 to 40 seconds, with the best birds holding it for a full minute. The birds are black, with a forward-leaning black crest, a V comb and mostly olive-green or gray legs; cocks may show a few red or gold wing feathers. Cocks weigh about 4.5 to 7 pounds and hens about 3.5 to 4.5 pounds. Hens start laying at eight months, produce around 160 white eggs a year and rarely go broody.

value: "Dobbelung" broad feather lacing in silver/gold birds

history_summary.value: The Kruper is an old German creeper breed from the Bergisches Land, related to two other local breeds with the same short-leg trait. It has become rare, and a genetic reserve of frozen semen was created after a 2013 census found fewer than 400 birds.

summary.value: The Kruper is an old German creeper chicken from the Bergisches Land and Westphalia in western Germany. Creepers are chickens with very short legs, a type written about since the 1500s, and the Kruper's shanks measure only about 3 to 4 inches. The body is long and rounded like a roller, with a single comb, round white earlobes and slate gray legs. Colors include black, white, cuckoo, partridge and two laced patterns found only in the local Berg breeds. Cocks weigh up to about 5 pounds and hens about 3.5 to 4.5 pounds, and a bantam form exists. Hens lay around 180 white eggs a year. The birds are kept for eggs, meat and as a hobby. The breed is gravely endangered in Germany: a 2013 count found fewer than 400 birds, and semen has been frozen as a genetic reserve.

history_summary.value: The Kraienkopp was bred in the late 1800s on the German-Dutch border by crossing local chickens with Malay and later silver duckwing Leghorn stock. It was first exhibited in the Netherlands in 1920 and in Germany in 1925.

summary.value: The Kraienkopp, called Twents Hoen in Dutch, is a rare chicken from the border country between Germany and the Netherlands. Farmers there crossed local hens with Malay and later with silver duckwing Leghorn blood, and the breed made its show debut in 1920 on the Dutch side and in 1925 on the German side. It has yellow skin, a small walnut comb and a slightly fierce Malay look, and comes mostly in silver or gold. Cocks weigh about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds and hens about 4 to 5.5 pounds, and the cocks crow loudly. Hens lay around 150 to 180 off-white eggs a year, keep laying in cold weather and will go broody. Though it looks stern, the bird is generally good-natured. It is active and hardy and forages well, so it does best on free range rather than in a small pen.

origin_year_or_period.value: traced by many authors to the 15th century; first described 1846

history_summary.value: The La Fleche is an old French breed from the Sarthe area, prized historically for fine meat and once exported to the US, Germany and Britain in the 1800s. Numbers collapsed after World War Two and it came close to disappearing in the 1960s-70s before regional conservation efforts began a slow recovery.

summary.value: The La Fleche is a rare French chicken named after the town of La Fleche in the Sarthe, near Le Mans. Its roots are often traced back to the 1400s, and it was long famous for fattened capons and pullets sold in Paris markets. The bird is mostly black, with tight feathers, large red wattles, white earlobes and a comb made of two upright spikes that look like horns. France also recognizes blue-laced, cuckoo, pearl-grey and white. It is heavier than it looks, with roosters near 8 pounds and hens around 6.5 to 7 pounds. Hens lay about 140 to 220 large to extra large white eggs a year, mostly from spring to fall, and they do not go broody. These are active, flighty birds that avoid people and fly well, so they need a high fence. They like warm weather and struggle in the cold, and they are a poor choice as pets.

conservation_status.value: Threatened (Livestock Conservancy); watch/vulnerable in Germany and the Netherlands as of 2024

history_summary.value: The Lakenvelder is an old black-and-white breed from the German-Dutch border area, first recorded in 1727 and shown from 1835. It lost popularity after more productive breeds like the Leghorn arrived in the late 1800s, and is now considered threatened.

summary.value: The Lakenvelder is an old breed from the border country between Germany and the Netherlands, recorded as early as 1727. Its Dutch name suggests a white sheet laid over a dark field, and English speakers call it Shadow on a Sheet. The body is pure white while the head, neck hackle and tail are solid black, set off by slate blue legs and a red single comb. Full markings often appear only after the third molt. It is a small, light bird: roosters weigh about 5 pounds and hens about 4. Hens lay roughly 150 to 200 small to medium white eggs a year and do not go broody. Lakenvelders are active, wary and quick to take flight, much like Leghorns. They forage well, hate close confinement and dislike cold. They are poor pets for children and better for experienced keepers with room to free range.

conservation_status.value: critical / possibly extinct - American Livestock Breeds Conservancy could not find surviving stock in 2013

value: stays tender as meat even after its laying career, unlike most layer breeds

history_summary.value: Harry S. Lamon of the USDA developed the Lamona from 1912 by crossing white Plymouth Rocks, silver-gray Dorkings and white Leghorns to get a good layer that also gave a decent carcass. It was recognized in 1933 but had nearly disappeared by the 1980s.

summary.value: The Lamona is an American chicken bred at the USDA research station in Beltsville, Maryland. Starting in 1912, government poultry scientist Harry Lamon blended three breeds: the white Plymouth Rock, the white Leghorn and the silver-gray Dorking. He wanted a hen that laid well and could still go to the table as a reasonably tender bird once her laying days were over, which most laying breeds cannot do. The APA accepted the Lamona in 1933 and the bantam in 1960. It is a mid-sized bird, heavier than a Leghorn but lighter than a Plymouth Rock or Dorking, with white feathers, yellow skin and a single comb. It lays white eggs yet has red earlobes, an unusual mix. Numbers fell sharply by the 1980s, and by 2013 no flock descended from the original birds could be traced, so the breed may be extinct.

conservation_status.value: rare breed, on the Rare Breed Survival Trust watchlist (not priority)

history_summary.value: The Legbar was bred in the early 1900s by Reginald Punnett and Michael Pease at Cambridge University by crossing Plymouth Rock and Leghorn birds to create an auto-sexing layer. The cream Legbar, which lays blue-green eggs and has a crest, arose later from an accidental cross with Araucana stock.

summary.value: The Legbar is a British egg breed made at Cambridge University by the geneticists Reginald Punnett and Michael Pease, who crossed barred Plymouth Rocks with Brown Leghorns. Its big selling point is autosexing: female chicks hatch with a dark brown stripe down the back, males with a paler, less distinct one, so keepers can tell them apart on day one. There are gold, silver and cream varieties. The cream Legbar, the one most US hatcheries sell, carries Araucana blood, wears a small swept back crest and lays sky blue or pale green eggs. Hens lay roughly 160 to 200 medium eggs a year and seldom go broody. Adults are light birds, about 4.5 to 7.5 pounds under the British standard. Legbars are active, curious and talkative, forage well and do best with room to roam. Their large single comb can get frostbite, so very cold areas need extra care.

history_summary.value: The Leghorn descends from light chickens of rural Tuscany and was exported from the port of Livorno to America in the late 1820s, where it was renamed after the city's English name. White Leghorns went on to become the basis of most commercial white-egg laying hybrids worldwide.

summary.value: The Leghorn is an Italian laying breed from the Tuscan countryside, named after Leghorn, the old English name for the port of Livorno that shipped the first birds to America around 1828. It is a light, upright bird with a large red comb, white earlobes and yellow legs, and the white variety is the most common, though many other colors exist. Roosters weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4.5 in the US standard; British birds run heavier. Hens lay roughly 280 to 300 large white eggs a year, and White Leghorns are the base of most commercial white egg layers. They seldom go broody. Leghorns are busy foragers that fly well and can be flighty and noisy, so they are not ideal as pets for children or for tight suburban lots. They handle both heat and cold.

history_summary.value: The Luikse Vechter was developed in the Liege area of Wallonia in the late 1800s by crossing the older Brugse Vechter fighting breed with Oriental fighting birds to improve its fighting ability. Cockfighting is now illegal in Belgium, so the breed survives mainly through exhibition and cross-border fighting in France.

summary.value: The Luikse Vechter, or Combattant de Liege in French, is a Belgian gamecock from the Liege area of Wallonia. Breeders there developed it in the late 1800s by crossing the older Brugse Vechter with fighting birds of Asian origin. It is a big, powerful bird: the standard asks for cocks of at least 9 pounds, ideally about 11, and hens of at least 7.5 pounds. The face is dark, from purplish red to nearly black, the triple comb is small, wattles are tiny or missing, and the thick legs are slate blue. Its back slopes steeply, unlike the flatter line of the Brugse Vechter. Hens lay tinted eggs. Cockfighting is banned in Belgium, and many birds are now bred only for shows. The breed is endangered, with fewer than 300 birds counted in 2010, and a bantam form also exists.

history_summary.value: The Lyonnaise was developed in Lyon, France, in the 1950s by Etienne Tamburini, but took nearly two decades to be recognized as an official distinct breed.

summary.value: The Lyonnaise is a French chicken created in the Lyon area in the 1950s by Etienne Tamburini. Recognition was slow, and the breed was approved around 1969. It is a light bird with frizzled, glossy black feathers, gray legs, white earlobes and white skin, and the comb is rough and ends in three points. The French standard asks for cocks of about 5.5 pounds and hens of about 3.3 pounds, and there is also a bantam. Hens lay about three medium-sized white to cream eggs a week. The birds are friendly with people, calm and quiet, and they do well on free range. Today it is kept mainly as a fancy breed, and it has become very rare, close to extinction in its home country.

history_summary.value: The Malay Game is an ancient breed from the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, brought to England around 1830 where it became fashionable and was refined by breeders, especially in Devon and Cornwall. It has mostly been used since to add height and vitality when crossed into other Asian fowl breeds, rather than kept as a farm bird.

summary.value: The Malay is an ancient Asian game fowl and one of the tallest chickens, often standing close to 3 feet. Large birds of this type were common from northern India to the Malay Peninsula, and English breeders, mostly in Devon and Cornwall, shaped the breed after imports began around 1830. It has long legs and neck, an upright stance, tight glossy feathers, yellow legs, a small walnut comb and heavy brows that give it a fierce look. Cocks weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 7. Hens are poor, seasonal layers of perhaps 20 to 100 medium brown eggs a year. They mother well, but males can be rough with chicks. Malays are active and quarrelsome and do badly in tight quarters or mixed flocks. They handle heat better than cold. The breed suits experienced keepers and exhibitors, not beginners or children.

history_summary.value: The Malines was created in the Mechelen area of Flanders from the 1850s by crossing local cuckoo-patterned farm chickens with imported Oriental breeds such as Shanghai, Brahma, Langshan and Cochin, for meat quality. It became famous as the "Poulet de Bruxelles" in the early 1900s but declined after World War II as specialised meat breeds took over.

summary.value: The Malines, known in Dutch as the Mechelse Koekoek, is a big Belgian meat chicken from the country around Mechelen, between Antwerp and Brussels. From the 1850s, local cuckoo-barred farm hens were crossed with Shanghai birds from the Antwerp zoo, and later with Brahma, Langshan and Cochin. The result kept the fine local meat on a much larger frame, and the breed was officially recognized in 1898. Along with the Jersey Giant it ranks among the heaviest chickens: cocks reach about 11 pounds and hens about 9. It usually has a single comb and pale, lightly feathered legs, and comes in several colors, cuckoo being the classic. Hens lay about 140 to 160 large tinted eggs a year and are devoted sitters and mothers. Sold as the Poulet de Bruxelles, its white, fine-grained meat was once in high demand. It is rare today.

history_summary.value: The Marans developed around the port town of Marans in south-west France from a mix of local birds, stock brought by British ships, and imported Croad Langshans. It was first exhibited in 1914 and a breed society and standard followed in the early 1930s, with a separate British strain later developed from a different set of crosses.

summary.value: The Marans is a French chicken named after the town of Marans on the Atlantic coast, where local hens were crossed with birds from passing ships and with Croad Langshans. It was first shown in 1914 and reached Britain around 1929. Its fame rests on its eggs: hens lay about 150 to 200 a year, medium to large, with deep chocolate brown shells, and the Black Copper line is known for the darkest. Other common colors include cuckoo, wheaten and white, and some lines carry light feathering on the legs. Hens weigh roughly 6.5 to 8 pounds and roosters 8.5 to 9.5. Marans are calm, quiet and easy to handle, and many hens will sit on eggs. They cope well with cold winters but can suffer in hot weather. They suit beginners and suburban keepers who want a gentle bird and an unusual egg basket.

history_summary.value: The Marsh Daisy was created in Lancashire from the 1880s by crossing Old English Game with Malay hens, then adding Black Hamburg, White Leghorn and Sicilian Buttercup blood, becoming a set breed by 1913. It has always been rare and confined mostly to England, and there is no bantam version.

summary.value: The Marsh Daisy is a rare English chicken from Southport in Lancashire. Breeding began in the 1880s with an Old English Game cock and Malay hens, and Hamburgh, Leghorn and Sicilian Buttercup blood was added later; the type was settled by 1913. The name may come from its marshy home or from its large rose comb, said to look like the sea thrift flower. It has white earlobes and willow green legs, and the usual colors are wheaten, brown, buff and black. It is a light bird: cocks weigh about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds and hens about 4.5 to 5.5. Hens lay around 160 to 210 tinted eggs a year. Birds grow slowly but are hardy once grown, forage well and do best on free range. They are mostly calm but active, can fly and may be flighty. There is no bantam form.

history_summary.value: The Mericanel della Brianza is a small traditional bantam breed from the Brianza area near Milan, bred from local dwarf stock in the early twentieth century. Its breed standard was approved in 1996 and it remains rare, with only a few hundred birds recorded.

summary.value: The Mericanel della Brianza is a true bantam from Lombardy in northern Italy, named for the hilly Brianza district north of Milan. Local farmers seem to have shaped it from small native birds in the early 1900s, and Italy's poultry federation approved a standard in 1996. It is a tiny bird: cocks weigh about 1.5 to 1.8 pounds and hens about 1.3 to 1.5 pounds. It has a single comb with five points, red earlobes and yellow legs, and it comes in several colors, including white, black, silver, gold and pyle. Hens lay roughly 120 to 170 small eggs a year, cream to light brown and about 35 grams each. The breed is still rare, with only a few hundred breeding birds counted, so it mostly suits keepers who want to help preserve an old Italian bantam.

history_summary.value: The international Minorca was developed by the British from local Menorcan chickens during and after Britain's occupation of the island in the 1700s, and became a well-known egg-laying and exhibition breed in Devon and Cornwall. It is now rare on Menorca itself, with conservation programmes underway there since the 2000s.

summary.value: The Minorca takes its name from Menorca, a Spanish island in the Mediterranean, but British breeders shaped the modern show and farm bird, especially in Devon and Cornwall. It reached the United States in 1884. It is the largest of the Mediterranean breeds, with glossy greenish black feathers in the best known variety, a big red comb and large white earlobes. White, buff and rose comb forms also exist. Under the US standard, roosters weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 7.5, though the native Spanish birds are much smaller. Hens lay about 140 to 220 very large white eggs a year, depending on the strain, and do not go broody. Minorcas are active, flighty and hardy foragers that dislike close confinement. They cope well with heat, but their big combs are prone to frostbite. They are not cuddly and are a poor fit for children.

history_summary.value: After cockfighting was banned in Britain in 1849, breeders crossed Old English Game and Malay stock to create a purely ornamental exhibition bird, first called the Game and later the Modern Game. It was refined through the late 1800s into today's tall, upright show type and has never been valued for eggs or meat.

summary.value: The Modern Game is a tall, slender show chicken created in England in the second half of the 1800s. When cockfighting was banned in 1849, fanciers crossed Old English Game with Malay birds and chose for height and hard, close feathering. The result stands very upright on long legs with a long neck and a short flat back, and it can look as if it is on tiptoe. Britain recognizes 13 colors. Under the US standard, cocks weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4.5, though British large fowl run heavier. Hens lay only 50 to 80 small white eggs a year, and some go broody and mother well. The birds are calm, easy to tame and active, but noisy, and they dislike being shut in. Their tight feathers give little protection from cold, so they do best in warm climates. Most are kept for exhibition, often as bantams.

history_summary.value: The Modern Langshan was bred from the Croad Langshan, imported to Britain from northern China in 1872, by selecting for a taller, tighter-feathered bird to distinguish it from the Black Cochin. It was popular for a time but declined through the twentieth century and is now rarely seen.

summary.value: The Modern Langshan is a rare British show chicken that grew out of the Croad Langshan, a black bird Major Croad brought to England from northern China in 1872. Some keepers felt the Croad looked too much like the Black Cochin, so in the 1890s they bred a taller bird with longer legs, tighter feathers and a more upright stance. The result has a lighter, game-like frame and is often likened to the Modern Game. Its legs carry only light feathering. The split led to separate clubs, and the Croad Langshan Club formed in 1904 for the older type. The Modern Langshan is kept for looks and showing; it is not a useful layer or table bird. It faded through the 1930s and barely survived, with fewer than 100 birds recorded in 2002.

history_summary.value: The Mugellese is a traditional small dual-purpose chicken from the Mugello area near Florence, once common both on farms and as a dooryard or balcony pet. It became rare in the later twentieth century and is now being revived, though it is still not an officially recognised Italian breed.

summary.value: The Mugellese is a true bantam from the Mugello valley northeast of Florence, in Tuscany. Its origins are unclear, but it was once a common farm bird and was also kept in town gardens and on balconies. Grandparents often gave a pair to a child old enough to look after them. Numbers fell sharply after 1950, and breeders are now bringing it back, though Italy has not yet approved an official standard. Cocks weigh about 1.8 pounds and hens about 1.5 pounds. Most birds are dark gold partridge, and hens can also be wheaten. Hens lay small ivory eggs and are famous sitters that will go broody through much of the year. The birds are lively and always on the move, and cocks fight other cocks. They are tough, handle both heat and cold, and happily roost in trees.

history_summary.value: The Naked Neck's origins are unclear but it is thought to trace back to Asia and was documented in Transylvania by the late 1800s before being refined in Germany and spread across Europe and the Americas. It became a recognised American breed in 1965 and reached Britain in the 1920s.

summary.value: The Naked Neck, often called the Turken or Transylvanian Naked Neck, is a chicken with a bare band of red skin from the shoulders to the head. It is all chicken; the old idea that it is a turkey cross is a myth. One dominant gene causes the bare neck, and the bird has only about half the usual number of feathers. Its recorded history centers on Transylvania in Romania, and Germany later refined it. The APA accepts black, white, buff and red. Cocks weigh about 8.5 pounds and hens about 6.5. Hens lay light brown eggs of medium size at a fair rate. The breed is kept for both eggs and meat, since the carcass is meaty and quick to pluck. Turkens are calm, friendly and easy to tame, forage well and handle cold better than their looks suggest.

history_summary.value: The Nankin is thought to be one of the oldest true bantam breeds, likely originating in Southeast Asia and present in England since before the 1500s. It gave rise to many later bantam breeds such as the Sebright, and survived partly through its use as a broody hen for hatching game bird eggs, though it is now critically endangered.

summary.value: The Nankin is one of the oldest true bantams, a naturally tiny chicken with no large version. It most likely came from Southeast Asia and was in England by the 1500s, and it helped create later bantams such as the Sebright. Birds are a warm buff or chestnut with black tails, and males are darker with black flight feathers. Combs are either single or rose, and the legs are slate blue. Roosters weigh about 24 ounces and hens about 22. Hens lay some 80 to 100 small creamy white eggs a year and are famous sitters, long used to hatch pheasant, quail and partridge eggs. Nankins are calm and friendly, stay close together as a flock, and make good pets for responsible children. The single comb can get frostbite, so they are a weaker pick for cold northern winters.

history_summary.value: The Indio Gigante was developed in Brazil's Minas Gerais and Goias states in the late 1980s or early 1990s by crossing large gamecock breeds with local caipira farm chickens. Its breed association is seeking official recognition, which would make it Brazil's first native pure chicken breed.

summary.value: The Indio Gigante, Portuguese for Giant Indian, is a Brazilian chicken known above all for its height; it ranks among the tallest chickens anywhere. Breeders in Minas Gerais and Goias, two inland Brazilian states, created it in the late 1980s or early 1990s. They mated big fighting breeds, among them Shamo, Malay and Indian Game, with caipira hens, the hardy mixed farm chickens of rural Brazil. The breed standard sets minimum weights of about 10 pounds for roosters and about 6.5 pounds for hens. A Brazilian breeders' association keeps that standard and is working toward official recognition. If it succeeds, the Indio Gigante would become the first pure chicken breed to come from Brazil. Reliable figures on egg laying and temperament are not yet available, so it is best seen as a large, upright bird for fanciers.

history_summary.value: The New Hampshire Red was bred over about thirty years in the early 1900s by selecting Rhode Island Red stock for faster growth and feathering, without introducing any other breed, and was standardised in 1935. It became important to the region's poultry industry and was named New Hampshire's official state poultry in 2018.

summary.value: The New Hampshire, often called the New Hampshire Red, is an American chicken bred from Rhode Island Reds in the early 1900s. Farmers and researchers in New Hampshire picked birds that grew, feathered and matured faster, and the APA accepted the breed in 1935. It is lighter red than its parent stock, with black in the tail and wings, and the sun can fade it further. Roosters weigh about 8.5 pounds and hens about 6.5. Hens lay around 200 to 220 large brown eggs a year, and many go broody and raise chicks well. The breed serves for both meat and eggs and suits pasture flocks. Temperament depends on the line: some birds are gentle, others pushy toward calmer breeds. It handles cold winters well and copes with warm areas given good housing. It is the official state poultry of New Hampshire.

history_summary.value: The Niederrheiner was created in western Germany's Lower Rhine region before World War Two by crossing the Dutch North Holland Blue with various other heavy and light breeds, gaining official recognition in 1943. It is now an endangered breed with roughly 1,600 birds recorded in 2021.

summary.value: The Niederrheiner is a German chicken from the Lower Rhine region near the Dutch border. Breeders created it in the years before World War Two by crossing the North Holland Blue with several heavy and light breeds, and Germany recognized it in 1943. It looks much like the North Holland Blue but has bare legs. Recognized colors include birchen, crele, silver and two cuckoo patterns, lemon and blue, and a bantam version exists. Roosters weigh about 7.5 to 9 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. The bird grows fast and has white skin and fine white meat, and hens lay around 200 cream to light brown eggs a year of about 55 grams. Niederrheiners are docile and seldom fly, but hens rarely go broody. The breed is endangered, with about 1,660 breeding birds counted in 2021.

history_summary.value: The Norfolk Grey was created by Frederick Myhill near Norwich around 1910, originally under the name Black Maria, likely from Birchen Game and Duckwing Leghorn stock. It nearly disappeared in the early 1970s and was revived from a single small flock found in 1974.

summary.value: The Norfolk Grey is a rare English utility chicken bred by Frederick Myhill near Norwich around 1910. He first called it the Black Maria, and it most likely came from Birchen Game and Duckwing Leghorn crosses. His flock mixed with other birds while he served in World War One, so he had to rebuild the strain, and he renamed it Norfolk Grey in 1925. The breed almost vanished in the 1970s until a flock of four birds turned up in 1974. It is black with a silver hackle striped in black, a single comb and slate legs. Roosters weigh 7 to 8 pounds and hens 5 to 6 pounds, lighter than most heavy breeds. Hens lay about 150 to 220 medium, pale brown eggs a year and keep laying through winter. The birds forage well on free range, and slow grown cockerels give a gamey roast.
