history_summary.value: The North Holland Blue was developed around Purmerend, Netherlands, about 1900 by crossing imported Malines chickens with local stock to meet demand for white chicken meat in Amsterdam. It was a major Dutch commercial meat breed until faster-growing American breeds took over after World War Two.

summary.value: The North Holland Blue is a heavy Dutch meat chicken bred around Purmerend, north of Amsterdam, in about 1900. Farmers crossed Belgian Malines birds with hardier local hens to feed the city's demand for white chicken meat. After World War Two faster American meat breeds pushed it aside, and the last big farm closed in 1977. It comes in one color, cuckoo, and males are paler than females. Dutch birds have clean legs, while the British standard asks for lightly feathered shanks. Roosters weigh about 7.5 to 9 pounds and hens about 6 to 7 pounds. Hens lay roughly 180 to 240 tinted eggs a year. The breed is quiet and docile, grows quickly, and is valued for firm, high quality meat. Hens crossed with suitable males give sex-linked chicks, and a bantam form exists.

history_summary.value: The Jaerhon was Norway's principal chicken breed until foreign imports began in the 19th century. It was selectively bred at a state-controlled station at Bryne from 1916 to 1973 and is now recognized as autosexing and a national conservation breed.

summary.value: The Jaerhon is Norway's only native chicken breed, named for the Jaeren district in Rogaland on the southwest coast. It was the country's main farm chicken until foreign breeds arrived in the 1800s. From 1916 to 1973 a state breeding station at Bryne kept and selected the breed, and that work made it autosexing, so chicks can be sorted by sex from their down color at hatch. Two color varieties are recognized, dark brown with yellow and light brown with yellow. Birds have a single comb and bright yellow beak and legs. It is a light layer type: roosters weigh about 5.5 pounds and hens about 3.3 pounds. Hens lay around 215 white eggs a year, each at least 55 grams. A bantam version was approved in 1994, and Norway treats the breed as a national conservation priority.

history_summary.value: The Ohiki is a Japanese true bantam from Kochi Prefecture, thought to have arisen during the Edo period from crossing long-tailed breeds such as the Onagadori with small bantams such as the Chabo. It was declared a Natural Monument of Japan in 1923 and was not bred in Britain until the 1990s.

summary.value: The Ohiki is a small Japanese show chicken from Kochi Prefecture on the island of Shikoku. Its name means roughly tail dragging, and that is its signature: older roosters grow tail feathers so long they trail along the ground. It is a true bantam with no large version. Breeders probably made it in the 1800s by crossing long-tailed birds such as the Onagadori with little bantams like the Chabo. The bird has short legs and a round body. Japan named it a Natural Monument in 1923. Japan recognizes white plus two black-breasted colors, red and silver, while the British standard lists white, black-red and the gold and silver duckwings. It reached British breeders only in the 1990s and remains rare in Europe, kept mainly by exhibitors who can give a long-tailed rooster the care it needs.

history_summary.value: The Old English Game descends from ancient fighting cocks brought to England by the Romans and changed little in appearance for centuries while bred for the cockpit. Since cockfighting was banned in 1849 it has been kept purely for exhibition, retaining its compact, muscular, hard-feathered build.

summary.value: The Old English Game is an ancient British fowl whose ancestors were fighting cocks brought over in Roman times. After cockfighting was outlawed in 1849, breeders turned to showing it, and the British clubs later split it into the Carlisle and Oxford types. It is a small, upright bird with a broad chest, tight glossy feathers and a large tail, and it comes in many colors. American birds weigh about 4 pounds for males and 3.5 for females. Hens lay small white or lightly tinted eggs, anywhere from about 40 to 160 a year depending on strain, and they go broody and guard chicks fiercely. The birds are active, noisy and flighty, fly well, and fight other roosters. They handle cold but not heat and can live 15 years. They suit experienced keepers and exhibitors rather than beginners or children.

history_summary.value: The Old English Pheasant Fowl is an old utility breed from rural Yorkshire and Lancashire, named for its pheasant-like plumage and formally named with a breed club in 1914. It is thought to be one of the ancestors of the Hamburg and remains rare today.

summary.value: The Old English Pheasant Fowl is a light utility chicken from the farms of northern England, chiefly Yorkshire and Lancashire, with roots in Cumberland and Westmorland too. It is a very old breed, known earlier as the Yorkshire Pheasant, Golden Pheasant or Old-fashioned Pheasant, and it got its present name and a breed club around 1914. Some think it helped give rise to the Hamburg. Its mahogany feathers edged with darker lacing recall a wild pheasant. It has a rose comb and white earlobes. Roosters weigh about 6 to 7 pounds and hens about 5 to 6 pounds. Hens lay white eggs, around 160 a year, and the birds carry a meaty breast for a light breed. They are hardy and thrive on free range, which made them a farm favorite. Today the breed is rare.

history_summary.value: Olive Eggers are a hybrid, not a recognized breed, created deliberately by backyard and hatchery breeders who cross a dark-brown-egg breed with a blue-egg breed so the offspring's blue and brown eggshell pigments combine into an olive-green shell.

summary.value: The Olive Egger is a crossbred chicken, not a standard breed. Breeders make it by pairing a bird from a line that lays dark brown eggs with a bird from a line that lays blue eggs. The brown pigment coats the blue shell, and the result is an egg in some shade of olive green. Because the parents can be many different breeds, no two flocks look quite the same, and both the feather colors and the exact egg shade vary from bird to bird. Hens usually start laying at about five to six months old and give around 150 to 200 eggs a year. The main reason people keep Olive Eggers is to add green eggs to a mixed basket. They suit backyard keepers who enjoy variety and do not need birds that match a show standard.

history_summary.value: The Onagadori was bred in the 1600s in what is now Kochi Prefecture from other long-tailed Japanese breeds, prized purely for its extraordinary, continuously growing tail. It was named a Special Natural Treasure of Japan in 1952 and is now endangered, kept by only a small number of dedicated breeders.

summary.value: The Onagadori, whose Japanese name means long-tailed chicken, comes from the old Tosa Province, now Kochi Prefecture on the island of Shikoku. Breeders there created it in the 1600s from other long-tailed Japanese fowl, and it is still raised mainly around Nankoku. Its fame rests on a tail of 16 to 18 feathers that, in the right conditions, never molt and keep growing by roughly 2 to 4 feet a year. Tails pass 5 feet as a matter of course, and a few have been reported at close to 40 feet. Japan recognizes three colors, the oldest being white with a black breast, and British clubs recognize five. The bird has a single comb and white earlobes. It is kept only for ornament, in tall hutches that hold the tail off the ground. Japan named it a Special Natural Treasure in 1952, and only a few hundred birds remain.

history_summary.value: Long thought to be Russian, the Orloff is now believed to have originated in Persia and spread across Europe and Asia by the 1600s, later becoming associated with Russia through the promotion of Count Alexei Orlov in the 1800s. It reached Central Europe in 1884 and Britain in the 1920s, and remains a rare, critically endangered breed in the West today.

summary.value: The Orloff is a tall, tough chicken that began in Gilan province in northern Iran and spread through eastern Europe and Asia by the 1600s. It carries the name of Count Alexei Orlov, who promoted it in Russia, which is why many people call it the Russian Orloff. It reached western Europe in the late 1800s, and German breeders made a bantam by 1925. The bird has a game-like build, a muff and beard, a heavily feathered neck, a tiny comb and very small wattles, so it copes with severe cold. Roosters weigh about 8 to 8.5 pounds and hens about 6.5 pounds. It was kept mostly for meat, and hens are modest layers, giving around 100 small to medium light brown eggs a year, and they seldom go broody. Orloffs are calm and friendly but not pushovers.

history_summary.value: The Orpington was bred in the 1880s by William Cook in Kent by crossing Minorcas, Langshans and Plymouth Rocks, originally intended as a dual-purpose bird laying well while producing good meat. Other breeders soon created larger, showier versions marketed under the same name, and the breed shifted almost entirely to exhibition, while the related Australorp kept the original utility qualities.

summary.value: The Orpington is a big, soft-feathered English breed. William Cook developed it on his farm at Orpington, Kent, during the 1880s. Using Minorca, Langshan and Plymouth Rock blood, he set out to make a useful farm bird that laid well and dressed out with the white skin British buyers liked. The first birds were black, and buff, white, blue, jubilee and other colors followed. Other breeders soon made larger, fluffier show strains, and in Britain the breed is now mostly exhibited. Roosters weigh about 10 pounds and hens about 8. Hens lay around 180 to 200 light brown eggs a year. Orpingtons are calm and friendly, and the Buff in particular is known as a gentle family pet. There is also a bantam form. The Australorp of Australia was bred from the original black line.

history_summary.value: The Orust is a Swedish landrace from the rocky west coast, where birds ranged freely and fed themselves on whatever they found, fish included. That hard life produced a hardy survivor. It is recorded as at risk, with about 520 birds counted in 2023.

summary.value: The Orust is a landrace chicken from the rocky west coast of Sweden. For generations the birds roamed free along the shore and fed themselves on whatever they could find, fish included, which made them tough survivors. Feathers are mottled black and white. When a rooster is roused to guard his hens, his wattles change from red to bright violet, a trait few breeds share. It is a small, light bird: roosters weigh about 4.4 pounds and hens about 3 pounds. Hens are good layers of small to medium white eggs, averaging around 150 a year. Sweden counts it as a native breed at risk, with about 520 birds recorded in 2023, so it mainly suits keepers who want to help conserve a rare Nordic landrace.

It remains rare, with under 1,200 birds recorded in Germany in 2016.

summary.value: The Ostfriesische Mowe, or East Frisian Gull, is an old German chicken that grew out of the farm flocks of East Friesland in northwest Germany and nearby West Friesland in the Netherlands. It is a close cousin of the Westfalische Totleger and the Braekel. Birds come in two pencilled colors, silver and gold. Roosters weigh about 5 to 6.5 pounds and hens about 4 to 5.5 pounds, and a bantam version is also kept. Hens lay around 170 white eggs a year, each about 55 grams, and the breed serves for both eggs and meat. It is rare and listed as endangered in Germany, where about 1,200 birds were recorded in 2016, so it mostly suits keepers who want an old regional farm breed and would like to help keep it going.

summary.value: The Pepoi is a small, hardy farm chicken from northeast Italy, mostly Friuli-Venezia Giulia and the eastern Veneto. It is one of Italy's few true bantams, and a regional conservation project in the Veneto looks after it along with the Padovana and three other local breeds. Italy has not yet given it official breed status, partly because birds still vary a lot in type. Plumage is golden partridge, and the skin and legs are yellow. Roosters weigh about 3 pounds and hens a little over 2 pounds. Hens lay some 160 to 180 small, pinkish eggs a year and are keen sitters and good mothers. Young birds reach about 1.5 pounds at four months, a handy single serving or spit roast, and the meat is full of flavor. Numbers are low, with a few hundred breeding birds.

history_summary.value: The Padovana is an old small crested and bearded chicken from Padova in Italy's Veneto region, with crested chickens depicted in the area as far back as a 1397 fresco. Its precise origins and relationship to similar Polish and Dutch crested breeds remain debated, and it survives today in low numbers of around 1,200 birds.

summary.value: The Padovana is an old crested and bearded chicken named for the city of Padua in northeast Italy. Where it first came from is still argued over, and links to Polish and Dutch crested breeds are unclear, but a 1397 fresco in Padua already shows a crested hen, and the naturalist Aldrovandi pictured the bird in 1600. It has a huge round crest, a full beard, no comb, and tiny hidden earlobes. Recognized colors include white, black, sparrowhawk and laced silver, gold and buff. Roosters weigh about 4 to 5 pounds and hens about 3 to 4 pounds. Hens lay good numbers of eggs weighing 50 to 60 grams; the Italian standard calls for white shells. The birds are lively and trusting, and today they are kept mostly for show, though they also give fine meat.

history_summary.value: The Pavlovskaya is considered Russia's most ancient chicken breed. It came close to extinction in the 1990s, when only two roosters remained and one was infertile, and remains rare and little known outside Russia today.

summary.value: The Pavlovskaya is thought to be the oldest chicken breed in Russia, and it is said to have helped shape later crested breeds such as the Polish and the Brabanter. It is a small bird of only 3 to 4 pounds. Its looks are busy for its size: a V-shaped comb, a crest, a beard and muffs, and feathers that cover the legs right down to the toes. The breed came very close to dying out. In the 1990s the whole known population was down to two roosters, and one of them could not breed. Numbers have recovered a little, and Russia now reports a few hundred birds. Hens are poor layers, giving only about 70 to 90 white eggs a year, so the breed suits people who want an unusual, pleasant bird and a hand in saving it.

history_summary.value: The Pedres Portuguesa is a traditional Portuguese dual-purpose breed centred on the Minho region in the north-west of the country. Once considered at risk with only around 4,500 breeding hens in the early 2000s, its population had recovered substantially by 2024 and is no longer considered at risk.

summary.value: The Pedres Portuguesa is a traditional farm chicken from Portugal and one of the country's four native breeds. It is found across mainland Portugal but is most common in the northwest, and its home area is the old province of Minho and nearby parts of Douro Litoral and Tras-os-Montes. It comes in just one pattern: fine dark gray bars on a white or pale gray background, which gives the breed its name. The single comb has five or six points, the face and earlobes are bright red, and the bare shanks are pale yellow marked with slate. Roosters weigh about 5.7 to 7 pounds and hens about 4.9 to 6 pounds. Birds are active, resist disease and do well on free range, and they are raised for both meat and eggs. Anglers also use the barred feathers to tie trout flies.

history_summary.value: The Pekin Bantam descends from birds brought from China to Europe in the 1800s, with accounts crediting both an 1835 gift to Queen Victoria and an 1860 wartime looting for the breed's origin. It developed in Britain as a true bantam distinct from the Cochin, though other countries still treat it as the Cochin's bantam form.

summary.value: The Pekin is a small, round bantam recognized as a breed in Britain, though its ancestors came from China in the 1800s. One story says British soldiers took the first birds from the Emperor's collection in Peking around 1860; another credits birds sent to Queen Victoria about 1835. It is a true bantam with no large version, and in the US and Canada birds of this type are sold as Cochin Bantams. Pekins are so heavily feathered that their legs and feet almost disappear under a ball of fluff. The British standard lists twelve colors, including buff, black, cuckoo, lavender and white. Hens weigh about 20 ounces and cocks about 23. Hens lay few eggs but go broody readily and make good mothers. Pekins are docile and tame quickly with handling, which makes them good pets and a common choice for small gardens.

history_summary.value: The Penedesenca comes from the Penedes region of Catalonia, where dark-egg-laying farm chickens were traditionally kept, with efforts to save the type from extinction beginning in 1928. The black variety was standardised in 1946 as the Villafranquina Negra, and the breed nearly died out again before being revived by dedicated breeders in the 1980s.

summary.value: The Penedesenca is a rare Spanish chicken from Catalonia, named for the area around Vilafranca del Penedes. Farm families there kept hens that laid very dark eggs for a long time before anyone wrote about them. The first records date from 1928, when people tried to stop the type from dying out, and a standard for a black strain was approved in 1946. The breed nearly vanished again before breeders revived it in the 1980s. Colors include black, crele, partridge and wheaten, and the birds have white earlobes and an unusual carnation comb. Roosters weigh about 5 to 6.5 pounds and hens about 3.7 to 5 pounds. Hens lay around 150 to 160 large eggs a year, about 60 grams each, in a deep brown that ranks among the darkest of any breed. It suits keepers who prize egg color.

history_summary.value: The Phoenix was created in Germany in the late 1800s by Hugo du Roi, who crossed delicate imported long-tailed Japanese birds related to the Onagadori with hardier European breeds to produce a more cold-tolerant long-tailed exhibition bird. It lost the Onagadori's non-moulting gene, so its tail, while still impressive, is shorter, and the breed remains endangered today.

summary.value: The Phoenix is a long-tailed show chicken made in Germany in the late 1800s by Hugo du Roi, the first head of the German national poultry club. Japanese long-tailed birds related to the Onagadori did poorly in the European cold, so he crossed them with hardier breeds such as the Leghorn, Malay and Old English Game. The Phoenix lost the gene that stops yearly molting, yet a rooster's sickle feathers can still reach 2 to 5 feet with good care. Only males grow the long tail. Common colors include silver, gold and black-breasted red. Roosters weigh about 5.5 pounds and hens about 4 pounds. Hens are fair layers of roughly 52 to 126 small to medium cream or tinted eggs a year, and they go broody and raise chicks well. The birds are docile but aloof and need high perches to keep tails clean. They do best in warm climates with room to roam.

history_summary.value: The Pictave was developed from about 1900 by Raymond Lecointre near Poitiers from small European partridge-coloured bantam stock, and he used the hens to hatch and raise his pheasant chicks. It nearly went extinct after World War Two, and later cross-breeding to save it caused the breed to drift from its 1928 standard, prompting a 1998 effort to restore the original type.

summary.value: The Pictave is France's only true bantam, a naturally tiny chicken with no large version. It takes its name from the Pictavi, the ancient tribe behind the name Poitou. Around 1900 Raymond Lecointre began shaping it south of Poitiers from the small partridge-colored bantams common across Europe, and he used the hens to hatch and rear his pheasants. A standard followed in 1928. The breed nearly died out after World War Two, and rescue crosses pulled it away from the old type until breeders set out in 1998 to restore it. Birds are partridge colored with long tails, low wings and pinkish-white legs. Roosters weigh about 1.8 pounds and hens about 1.3 pounds. Hens lay around 130 small creamy white eggs a year and are superb sitters and mothers. It remains endangered.

history_summary.value: The Pita Pinta Asturiana is the only chicken breed native to the Asturias region of north-west Spain, related to other Atlantic-branch Spanish breeds like the Basque Euskal Oiloa. Industrialised egg production in the 1950s and 60s nearly wiped it out, but a recovery effort from the 1980s, backed by a breeders' association founded in 2003, has rebuilt its numbers.

summary.value: The Pita Pinta Asturiana is the only native chicken of Asturias, a region on the north coast of Spain. Its name means painted or mottled hen in the local language. It belongs to the Atlantic group of chickens and shares roots with other northern Spanish breeds such as the Basque Euskal Oiloa. Factory egg farming in the 1950s and 1960s nearly wiped it out, but breeders began rebuilding it in the 1980s, and a breed society followed in 2003. The bird is compact, with yellow skin, red earlobes, orange eyes and a single comb. Colors are mottled black, mottled red-brown, white and solid black. Roosters weigh about 9 to 10 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 6.5 pounds. Hens are steady layers of large light brown eggs, and the birds are tough and adapt well to their surroundings.

history_summary.value: The Plymouth Rock traces to 1869 crosses of Black Java hens with a barred, single-combed cock in Massachusetts, though genetic analysis points mainly to Dominique ancestry with input from the Java and Cochin. It became America's most common chicken breed by the early twentieth century and later became foundational to the commercial broiler industry through crosses with white Cornish stock.

summary.value: The Plymouth Rock is an American dual-purpose chicken from Massachusetts, first shown in the mid 1800s. Until about World War II it was the most common chicken on US farms. The first birds were barred, with crisp black and white stripes, and later colors include white, buff, blue, partridge and Columbian. It has a single red comb, yellow legs and yellow skin. Hens weigh around 7.5 pounds and roosters around 9.5. A hen lays roughly 200 large brown eggs a year, and the breed also gives a good table bird; white Rocks helped found the modern broiler industry. Rocks are calm, docile and easy to manage, and many hens will go broody. They feather early and handle cold winters well. They like to free range but accept a roomy run, which makes them a good first flock for families.

history_summary.value: The Polbar was created between 1946 and 1954 by Laura Kaufman, who crossed the Polish Green-legged Partridge with the American Plymouth Rock to give chicks a sex-linked eye-stripe so they could be sexed at hatch. It now survives only as a single conservation flock at a Polish agricultural research station.

summary.value: The Polbar is a Polish chicken bred between 1946 and 1954 by Laura Kaufman. She crossed the native Green-legged Partridge with Plymouth Rock roosters to bring in the barring gene, which makes the breed autosexing. At one day old, female chicks show a longer black stripe by the eye than males, so they can be sorted at hatch. Adult males are creamy white and hens grayish brown, with a single comb and gray to yellow legs. Roosters weigh about 5.5 pounds and hens about 4.4 pounds. Hens lay cream-colored eggs, around 160 a year on average. Today the whole breed lives in a single conservation flock of roughly 1,000 birds at the University of Life Sciences research station in Lublin, eastern Poland, so it is not something backyard keepers can easily find.

history_summary.value: The Polish chicken's crested type appears in European paintings from at least the 1400s-1600s, and its exact origin, whether Poland or elsewhere, remains uncertain. It was kept for eggs in places like France before losing favour as a layer to breeds like the Leghorn in the mid-1800s, after which it became mainly an exhibition bird.

summary.value: The Polish is an old European crested breed. Nobody knows for sure where it began, but Dutch breeders shaped the big feathered crest that sits on a bony dome on top of the skull. Hens wear a neat round pom-pom, while roosters carry a looser, shaggier mop. Some strains are bearded and some are frizzled. Roosters weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4.5. Hens lay roughly 150 to 200 white eggs a year, start a little late, and almost never go broody. The birds are calm and friendly but spook easily, because the crest blocks much of their view, so hawks are a real risk. Speaking softly when walking up helps. They handle heat well when given shade but do poorly in cold, wet weather, when the crest can soak or freeze. They suit families who want a showy, gentle bird in a dry, covered run.

history_summary.value: The Polverara is an old crested breed named for a town in the Padova countryside, described in Italian writing as far back as the 1500s and possibly related to the Padovana breed. It declined through the twentieth century, dropping to just seven birds, before recovery efforts starting in the 1980s and official Italian recognition in 1996.

summary.value: The Polverara is an old crested chicken named after a small town in the countryside near Padua, in the Veneto region of northern Italy. Writers praised the large chickens of this village as early as the 1500s. The breed nearly died out in the 1900s, falling to only seven birds, and was rebuilt from the 1980s before Italy recognized it in 1996. It comes in glossy black with a green sheen or pure white. It wears a small upright crest, a beard, a tiny V-shaped comb and white earlobes. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 6.2 pounds and hens about 4 to 4.6 pounds. Hens lay at least 150 whitish eggs a year, and the dark meat is prized for its flavor. This is a hardy, free-ranging bird that does poorly when shut in and will roost in trees, so it suits keepers with open space rather than a small pen.

history_summary.value: The Potchefstroom Koekoek was developed in the 1960s by Chris Marais at the Potchefstroom Agricultural College by crossing Black Australorp, White Leghorn and Barred Plymouth Rock stock to create a dual-purpose bird suited to South African free-range conditions. summary.value: The Potchefstroom Koekoek is a South African dual-purpose chicken bred at the Potchefstroom Agricultural College by Chris Marais. He crossed Black Australorps, White Leghorns and Barred Plymouth Rocks to get a bird that lays well, carries enough body for the table and copes with local farm conditions. The name comes from the Afrikaans word for its barred pattern, and every pure bird is barred black and white. Chicks can be sexed soon after hatching because males and females show different markings. Hens lay brown eggs with deep yellow yolks, and studies put output at close to 200 eggs a year. Reported weights vary widely, from about 8 pounds for hens and 9 for roosters down to under 5 pounds for hens. The breed forages well, holds up on poor feed and is popular with small farmers in South Africa and Ethiopia.

history_summary.value: The Preta Lusitanica is a traditional black breed from north-western Portugal that declined sharply in the mid-1900s as imported industrial chicken strains took over farming. summary.value: The Preta Lusitanica is an old farm chicken from north-western Portugal and one of the country's four native breeds, alongside the Branca, Amarela and Pedres Portuguesa. Its name means black, and black is its only color, often with a green or blue shine on the neck, back and tail of the roosters. It has a red single comb with five or six points, red face and earlobes, and dark slate legs with no feathers. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 6.6 pounds and hens about 3.7 to 5.5 pounds. It is kept for both meat and eggs. Numbers crashed once factory strains arrived in the mid 1900s, but breeders rebuilt the flock, and by 2024 it was no longer rated at risk. It sits on the Slow Food Ark of Taste list and is mostly raised outdoors on small farms.

summary.value: The Pyncheon is a rare true bantam, meaning it has no large fowl version. It was bred in the northeastern United States from birds thought to have come over from the Netherlands or Belgium, and it is one of the older American bantams. Nathaniel Hawthorne kept the breed and wrote its birds into The House of the Seven Gables. The Pyncheon wears a small crest behind a single comb that often bends into an S shape, and most birds show a Mille Fleur type of spotted pattern. Hens are fair layers of small white eggs and go broody often, so they make willing mothers. The birds are friendly and docile, but like most bantams they fly well, so a covered run helps. The American Bantam Association recognizes the breed, while the American Poultry Association does not.

summary.value: The Ramelsloher is a German dual-purpose chicken from the village of Ramelsloh, just south of Hamburg. A Hamburg shipowner, A.D. Wichmann, shaped it from plain white farm hens in the 1870s and showed it in 1874. Around 1900 it was one of the main utility birds in Germany, but it faded after the Second World War and is now listed as extremely endangered. It comes only in white and buff, with no bantam form. Its legs are slate blue, the earlobes bluish, and the eyes so dark they look black, a trait no other breed shares. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 6.6 pounds and hens about 4.4 to 5.5. Hens lay roughly 150 to 170 white or pale cream eggs a year and keep laying in winter. The birds are lively but grow very tame, forage well and stand up to rough weather.

history_summary.value: Red sex-links are crossbred hybrids developed so that chick down color is linked to sex, making chick sexing easy. Different hatcheries sell their own strain of this cross under different trade names, all functioning as heavy brown-egg production layers.

summary.value: The Red Sex Link, often sold as the Red Star, is a hybrid rather than a true breed. It comes from putting a male of a red breed, usually the Rhode Island Red or the New Hampshire, over a light-colored hen such as a White Rock, Delaware, Rhode Island White or Silver Laced Wyandotte, a cross American hatcheries were using by the 1950s. Several hatchery strains, including the Golden Comet, follow the same idea. Chicks can be sexed by down color at hatch: pullets are red and cockerels pale. Grown hens are red with some white, and roosters are mostly white. Hens weigh about 6 pounds and roosters about 8. A hen lays roughly 240 to 300 large brown eggs a year and rarely goes broody. The birds are friendly and docile and cope with cold and heat. They suit beginners who want a steady supply of eggs.

history_summary.value: The Red Shaver is a Canadian sex-linked hybrid bred as a prolific, cold-hardy brown-egg layer, with chicks that can be sexed by down color at hatch.

summary.value: The Red Shaver is a sex-linked laying hybrid that comes from Canada, where the Shaver line has its roots. Because of the cross, chicks can be sorted by color the day they hatch. Pullets are reddish brown with white underfeathers, while cockerels are white with a few red marks. Grown birds are light, at roughly 3 to 5 pounds. Hens are known for heavy laying, with reports of about 305 to 315 large brown eggs a year. They have a name for being quiet and calm, which makes them easy to keep in a backyard flock. Their Canadian background means they handle cold weather well. This bird suits keepers who care most about a steady supply of eggs rather than showing or breeding their own chicks.

history_summary.value: The Rhode Island Red was developed in Rhode Island and Massachusetts in the late 1800s by crossing Oriental breeds such as the Malay with brown Leghorns from Italy. It was first bred for both meat and eggs, though modern strains focus on egg production.

summary.value: Rhode Island Reds were shaped on farms in Rhode Island and southern Massachusetts in the late 1800s, using Asian fowl such as the Malay, Java and Shanghai together with brown Leghorns. The Malay gave it the deep red feathers, which run from rich red to nearly black, with a mostly black tail. Combs can be single or rose. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6. Hens lay 200 to 300 large brown eggs a year and may start at six months old. Since the 1940s, production strains have become smaller, paler and less likely to go broody, while the old type stays larger and darker. Most hens are calm and peaceful. The breed is hardy, handles cold well and asks for little care, which makes it a common first choice for beginners. Rhode Island has made it the official state bird.

history_summary.value: The Rhode Island White was developed from around 1888 by John Alonzo Jocoy in Rhode Island by crossing Partridge Cochins, White Wyandottes and rose-comb White Leghorns. It is treated as a distinct breed from the Rhode Island Red in the United States, though some other countries classify it as a color variant.

summary.value: The Rhode Island White is an American dual purpose chicken from Peacedale, Rhode Island. John Alonzo Jocoy began breeding it around 1888 from Partridge Cochins, White Wyandottes and rose comb White Leghorns, and sold his first birds in 1903. In the United States it counts as its own breed, separate from the Rhode Island Red, though it shares that bird's long, brick shaped body. It comes only in white, with a bright red rose comb and yellow legs. Cocks weigh about 8.5 pounds and hens about 6.5 to 7 pounds. Hens lay some 200 to 250 large eggs a year in shades from light to dark brown, lay well in winter and seldom go broody. The birds are calm and friendly with people but can push around gentler breeds, so they need a roomy coop. They handle both hot and cold weather and suit family farms.

summary.value: The Rhodebar is an autosexing chicken built to have the laying power of the Rhode Island Red. The first birds were bred in Canada during the 1940s at a university in British Columbia, crossed from Rhode Island Reds and Barred Plymouth Rocks. British breeders made their own strains in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and it was standardized in Britain in the early 1950s. Chicks can be sexed on the day they hatch: males are yellow, while females show dark stripes down the back. Adults are medium sized and shaped like a utility Rhode Island Red, with red, barred plumage and a barred black and silver tail. Hens lay about 180 to 200 light brown eggs a year, and birds weigh roughly 6 to 9 pounds. It caught on just before commercial hybrids took over and is now very rare, with an even rarer bantam.

summary.value: The Robusta Lionata is a modern Italian dual-purpose chicken from Rovigo in the Veneto. Staff at the local poultry research station made it in the early 1960s by crossing Buff Orpingtons with a white commercial strain known as White America. It looks much like a Buff Orpington, warm buff all over with a black tail that shines green, but it has yellow skin and yellow legs, which Italian meat buyers prefer. It has a single comb and red earlobes. Roosters weigh about 8.8 to 9.9 pounds and hens about 6.2 to 7.3. Hens lay some 160 to 170 pinkish eggs a year, and they go broody readily and raise their own chicks. Young birds reach about 4 pounds in four months. The breed is rare, with only a few hundred breeding birds counted in 2007, and it is part of a regional conservation program.

summary.value: The Robusta Maculata is a modern Italian chicken kept for both meat and eggs. It was bred in the early 1960s at the poultry research station in Rovigo, in the Veneto, from Buff Orpingtons and a white commercial strain called White America. The name means spotted: birds are silvery white with scattered black or dark grey patches, a silver and black neck, and a black tail with a green shine. Skin and legs are yellow, the comb is a large single one and the earlobes are red. Roosters weigh about 8.8 to 9.9 pounds and hens about 6.2 to 7.3. Hens lay around 140 to 160 pinkish brown eggs a year. The birds are hardy and suit free-range and organic farms, and young stock reach about 4 pounds by four months. Numbers are small, and the breed is in a regional conservation program.

history_summary.value: The Romagnola is a traditional Italian dual-purpose breed once common in central Italy, which nearly went extinct in the late twentieth century. A recovery programme run with the University of Parma and a breeders' association formed in 2007 helped bring the population back, though numbers stayed low and the breed was still awaiting official recognition as of 2012.

summary.value: The Romagnola is an old farmyard chicken from Emilia-Romagna in Italy, once common around Ravenna, Forli-Cesena and Bologna. In the mid 1900s breeders at Rovigo and Ravenna fixed two color types, a silver and a golden, both flecked with black, though the breed still varies a lot in color. Skin is mostly creamy white, the legs run from yellow to almost black, the earlobes are cream with a hint of blue and the comb is single. It is a light, fine-boned bird: roosters weigh about 4.4 to 5.5 pounds and hens a little over 4. Hens lay around 150 white eggs a year, each fairly large at about 60 grams. It is kept for both eggs and meat, and the young grow fast and have good flavor. The breed nearly vanished before a recovery project led from Parma began, and numbers are still very small.

history_summary.value: The Rosecomb is one of the oldest true bantam breeds, with records going back to 14th-century Britain and a boost in popularity credited to King Richard III. It has long been bred purely for show, which has left it with poor fertility, low broodiness and high chick mortality.

summary.value: The Rosecomb is a true bantam, a naturally tiny chicken with no large version, and one of the oldest bantam breeds. Records place it in England as far back as the 1300s. Its name comes from the broad rose comb, which is big for such a small bird, and it also has large white earlobes, a full sweeping tail and a compact body. Black, white and blue are the standard colors, though many others exist. Cocks weigh roughly 1.3 to 1.6 pounds and hens about 1 to 1.4 pounds. Hens lay very few eggs, often about one small cream egg a week, and seldom go broody. The birds are alert, active and fly well. Because the breed has been shaped almost entirely for the show pen, fertility is low and chicks are delicate, so it suits serious exhibitors more than people who want eggs or an easy backyard pet.

history_summary.value: The Rumpless Game is a tail-less British breed possibly originating on the Isle of Man. A separate American line called Manx Rumpy was created in 1958 by crossing tail-less birds of supposed Iranian origin with other breeds, though it is not recognised by the American Poultry Association.

summary.value: The Rumpless Game is a British hard-feathered game fowl with no tail. Like other rumpless breeds it lacks the small bone and gland at the base of the spine that a tail grows from. It most likely began as a chance mutation in Old English Game, and it may have come from the Isle of Man, which is why it is sometimes called the Manx Rumpy. The comb is single, the wattles and lobes are small, and any color is allowed in the British standard. Males weigh about 5 to 6 pounds and hens about 4 to 5. The bantam is far more popular than the large fowl, which is seldom seen. The British breed has never been brought to the United States; the American birds sold as Manx Rumpy or Persian Rumpless come from a different 1958 cross and are not the same breed.

history_summary.value: The Sapphire Gem is a hatchery hybrid developed in the Czech Republic. It combines commercial brown-egg laying traits with a blue dilution gene, so a single cross produces slate-blue, splash and other color variants in the same batch of chicks.

summary.value: The Sapphire Gem is a hatchery hybrid, not a recognized standard breed. It comes from the Czech Republic and is sold in the US under a trademarked name. Its feathers are slate gray to light gray, a shade the poultry trade calls blue or lavender, and some chicks in a hatch come out splash. The bird is built for egg production. Hoover's rates hens at about 290 extra large brown eggs a year, and adults weigh roughly 6 to 7 pounds. They are described as docile and easy to care for, good foragers, and able to cope with both cold winters and hot summers. Hens only go broody now and then, so they are a poor pick for hatching chicks but a sensible one for a steady supply of eggs in a backyard flock.

history_summary.value: The Satsumadori originated in Kagoshima Prefecture in southern Japan, bred originally for steel-spur cockfighting, a practice no longer legal there. It was named a Natural Monument of Japan in 1943 and is now kept mainly for exhibition.

summary.value: The Satsumadori is a Japanese game fowl from Kagoshima Prefecture on the southern tip of Kyushu, an area once called Satsuma. It was bred for fighting with steel blades fixed to the legs, a sport now banned in Japan, and today it is kept for show. Japan named it a Natural Monument in 1943. Roosters stand tall and carry a wide, fanned tail held above level, giving the bird a bold, flashy look. The comb is small and triple in cocks and tiny or missing in hens, with bright red face and yellow legs. Traditional Japanese colors include red, golden and white hackled types plus solid black and white. Cocks weigh about 7.5 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 5.8. Hens make good broody mothers. The breed is rare outside Japan and best suited to experienced keepers who show game birds.

history_summary.value: The Schweizer was created in 1905 by Alfred Weiss in Amriswil, Switzerland, mainly by crossing white Orpingtons and Wyandottes into a dual-purpose breed. Numbers fell sharply after the Second World War, and a conservation programme launched in 1991 has since helped the breed slowly recover.

summary.value: The Schweizer, or Swiss hen, is a dual-purpose chicken that Alfred Weiss of Amriswil, in north-east Switzerland, created in 1905 mainly from white Orpingtons and Wyandottes. It is pure white with a deep red rose comb, so it carries the Swiss national colors. The body is compact and heavy with a straight back. Roosters weigh about 6.2 to 7.7 pounds and hens about 5.3 to 6.2. Hens lay roughly 120 cream eggs a year, and some lines lay more. The small rose comb resists frostbite, and the birds are long lived and cope well with cold nights, which suits cold climates. They are calm and trusting, and they are poor fliers that seldom try, so a low fence usually holds them. Numbers fell to about fifty birds by 1991, when a rescue program began, and the breed has been slowly recovering since.

history_summary.value: The Scots Dumpy is a traditional Scottish short-legged breed bred for more than two centuries, which became very rare and was unsuccessfully searched for in Scotland in 1975. The breed was rebuilt from birds imported from Kenya in 1977, descendants of a flock taken there in 1902.

summary.value: The Scots Dumpy is an old Scottish farm chicken known for its very short legs, which leave the body only a few inches off the ground and give it a waddling walk. The trait comes from a dwarfing gene, so some chicks from two short-legged parents hatch long legged and some never hatch. Over the years it has also been called the Bakie, Crawler and Creeper. Birds are usually cuckoo, black or white, with a bright red single comb, and there is a bantam version. Roosters weigh about 7 pounds and hens about 6. Hens lay up to about 180 white or lightly tinted eggs a year. They are docile, and they are famous as broodies and careful mothers, often used to hatch game bird eggs. Short legs also mean they do little damage to gardens. The breed nearly died out and was rebuilt in 1977 from birds kept in Kenya.

history_summary.value: The Scots Grey is a dual-purpose chicken developed in Scotland and bred there for more than two centuries, once known as the Scotch Grey. It was widely kept in Scotland until around 1930 and is now listed as an at-risk native breed.

conservation_status.value: Native Poultry Breeds at Risk (Rare Breeds Survival Trust)

summary.value: The Scots Grey is the traditional farmyard chicken of Scotland, bred there for well over two hundred years and at its most popular from the 1880s until about 1940. It is a tall, upright bird on long, pale legs, with a single red comb, red earlobes and a full tail. It comes in one pattern only: steel grey with black barring that has a metallic shine. Roosters weigh about 7 pounds and hens about 5, and a bantam exists. Hens lay around 150 to 180 white eggs a year and rarely go broody. The birds are hardy, handle rough weather and do best free ranging, since they are alert, active foragers. They can be flighty when disturbed, and roosters may turn feisty in the breeding season, so they are not the first pick for homes with small children. The breed is now on the British rare breeds list.

history_summary.value: The Sebright was bred as an ornamental bantam by Sir John Saunders Sebright in the early 1800s, combining several small laced and game fowl to fix a sharply laced feather pattern. It became the first breed with its own specialist club and remains one of the oldest British bantam breeds.

summary.value: The Sebright is a tiny English bantam created by Sir John Saunders Sebright, who spent years crossing small local birds before presenting it around 1810. It is a true bantam, so there is no large version, and it ranks among the oldest British bantam breeds. Every feather is gold or silver with a crisp black edge, and cocks are hen feathered, lacking the long curved tail plumes of most roosters. Males weigh about 22 ounces and females about 20. Hens lay only 60 to 80 small creamy white eggs a year and seldom go broody. Sebrights are active and spunky and tame easily when handled young, though they fly well and can be hard to catch. They prefer warm climates and dislike cold, damp weather. The breed is kept for shows and ornament, suits 4H projects, and is a poor choice for anyone wanting eggs.

history_summary.value: The Sentul chicken originated in Ciamis Regency, West Java, Indonesia, as a dual-purpose meat and egg breed. It is noted for growing faster and resisting disease better than other local Indonesian breeds.

summary.value: The Sentul is a native chicken of Indonesia. It comes from Ciamis Regency in West Java, where local birds descended from the red junglefowl were kept and shaped over a long period. Farmers raise it for both meat and eggs, and some people also keep it as a hobby or show bird. Most Sentuls carry a pea comb, though a share of the flock has single combs. Compared with other Indonesian village chickens, it is said to grow faster and to resist disease better, and young birds are reported to reach eating size in about twelve weeks. Reliable figures on egg numbers, egg color and adult weight are hard to find outside local studies, so it remains a breed known mainly within its home region.

history_summary.value: The Serama was developed in Kelantan, Malaysia, in the early 1970s from a mix of small local and Japanese-type bantams, and was named after a figure from traditional shadow puppet theatre. It is bred mainly as a show bird, prized in Malaysia for its tiny size and confident, upright carriage.

summary.value: The Serama is the smallest chicken breed in the world, a true bantam from Kelantan state in Malaysia. Breeders there created it in the early 1970s from tiny local pet bantams, small game-type birds and early Japanese bantam stock, and named it after Sri Rama, a hero of shadow puppet plays. It stands about 10 inches tall or less and usually weighs under about a pound, with some Malaysian birds far lighter. The bird has a full, high chest, an upright tail held tight to the body and wings pointing almost straight down, giving a V shape. Seramas carry themselves boldly but are calm, easy to handle and not aggressive. In Malaysia they compete in tabletop shows where judges score their pose and bearing. They reached the UK in 2004, and the APA accepted the white variety in 2011. Chicks are sensitive to cold because of their small size.

history_summary.value: Shamo is a designation for Japanese game fowl descended from Thai fighting stock brought to Japan in the early 1600s. Seven recognized Shamo breeds are protected as Natural Monuments of Japan; outside Japan they are kept mainly for exhibition.

summary.value: Shamo is the Japanese name for a family of large game fowl. Their ancestors came to Japan from Siam, now Thailand, in the early 1600s, and the name comes from that old country name. Japan protected the breed by law in 1941, and regional types range from the big O-Shamo to the medium Chu-Shamo and smaller birds. The Shamo stands very upright, often near 30 inches tall, with a wide muscular body, yellow legs, a pea comb, pearl eyes and hard, sparse feathers that leave skin showing. The US standard calls for 11 pound males and 7 pound females. Hens are fair to poor layers of light brown eggs but devoted mothers. Shamos are friendly with people yet fight other birds of the same sex, so roosters must be kept apart. They rarely fly and need room to forage. Most are kept for show or as curiosities.

history_summary.value: The Showgirl comes from crossing Silkies with Turkens (naked neck chickens), giving a bird with Silkie plumage and a bare neck.

summary.value: The Showgirl is a cross between two odd looking chickens, the Silkie and the Turken, also called the naked neck. It carries the Silkie coat of soft, hair-like feathers that lack the tiny hooks that normally hold a feather together, so the bird looks and feels furry. It also keeps the Silkie's black skin, dark beak and eyes, deep mulberry comb and turquoise earlobes. From the Turken side it gets a bare neck, while a fluffy crest still sits on top of the head. Some birds keep a small patch of feathers on the neck that looks like a brooch. Both hens and roosters go by the name Showgirl. Most share the sweet, docile manner of the Silkie, so they are kept mainly as pets and show birds rather than for eggs or meat.

history_summary.value: The Sicilian Buttercup descends from the older Siciliana breed of Sicily and was brought to the United States in the 1800s, later reaching Britain and Australia in the early 1900s. It is best known for its distinctive cup-shaped comb, a trait depicted in Italian paintings dating back to the sixteenth century.

summary.value: The Sicilian Buttercup comes from Sicily and reached the United States in the 1800s, where a Massachusetts breeder named C. Carroll Loring promoted it for decades. It went into the American Standard in 1918 and later spread to Britain. Its trademark is a cup-shaped comb, really two single combs joined front and back into a crown of points. Hens are golden buff with rows of black spangles, roosters are reddish orange with a black tail, and both have willow-green legs. Roosters weigh about 6.5 pounds and hens about 5. Hens lay some 140 to 180 small to medium white eggs a year and seldom go broody. The birds are busy foragers that hate confinement, do well in hot weather and dislike cold. Temperament varies by strain, from friendly and tame to nervous and flighty, and they are chatty. The breed is listed as threatened.

history_summary.value: The Siciliana is an old Sicilian breed likely descended from crosses of local birds with North African stock, depicted in Italian paintings as early as the sixteenth century. It nearly went extinct in the twentieth century but was revived from the 1980s onward and gained official Italian breed standard recognition in 2004; it is also the ancestor of the Sicilian Buttercup.

summary.value: The Siciliana is an old laying breed from Sicily, most likely formed long ago by crossing island chickens with birds from North Africa. Birds much like it appear in paintings from the 1500s. It had nearly vanished by the 1980s, was revived after that, and entered the Italian breed standard in 2004. It is the parent stock of the Sicilian Buttercup, which has since drifted away from it. Its trademark is a cup-shaped comb, open like a crown with points around the rim. Other traits are willow-green legs, yellow skin and red earlobes. Colors are golden duckwing, black, white and blue. Roosters weigh about 4.4 to 5.3 pounds and hens about 3.5 to 4 pounds. The breed matures very early, and pullets begin laying at four to five months. Eggs are white to light brown, long and pointed, and weigh at least 45 grams. The birds are lively, roam widely, forage well and handle cold fairly well.

history_summary.value: Silkies are an ancient Chinese breed first described in the West by Marco Polo in the 13th century as a furry chicken, though other parts of Asia have also been proposed as their origin. They reached the West via trade routes and became one of the most popular ornamental chicken breeds, valued for their fluffy plumage, black skin, and strong broodiness.

summary.value: The Silkie is an ancient breed from China, or possibly elsewhere in Asia, named for its soft, hair-like feathers that feel more like fur than plumage. It has black skin and bones, a small walnut comb, turquoise earlobes and five toes on each foot. Standard birds are small, with roosters near 4 pounds and hens near 3, and nearly all Silkies in North America are bantams. Hens lay about 100 to 120 small cream eggs a year, but they go broody so often that laying stops and starts. That same habit makes them famous mothers that will hatch almost any egg. Silkies are docile and friendly, easy to handle, and good with children, though gentle enough to get picked on by bolder breeds. They cannot fly and their fluff is not waterproof, so they need a covered, dry run in wet or snowy weather.

history_summary.value: The Silverudd Blue was developed in Smaland, southern Sweden, by Martin Silverudd, crossing New Hampshire and Rhode Island Red stock with Cream Legbars from the UK to produce a blue-egg layer. Silverudd died in 1986 before the breed was fully fixed, so modern birds still vary in size and egg color, and the breed was renamed after him in 2016.

summary.value: The Silverudd Blue is a Swedish chicken created by Martin Silverudd in the Småland region of southern Sweden. He started mainly from New Hampshire and Rhode Island Red birds and crossed in Cream Legbars from Britain to get colored eggshells. Hens lay blue to green eggs of roughly 50 to 65 grams. Silverudd died in 1986 before the work was finished, so birds today still differ in size and in egg shade. The breed went by names such as Isbar and Swedish green egg layer before it took its creator's name in 2016. It is a medium-sized bird with a square outline, a single comb, four toes, dark legs and a dark beak. Hens weigh about 3.3 pounds and roosters about 5.5 pounds. Because it carries the blue gene, chicks hatch in black, blue or splash in a steady ratio, with blue the most common.

history_summary.value: The Slovene Late-feathered Hen was developed from around 1960 from imported White Plymouth Rock stock brought to a farm near Pivka, with slow-feathering birds selected and refined at a research station and later at the University of Ljubljana. It is now the only traditional Slovenian meat-type chicken breed, kept in small numbers mainly for broiler breeding.

summary.value: The Slovene Late-feathered Hen is a heavy white chicken from Slovenia and the only meat-type breed left on the country's list of traditional farm animals. It grew out of White Plymouth Rocks imported to a farm near Pivka around 1960, and breeders at a research station picked out birds that grow their feathers slowly. Today the University of Ljubljana keeps most of the flock, which numbered 340 birds in 2020. Birds are plain white with a broad back, a red single comb, yellow eyes, small red earlobes and yellow skin and legs. Roosters average about 10 pounds and hens about 6.6 pounds. Hens give around 200 brown eggs a year of roughly 60 grams. The breed is mainly used as a grandparent line for the Prelux-BRO broiler, and a slow-feathering hen crossed with a fast-feathering rooster gives chicks that can be sexed by how fast their feathers come in.

history_summary.value: Developed in the 1970s at the University of Ljubljana's Biotechnical Faculty from Barred and White Plymouth Rock stock, this layer breed was bred for body mass, egg output and its barred plumage pattern. It now survives mainly at the university's poultry research center and serves as a parent line for the commercial Prelux crossbreeds.

summary.value: The Slovenian Barred Hen is a laying breed begun in 1970 by animal scientists at the University of Ljubljana, who built it from Barred and White Plymouth Rocks. They selected for body size, good laying and a clean barred pattern. The feathers show crisp alternating bands of black and white, and roosters look paler than hens. Birds have a medium single comb, small red earlobes, orange eyes and light yellow legs with darker toes. It is the heaviest of the Slovenian layer breeds: roosters weigh about 6.6 to 7.7 pounds and hens about 5 to 6 pounds. Hens begin laying at around 20 weeks and produce some 240 to 250 light brown eggs a year, averaging about 59 grams. The breed is also a parent of the Prelux Black and Prelux Barred commercial layers. Slovenia counted about 1,270 birds in 2020, most of them at the university's poultry center.

history_summary.value: Bred in the 1970s at the University of Ljubljana's Biotechnical Faculty from imported Rhode Island Red stock, the Slovenian Brown became a popular layer on both large and small farms. It is now kept mainly at the university's poultry research center and used as a parent for the Prelux commercial crossbreeds.

summary.value: The Slovenian Brown Hen is a laying breed created in the 1970s by animal scientists at the University of Ljubljana, working from Rhode Island Red stock that had long been a favorite on Slovenian farms. The birds are a solid dark brown with no pattern. Roosters have a metallic gloss and a tail of dark green and black feathers, and strong sun can fade the plumage. It has a medium single comb, orange eyes and yellow legs. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 6.6 pounds and hens about 4 to 4.9 pounds, making it the lightest of the Slovenian layer breeds. Hens start laying at about 19 to 20 weeks and give roughly 295 to 305 brown eggs a year, averaging about 61 grams each, while eating less feed per egg than their cousins. The breed is also a parent of the Prelux commercial layers, and in 2020 Slovenia counted about 2,900 birds.

history_summary.value: Developed at the University of Ljubljana's Biotechnical Faculty and consolidated as a breed by 1968, the Slovenian Silver was selected for a sex-linked white plumage gene useful in crossbreeding. It is kept mainly at the university's poultry research center and used as a parent for the Prelux commercial crossbreeds.

summary.value: The Slovenian Silver Hen is a white-feathered laying chicken bred by poultry scientists at the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, where the line was settled and tested around 1968. Breeders favored a sex-linked gene for silver-white plumage, which makes the hens useful as a parent line. Crossed with Slovenian Brown roosters, they produce the commercial Prelux Brown layer. The hens are plain white with yellow legs, yellow-orange eyes, a medium single comb and small pale red earlobes. Roosters weigh about 6 to 7 pounds and hens about 4.9 to 5.3 pounds. A hen starts laying at around five months and gives some 260 to 270 brown eggs a year, each weighing about 64 grams, larger than the eggs of the other Slovenian breeds. Most of the flock, a little over 900 birds in 2020, is kept at the university's poultry center.

history_summary.value: The Sombor Kaporka was created in the early 1900s in the Vojvodina region of northern Serbia by crossing imported Sulmtaler and Houdan chickens with local birds. A breed standard for it was set around 1918, and it is raised today as a dual-purpose egg and meat bird.

summary.value: The Sombor Kaporka, also called the Sombor Crested, is a rare chicken from Serbia. Breeders in Vojvodina, the northern province of the country, made it in the early 1900s and named it after the town of Sombor. They crossed local farm hens with Sulmtaler and Houdan birds brought in from abroad, and the tuft of feathers on the head comes from that mix. A written standard for the breed followed around 1918. It is a dual purpose bird, kept for both meat and eggs. Roosters weigh roughly 7.7 to 8.8 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 6.6 pounds. A good hen lays around 200 to 220 eggs a year, and the best layers can reach 260.

history_summary.value: The Speckledy is a modern hybrid from a Rhode Island Red and Marans cross, with feathering like a Cuckoo Marans, bred as a prolific layer of speckled chestnut-brown eggs.

summary.value: The Speckledy, also sold as the Speckled Ranger, is a modern hybrid laying hen made by crossing a Rhode Island Red rooster with a Marans hen. It takes after the Marans side in looks, with barred, cuckoo style feathers that are soft and plentiful. The birds are large but neat, with a deep breast, an upturned tail, pale legs, pale bay eyes and a medium red single comb. Hens are strong layers, putting out around 250 to 270 dark chestnut brown eggs a year, often with speckles. The shells are notably tough and the yolks a deep yellow. Speckledys are docile and easy to handle, and they enjoy foraging, so they do best with room to range on grass. Their calm nature and steady laying make them a common choice for first time keepers who mainly want brown eggs.

history_summary.value: The Stara Zagora Red was created around 1970 by crossing local hens from the Stara Zagora region of Bulgaria with Rhode Island Red cocks, with the red colour fixed by the second generation. It is now a rare breed, kept mainly by the Bulgarian Poultry Institute and a handful of breeders.

summary.value: The Stara Zagora Red is a rare laying chicken from the Stara Zagora region in south central Bulgaria. It was made around 1970 by mating local hens of mixed colors with Rhode Island Red roosters, and the even red plumage was fixed within two generations. The bird is of medium build, with bright red feathers, a broad flat back, a full breast and a large comb and wattles. Roosters weigh about 6.6 to 7.7 pounds and hens about 5 to 5.5 pounds. Pullets begin laying at around five and a half months, and a hen gives some 215 to 220 brown eggs a year, each about 2 ounces. Numbers are very low. The Bulgarian Poultry Institute and a small group of Bulgarian breeders keep the remaining flocks, and the breed is listed as at risk.

history_summary.value: A trademarked hybrid from Hoover's Hatchery, made by crossing its Prairie Bluebell Egger with a brown egg laying bird so that the hens lay green eggs in high numbers.

summary.value: Hoover's Hatchery in the United States developed the Starlight Green Egger as a crossbred laying hen. It comes from crossing the company's Prairie Bluebell Egger, a blue egg layer, with a brown egg laying bird, and the mix of shell colors gives green eggs. Hens lay around 280 large green eggs a year, and a small share of birds may lay brown instead. It is a light, active chicken that weighs about 5 to 6 pounds and forages well when allowed to roam. Feather colors vary a lot, so no two birds look quite alike. The birds are easy going, rarely go broody and carry a small pea comb. They are sold as hardy in both cold and hot weather. This bird suits backyard keepers who want a steady supply of colorful eggs rather than a show breed or a meat bird.

history_summary.value: The Sulmtaler descends from country chickens of the Styrian valleys of southern Austria, which were crossed with Cochin, Dorking and Houdan stock in the late 1800s to make heavier fattening birds. Around 1900 breeders gathered the remaining original-type stock and re-established the breed, which then spread to Germany, the Netherlands and England.

summary.value: The Sulmtaler is a heavy farm chicken from the Sulm valley and nearby valleys of Styria, south of Graz in Austria. Local birds there were fattened on maize for the table. In the late 1800s they were crossed with Cochin, Houdan and Dorking, then bred back to the old type, and by 1900 the breed stood on its own before spreading to Germany, the Netherlands and Britain. Roosters weigh about 6.6 to 8.8 pounds and hens about 5.5 to 7.7 pounds. Gold wheaten is the classic color, and both sexes carry a small crest. Hens rarely go broody and lay some 130 to 180 cream to light brown eggs a year. Birds grow fast, forage well and handle cold and wet weather. They can be flighty at first but calm down with handling, so they suit keepers who have room for them to range.

history_summary.value: According to legend the Sultan was kept as an ornamental bird in the palace gardens of the Ottoman sultans in Turkey, and all Western stock descends from birds sent to a London poultry editor in 1854. It remains a rare, purely ornamental breed prized for its unusual crest, beard, muffs, feathered legs and five toes.

summary.value: The Sultan is a rare ornamental chicken from Turkey, where its old name meant fowl of the sultan. Legend says these birds decorated the palace gardens of the Ottoman sultans, and every Sultan in the West descends from a few birds sent from Constantinople to London in 1854. Few breeds pack in so many odd features: a crest, beard and muffs, a small V comb, feathered legs and feet, vulture hocks and five toes. The plumage is pure white with slate blue legs. Under the American standard, cocks weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4 pounds. Hens lay only 50 to 70 small white eggs a year and rarely sit. Sultans are tame and friendly, like being held and chatter softly. They need shelter from wet and cold, since crests and combs can freeze, and they should live with other gentle breeds. They make good pets for urban yards.

history_summary.value: The Sumatra descends from fighting cocks brought from the Indonesian island of Sumatra to the United States in 1847, and later to Germany and Britain. Today it is kept purely as an ornamental and show bird, valued for its glossy black, low-carried tail and pheasant-like bearing.

summary.value: The Sumatra traces back to fowl from the islands of Sumatra, Java and Borneo in Indonesia, where men caught wild males for cockfights. The first birds reached Massachusetts in 1847, and the black variety entered the American standard in 1883. Today it is an ornamental and show breed with a long, flowing tail carried low, a pheasant-like way of moving and a green sheen on black feathers. It has a dark purple to black face, a small red pea comb, black skin, and often more than one spur on each leg. Blue, white and dun birds also exist. Cocks weigh about 5 pounds and hens about 4, though the feathers make them look bigger. Hens lay 100 to 130 small white or tinted eggs a year and are strong sitters, often used to hatch duck eggs. The birds are alert and flighty, fly well and dislike handling, so they suit fanciers more than families.

history_summary.value: One of Britain's oldest chicken breeds, the Sussex was shown as early as 1845 and given a formal breed standard in 1902, after which it and the Rhode Island Red became the two leading British meat breeds until commercial hybrids took over. A breed club revived it after near-extinction in the early 1900s, and it is now raised as a calm, cold-hardy dual-purpose bird suitable for beginners.

summary.value: The Sussex is one of England's oldest chicken breeds, from the counties of Sussex, Kent and Surrey, long known for fine table birds. It was shown at London's first poultry show in 1845 and nearly died out around 1900 before a breed club, formed in 1903, brought it back. It is a big, rectangular dual-purpose bird with a broad flat back, white skin and legs and a single comb. The Speckled, a dark mahogany bird dotted with black and white, is the oldest color; Light and Red are also recognized in the US, and Britain has several more. Roosters weigh about 9 pounds and hens about 7. Hens lay roughly 200 to 250 large tan to brown eggs a year and may go broody. Sussex are calm, curious and people friendly, good with children and beginners. They handle winter well but dislike heat.

history_summary.value: The Swedish Black (Svarthona) developed on the Norway-Sweden border, carrying fibromelanistic genes traced back to Indonesian stock, making it a close but more refined-looking relative of the Ayam Cemani. It remains an ultra-rare, exotic breed.

summary.value: The Swedish Black, or Svarthona, is a rare landrace chicken from Sweden, raised for centuries near the border with Norway. Like the Ayam Cemani and the Silkie, it carries the fibromelanosis gene, so its feathers, skin, comb, legs and even inner tissue are black, and the plumage can shine green and purple in the light. Its ancestors are thought to have reached Scandinavia from the tropics on ships hundreds of years ago. It is a small, sleek bird: roosters weigh up to about 4.4 pounds and hens around 3.3 pounds. Hens lay small cream or white eggs. The birds are friendly and relaxed, forage well on free range, fly better than most breeds and like to roost high. Having lived so long in the Nordic north, they handle cold weather well. Fewer than 500 were counted in a Swedish census.

value: largest of the Swedish breeds, up to 8 lb

history_summary.value: This landrace breed developed naturally in southern Sweden over centuries from the hardiest farmyard birds, without deliberate selection. It nearly died out in the 1970s and was rebuilt from three surviving flocks in the Skane region.

summary.value: The Swedish Flower Hen is a farmyard landrace from Skane, the far south of Sweden, and the largest of the country's native chicken breeds. It almost vanished in the 1970s, and today's birds descend from three village flocks found at that time. The name comes from the white tip on each feather, which gives a speckled, flowery look over a base of black, blue, buff, red or brown. Some birds carry a crest. Hens weigh about 4.5 to 5.5 pounds and roosters up to about 7.5. Hens lay around 150 to 175 tinted or cream eggs a year, usually large, and keep laying for several seasons. Only some hens go broody. The birds are calm and friendly with people yet independent, and they range and forage well. They handle cold winters and also adapt to warmer weather, so they suit free range keepers and small homesteads in most climates.

value: one of the largest and heaviest chicken breeds, may exceed 10 kg

history_summary.value: This very large game breed comes from the island of Taiwan and is similar in type to the Malay and to large Japanese Shamo birds, though it is not Japanese. Big game fowl of uncertain breed are sometimes sold under the Taiwan name, or in the US as Saipan or Chinese Shamo.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Taiwanese Game, often just called the Taiwan, is a huge game chicken from the island of Taiwan. It belongs to the Malay family of upright Asian fighting fowl and looks a lot like the Japanese Shamo, but it is usually bigger and longer in the leg. Some people call it the Taiwan Shamo, though the breed has no Japanese roots. Roosters usually weigh about 11 to 15 pounds and hens about 9 to 12 pounds, and exceptional birds can top 22 pounds, which puts it among the heaviest chickens anywhere. Wheaten is the most common color, though any color is allowed. The legs are yellow, sometimes marked with black, and the face, comb, earlobes and throat are bright red. In Europe and the US, large game birds of unknown breeding are sometimes sold under this name or as Saipan, so a true bird should be strong, agile and upright.

history_summary.value: This hard-feather fighting breed originates in Thailand, where it is known as gai chon. It has been recognised by the British Poultry Standards since 2009.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Thai Game is a hard feathered fighting chicken from Thailand, where it is called gai chon, meaning fighting chicken. Britain added it to its poultry standards in 2009. It is a Malay type bird that resembles the Shamo, but it is lighter, stands a little less upright and carries a full tail just above level. Standard weights are about 7.7 pounds for roosters and 5.5 pounds for hens. Red and black is the usual color, though any color is accepted, and the comb and wattles are small. Birds are fast, strong runners and keen foragers that handle heat, cold and rough weather. Hens lay around 100 tinted eggs a year and can be fierce toward one another, so many keepers house them in a mixed flock. They need a large range and strong, secure fencing, since they are clever at escaping.

history_summary.value: The Thuringian comes from the Thuringia region of Germany, where it was first recorded in 1793 and known as the Thuringer Pausbackchen before it was standardised as the Thuringer Barthuhn in 1907. Bred as a dual-purpose farm bird, it is now kept mainly for shows and has been exhibited in Britain since about 2000.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Thuringian is a rare bearded chicken from the Thuringian Forest area of central Germany. Records of it go back to 1793, and it was standardised under the German name Thuringer Barthuhn in 1907. It was meant as a dual purpose farm bird, but today it is mostly seen at poultry shows, and British exhibitors have shown it since about 2000, first in chamois and silver spangled colors. A full beard and muffs give it a round, chubby cheeked face, and the comb is very small, which helps in cold weather. Hens lay about 160 eggs a year. They seldom go broody, but a sitting hen guards her chicks fiercely. The birds are friendly and tame and like to explore, so they do best with room to free range and can make good pets.

value: cuckoo (most common, plus 20 other recognised plumage colours)

history_summary.value: This critically endangered Belgian gamecock breed was developed in the late 1800s around the town of Tienen by crossing the older Brugse Vechter with Oriental fighting birds, similar to how the related Luikse Vechter was created. It is now the most threatened of the three Belgian fighting-cock breeds, with only 33 birds recorded in 2010.

summary.value: The Tiense Vechter is a Belgian gamecock named after the town of Tienen in Flemish Brabant. Breeders made it in the late 1800s by crossing the older Brugse Vechter with fighting birds of Oriental origin, much as the Luikse Vechter was made near Liege. It is one of three Belgian fighting breeds and today the rarest of them, with only 33 birds counted in Flanders in 2010. It is a big, strong bird with a steeply sloping back. Unlike its two cousins, it has pale skin, face and legs with no dark pigment. It has a triple comb and tiny or missing wattles. Cuckoo is the most common of its many colors. Roosters weigh about 11 pounds and hens about 9 pounds, and a bantam version exists. Cockfighting is illegal in Belgium, and some strains are now kept only for shows.

history_summary.value: The Tomaru is one of four Japanese long-crowing breeds. Its name points to China's Tang dynasty, and the Japanese breed record says it came from crosses of Shokoku and Daitomaru birds imported from China in the 16th or 17th century. It was designated a natural monument in 1939.

summary.value: The Tomaru is a Japanese long-crowing chicken, one of four such breeds in Japan along with the Koeyoshi, Kurokashiwa and Totenko. Roosters are prized for a deep, drawn out crow that can last from about 18 to 25 seconds. The name refers to China's Tang dynasty, and Japanese breed records trace the bird to crosses of Chinese imports made several hundred years ago. It was made a natural monument in 1939. The Tomaru comes in one color only, black with a green sheen. It has a broad, compact body, a full breast, a single comb, a low carried tail and dark slate gray legs. The face and ears are red, though hens may have a fully black face. Roosters weigh about 7.3 pounds and hens about 4.6 pounds. It is kept as a fancy breed for its voice.

history_summary.value: The Tuzo is a German true bantam of gamecock type descended from Asian fighting fowl, possibly of Japanese origin, and was developed further in both Europe and the United States. It was officially recognised in Germany in 1983 and is now also recognised by the Entente Europeenne and the Poultry Club of Great Britain.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Tuzo is a true bantam gamecock, meaning there is no large version of the breed. It comes from Asian fighting stock, probably Japanese, and was developed further in Europe and the United States before Germany standardised it in 1983. Britain has had it since the 1970s, and it is shown there as an Asian hard feather breed. It is a small, muscular, upright bird. Roosters weigh roughly 2.5 to 3.3 pounds and hens around 2 to 2.6 pounds. Black, blue and white are the colors most widely accepted. Hens lay only about 80 to 100 small white or tinted eggs a year, and their hard keel makes them clumsy sitters. Tuzos are friendly and easy to handle, though males may fight each other. They do not cope well with cold, and today they are kept mainly for shows.
