history_summary.value: The Twentse, called Kraienkopp in German, originates from the border region between Germany and the Netherlands, developed in the late 19th century from local stock crossed with Malay and Leghorn birds. It is kept today as a rare layer or show bird.

summary.value: The Twentse, known in German as the Kraienkopp, comes from the border country between the Netherlands and Germany. Breeders made it in the late 1800s by crossing local hens with Malay fowl, then adding silver duckwing Leghorn blood. Dutch shows first saw it in 1920, and German shows in 1925. The bird has yellow skin and a small walnut comb, with bright red wattles and earlobes, and comes in silver, gold and several other colors. Roosters weigh about 6 pounds and hens about 4 pounds. Hens lay up to around 200 off-white eggs a year, go broody and raise chicks well. The Twentse is active, alert and independent, with a hint of Malay fire, though it tames if raised by hand. It forages very well and stands up to cold, so it suits free range keepers.

value: original population went extinct and was restored by crossing survivors with Czech gold brindle, yellow Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island, New Hampshire and Wyandotte

history_summary.value: The Sumava is an old breed from the Bohemian Forest whose original population died out. It was later recreated in the second half of the 20th century by crossbreeding a few remaining birds with several other established breeds.

summary.value: The Sumavanka, or Sumava chicken, is an old Czech breed named after the Sumava, the Bohemian Forest along the country's southwestern border. The original birds died out, so the breed seen today is a rebuilt one. In the second half of the 20th century, breeders took the few birds left from the old stock and crossed them with Czech gold brindle hens, yellow Plymouth Rocks, Rhode Island Reds, New Hampshires and Wyandottes. Roosters weigh about 6.4 to 7.9 pounds and hens about 5.3 to 6.8 pounds. A hen lays around 180 brown eggs a year, each close to 2 ounces. The breed is still rare, which makes it a bird for keepers interested in preserving Czech farm poultry.

value: slate-grey or black legs in partridge and black varieties, unpigmented in barred and white

history_summary.value: The Utrerana was developed from about 1926 by Joaquin del Castillo near Utrera in Andalusia, Spain, initially by selecting local rustic hens for better egg laying and later for distinct colour varieties. Four colour strains were eventually established: black, barred, white and partridge.

summary.value: The Utrerana is a Spanish chicken named after the town of Utrera, near Seville in Andalusia. Joaquin del Castillo created it on his farm there, starting around 1926 with the hardy local farm hens of the area. At first he selected only for better laying. From about 1930 he also bred for looks and fixed black, barred and white strains, and a partridge strain came later. The barred bird is known locally as the franciscana. It is a medium sized fowl: hens average about 5 pounds and roosters about 6.6 pounds. Earlobes are always white, and the legs are slate or black in the dark varieties and pale in the barred and white ones. Hens lay about 180 fairly large eggs a year, and the meat has a good flavor. The breed is listed as at risk.

history_summary.value: The Valdarnese is a white Italian breed from the upper Arno valley in Tuscany, first described in 1899 and nearly wiped out in the 20th century by intensive farming and competition from the White Leghorn. Conservation efforts from the 1990s onward have kept a small population going, with roughly 1200 birds recorded in a 2007 study.

summary.value: The Valdarnese is a big white meat chicken from the upper valley of the Arno river in Tuscany, between Florence and Arezzo. White chickens from this valley were first written about in 1899. The breed had a club by 1955, but it faded fast in the 1960s as old sharecropping farms broke up and cheap White Leghorn chicks took over, and by the end of the century it had nearly vanished. A rescue program began in the 1990s, and Tuscany now keeps a breed register and standard. Around 1,200 breeding birds were counted in 2007. The plumage is white, the skin yellow and the legs orange yellow, with a large red single comb. Roosters weigh about 6.4 to 7.3 pounds and hens about 4.4 to 5.5 pounds. Hens go broody often, so they lay only about 135 ivory eggs a year. Its firm meat is the main reason it is raised.

conservation_status.value: very low numbers, recovering after near extinction (approx. 200 breeding birds in 2007 study)

history_summary.value: This black Tuscan breed from the lower Arno valley was described as early as 1900 and standardized in 1905, but competition from the White Leghorn drove it to near extinction by the late 1900s. It was rebuilt from surviving countryside birds crossed with Bresse and Castellana Negra stock, with the restored breed shown in 1998.

summary.value: The Valdarno is a black dual purpose chicken from the lower Arno valley in Tuscany, in the farm country between Florence, Pisa and the sea. It should not be confused with the Valdarnese, a white breed from the upper valley. Writers praised it around 1900 for fast growth and good mothering, and a standard was set in 1905, when a local saying held that only a black chicken was a real one. Competition from the White Leghorn later pushed it almost to extinction. Breeders rebuilt it from a few birds found near Siena, crossed with Bresse and Castellana Negra, and showed the results in 1998. The bird is black with a green sheen, slate legs, white skin, a red single comb and white earlobes. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 6.2 pounds and hens 4.4 to 5 pounds. Hens lay white eggs. Only about 200 breeding birds were counted in 2007.

value: grows fast on low feed inputs

history_summary.value: Vanaraja is a dual-purpose backyard chicken developed by ICAR's Directorate of Poultry Research in Hyderabad for rural households that scavenge-feed their birds. It grows fast, resists disease, and is now distributed across many Indian states from the Hyderabad center.

summary.value: Vanaraja is a crossbred dual purpose chicken made in India by the ICAR Directorate of Poultry Research in Hyderabad. It was designed for village families who let their birds roam the yard and feed mostly on what they find, with only a little extra grain. The birds have multicolored feathers, resist disease well, grow quickly and need less feed than many breeds. They do best on free range. A hen lays up to about 110 eggs a year, and young birds reach roughly 2.2 to 2.6 pounds by six months of age. Keepers are advised to vaccinate them together with any native birds, and to avoid letting them get too heavy, since excess weight can cut egg output. Most flocks are in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, and the Hyderabad center supplies chicks to 26 Indian states.

value: black head, neck and tail with buff body

history_summary.value: Oskar Vorwerk created this German breed starting in 1900 by combining the Lakenvelder's belted pattern with a golden-buff base, using Lakenvelder, Buff Orpington, Buff Sussex and Andalusian stock, and it was standardized by 1913. It remains rare outside continental Europe and is often confused with the separate Golden Lakenvelder breed.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Vorwerk is a German utility chicken created from 1900 by Oskar Vorwerk in Hamburg. He wanted a mid sized farm bird with the belted pattern of the Lakenvelder but a golden buff body in place of white, and he drew on Lakenvelder, Buff Orpington, Buff Sussex and Andalusian stock. It was first shown in 1912 and standardised in 1913. The head, neck and tail are black and the rest is buff, with a single comb and white earlobes. It is often mistaken for the Golden Lakenvelder, a separate breed. Roosters weigh about 5.5 to 7 pounds and hens 4.5 to 5.5 pounds, and there is a bantam. Hens lay about 170 large cream eggs a year. Vorwerks are alert, lively and good natured, eat little, forage well and mature fast. Roosters get along with each other, and the birds fly well, so fences need height.

value: hardy, survives illness and hard winters

history_summary.value: The Welsummer was bred in the early 1900s in the Dutch village of Welsum from a mix of Rhode Island Red, Barnevelder, Partridge Leghorn, Cochin and Wyandotte stock, and reached a fixed standard by 1922-23. Birds were exported for the commercial egg trade and the breed was added to the British Standard in 1930.

summary.value: The Welsummer is a Dutch breed named for the village of Welsum in the eastern Netherlands. Farmers there made it in the early 1900s from Partridge Leghorn, Cochin, Wyandotte, Barnevelder and Rhode Island Red stock, and a standard was fixed in the early 1920s. Britain imported it in the late 1920s for its eggs. Roosters have the bright red and orange look of a storybook cockerel, while hens are a soft brown with gold in the neck feathers. Hens weigh about 5 to 6 pounds and roosters about 7. They lay around 150 to 200 large, deep terracotta brown eggs a year, often freckled with darker spots. Chicks can be sexed at hatch by their head markings. Welsummers are friendly, clever birds that like to forage but accept a run, and they cope with both cold and heat.

value: closely related to Ostfriesische Möwe and Braekel

history_summary.value: This rare German breed comes from the traditional farm chickens of Westphalia around Bielefeld and Herford, and its name evolved from old Low German words meaning a daily or long-lasting egg layer rather than from the word for dead. It lost ground to more productive foreign breeds from the 1880s onward and its numbers have kept falling, reaching gravely endangered status by 2016.

summary.value: The Westfalischer Totleger is an old German laying breed from Westphalia, mostly kept around Bielefeld and Herford, with a history of more than four centuries. The name sounds like dead layer in modern German, but it really grew out of older Low German words for a hen that lays every day. It is a close relative of the Ostfriesische Mowe and the Braekel. Once common on farms, it lost out to more productive imported breeds from the 1880s, and by 1904 it was mainly a show bird. It comes in gold pencilled and silver pencilled. Roosters weigh about 4.4 to 5.5 pounds and hens 3.3 to 4.4 pounds. Hens rarely sit and lay around 180 eggs a year, each about 2 ounces. Fewer than 1,000 birds were recorded in 2016, and the breed is rated gravely endangered in Germany.

history_summary.value: This ancient Spanish breed of unknown origin was refined in Great Britain in the 1700s and became one of the best-known laying breeds in America and England through the 1800s. Breeders' focus on ever-larger white faces weakened the birds' hardiness, and it lost popularity to hardier breeds like the Minorca and Leghorn.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The White-faced Black Spanish is one of the oldest laying breeds in the West. It traces back to old Spanish stock but took its modern form in Britain and Holland in the 1700s, and the American Poultry Association accepted it in 1874. For most of the 1800s it was a leading egg bird in England and the eastern US. The plumage is a glossy green black, and a huge white face and earlobes hang down below the wattles. Roosters weigh about 8 pounds and hens about 6.5 pounds, and a bantam form exists. Hens seldom go broody and lay some 160 to 180 large chalk white eggs a year. The birds are active, noisy and curious, and a little aloof with other breeds. Years of breeding for bigger faces left them delicate, so they need shelter in both hot and cold weather and suit experienced keepers.

value: plumage varies; most commonly chipmunk or grey
a modern production breed developed by poultry geneticist Dr. Tom Whiting specifically to lay a consistent blue egg at a commercial rate

history_summary.value: Poultry geneticist Dr. Tom Whiting developed the Whiting True Blue in Colorado in the 1990s by crossing White Leghorns with Ameraucanas, first in search of feathers for fly-tying. The result is a modern production layer bred to lay large blue eggs consistently, with a sister line, the True Green, that lays green eggs.

summary.value: The Whiting True Blue is a modern American laying breed, not a heritage one. Poultry geneticist Dr. Tom Whiting developed it in Colorado in the 1990s by crossing White Leghorns with Ameraucanas. He started out breeding for fly-tying feathers, and the birds turned out to be strong layers of blue eggs. Every True Blue lays a blue egg, while a sister line, the True Green, lays green ones. Feather colors vary widely, with chipmunk and gray patterns the most common. Hens lay about 280 to 300 large powder blue eggs a year. The birds are very active and do best on free range, where they eagerly hunt insects. Reports on their manner differ: one source calls them friendly and gentle, another says they are independent and slow to trust people unless handled young. They get along well with the rest of the flock.

history_summary.value: The Wyandotte was developed in the United States in the 1870s, first as the silver-laced variety originally called the American Sebright, and was standardized by the American Poultry Association in 1883. Further colour varieties were produced over the following decades by crossing in Hamburg, Brahma, Cochin and Plymouth Rock stock.

summary.value: The Wyandotte is an American dual-purpose breed from the 1870s, named for the Wyandot people. The first birds were silver laced, each white feather edged in black, and golden laced, buff, white, Columbian, partridge and other colors came later. Wyandottes are broad, full-breasted birds with yellow skin and legs and a low rose comb that stands up well to frostbite. Hens weigh about 6.5 pounds and roosters about 8.5. A hen lays around 150 to 200 large brown eggs a year. Some hens sit well and make good mothers, though others rarely go broody. The breed is calm and friendly, but it often ends up near the top of the pecking order in a mixed flock. It copes well with cold and also handles heat, which makes it an easy family bird in most of the US. Bantams are available too.

history_summary.value: The Yakido descends from the Shamo group of Japanese fighting fowl, themselves derived from Malay-type birds brought from Thailand in the 1600s, and was bred in Mie Prefecture in the mid-1800s as a smaller sparring partner for bigger gamecocks. Japan declared it a Natural Monument in 1950.

sources.publisher: The Poultry Club of Great Britain

summary.value: The Yakido is a small Japanese gamecock of the Shamo family, bred around 1850 in Mie Prefecture on the main island of Honshu. It was made as a sparring partner for bigger fighting cocks, a bird that would lose but build the larger bird's confidence. Japan named it a Natural Monument in 1950. The Yakido is compact, muscular and very upright, with hard, tight black feathers, yellow legs and beak, and a small triple comb. Its size falls between a bantam and a standard bird, and British shows class it as a bantam. Roosters weigh about 4.6 to 5.7 pounds and hens 3.7 to 4.6 pounds. Hens lay only about 80 cream eggs a year. The birds are confident and fairly hardy, and they handle cold well. Males will fight, so most keepers house just one rooster.

history_summary.value: The Yokohama was created in Germany in the 1880s by Hugo du Roi from long-tailed ornamental fowl imported from Japan through the port of Yokohama starting in the 1860s. Small surviving import stock forced breeders to outcross with Malay, Phoenix, game fowl and Sumatra chickens to keep the breed going, and it reached the US Standard of Perfection in 1981.

summary.value: The Yokohama is a long-tailed show chicken bred in Germany in the late 1800s from Japanese birds shipped out of the port of Yokohama. Hugo du Roi, first head of the German poultry association, developed it, and later breeders mixed in Malay, Phoenix, game and Sumatra blood because so few imported hens survived. The US recognizes two colors: white, and red shouldered, which is white with red across the back and breast. Tails and saddle feathers can trail three to four feet. It is a small bird, with males around 4.5 pounds and females around 3.5. Hens are poor layers, giving only 60 to 80 small cream or tinted eggs a year and going broody after a dozen or so. Yokohamas are alert and active but easy to tame, and they tolerate confinement. They like warm weather and suit fanciers who keep birds for looks rather than eggs or meat.
